title: 正德八年應天府鄉試錄
text:
應天府鄉試錄序
比以方隅嘉靖
皇上勵精有為思得才俊以自輔
適屆癸酉秋賓興鄉賢之期
爰
命右諭德臣文叙左中允臣詠往
司應天府試事雖按常式舉
===
行而
聖心視前則特至也雖與他政均
一而
聖知則以此為先務也故綱無不
舉有提調考試同考試監試
諸官之别焉目靡不張提調
則應天府府尹臣旦府丞臣

應天府鄉試錄序

比以方隅嘉靖，皇上勵精有為，思得才俊以自輔。適屆癸酉秋賓興鄉賢之期，爰命右諭德臣文叙、左中允臣詠往司應天府試事。雖按常式舉行，而聖心視前則特至也；雖與他政均一，而聖知則以此為先務也。故綱無不舉，有提調、考試、同考試、監試諸官之别焉；目靡不張，提調則應天府府尹臣旦、府丞臣
translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination

Recently, with the regions of the realm enjoying peace and good order, His Majesty has devoted himself energetically to effective government, seeking talented men to assist him. As the autumn of the guiyou year [1513] arrived, the appointed time for honoring and recommending worthy men from the localities, he commanded his servants Wenxu, Right Mentor, and Yong, Left Companion, to go and oversee the examination at Yingtian Prefecture. Although conducted according to established procedures, it received even greater attention from His Majesty than before. Although standing alongside other affairs of government, in his sagely discernment he regarded it as a matter of foremost importance. Thus every principal responsibility was provided for, with distinct offices for Proctors, Examiners, Associate Examiners, and examination monitors; every detail, too, was attended to. Serving as Proctors were his servant Dan, Prefect of Yingtian Prefecture, and the Vice Prefect, his servant …

title: 正德八年應天府鄉試錄
text:
梅焉同考試則教授臣德明臣
大有學正臣天祥教諭臣華臣大用
臣璧臣大廈訓導臣塤臣大韶焉
監試則御史臣鳳臣英焉曁
諸執事罔不咸備是以二旬
而竣事不為日薄務叢所縛
得士百三十有五人遵
===
定制也謹集為錄以
獻兼傳示遠邇而臣文叙當序諸
首惟漢孔融曰聞延陵之理
樂觀虞翻之治易乃知東南
之美非徒會稽之竹箭也臣
謂于時陸贄未出而范仲淹
尚遠隔世數耳使融見贄之
alt_text:
梅〔臣德明臣〕
焉同考試則教授〔臣〕
有學正〔臣天祥〕教諭〔臣華臣有〕
〔臣璧臣大廈〕訓導〔臣墳臣大韶〕焉
監試則御史〔臣鳳臣英〕焉暨
諸執事罔不咸備是以二旬
而竣事不為日薄務叢所縛
得士百三十有五人遵
===
定制也謹集為録以
獻兼傳示遠邇而〔臣文敘〕當序諸
首惟漢孔融曰聞延陵之理
樂觀虞翻之治易乃知東南
之美非徒會稽之竹箭也〔臣〕
謂于時陸贄未出而范仲淹
尚遠隔世數耳使融見贄之
punctuated:
梅焉。同考試則教授臣德明、臣大有，學正臣天祥，教諭臣華、臣大用、臣璧、臣大廈，訓導臣塤、臣大韶焉。監試則御史臣鳳、臣英焉。曁諸執事，罔不咸備。是以二旬而竣事，不為日薄務叢所縛，得士百三十有五人，遵定制也。謹集為錄以獻，兼傳示遠邇，而臣文叙當序諸首。
惟漢孔融曰：「聞延陵之理樂，觀虞翻之治易，乃知東南之美，非徒會稽之竹箭也。」臣謂于時陸贄未出，而范仲淹尚遠，隔世數耳。使融見贄之
translation_en:
…Mei. The Associate Examiners were your servants Deming and Dayou, Professors; Tianxiang, School Rectifier; Hua, Dayong, Bi, and Daxia, Instructors; and Xun and Dashao, Assistant Instructors. Those overseeing the examination were your servants Feng and Ying, Investigating Censors. Together with all the other functionaries, the staff was fully provided. Thus the work was completed in twenty days, unhampered by the shortness of time and the press of duties. One hundred and thirty-five men were selected, in accordance with the established regulations. We have respectfully compiled this record for presentation to the throne and for circulation far and near; I, your servant Wenxu, am charged with placing a preface at its beginning.
Kong Rong of the Han said: “Hearing of the Lord of Yanling’s understanding of music and observing Yu Fan’s study of the Book of Changes, I know that the fine things of the southeast are not merely the bamboo arrow shafts of Kuaiji.” I would say that Lu Zhi had not yet appeared in his time, and Fan Zhongyan still lay far in the future: it was simply a matter of the generations separating them. Had Kong Rong seen Lu Zhi’s …

title: 正德八年應天府鄉試錄
text:
論諫仲淹之萬言書當必舉
二子與季札並稱而翻在所
畧矣我
太祖高皇帝龍飛淮甸一時里閈
元臣若徐達之克成駿功常
遇春之平定中原是皆升陔
鷹揚之佐使融獲見二臣之
勳烈當盡置諸子而獨舉之
以激當時詔後世也今去
聖祖之興已百餘年
東南清淑之氣磅礴欝積復
鍾于人易武奮而為儒進將
尋
國初二□□年矣故頃者禮闈
alt_text:
論諫伸淹之藹言書當必舉
二子與季札並稱而翻在所
畧矣我
太祖高皇帝龍飛淮甸一時里閈
元臣若徐達之克成駿功常
遇春之平定中原是皆升陑
鷹揚之佐使融獲見二臣之
===
勳烈當盡置諸子而獨舉之
以激當時詔後世也令去
聖祖之興巳百餘年
東南清淑之氣磅礴鬱積復
鍾于人易武奮而為儒進將
尋
國初二□□年矣故頃者禮闈
punctuated:
論諫、仲淹之萬言書，當必舉二子與季札並稱，而翻在所畧矣。我太祖高皇帝龍飛淮甸，一時里閈元臣，若徐達之克成駿功、常遇春之平定中原，是皆升陔鷹揚之佐。使融獲見二臣之勳烈，當盡置諸子而獨舉之，以激當時、詔後世也。
今去聖祖之興已百餘年，東南清淑之氣磅礴欝積，復鍾于人，易武奮而為儒進，將尋國初二□□年矣。故頃者禮闈
translation_en:
…the remonstrances of Lu Zhi and Fan Zhongyan’s Letter of Ten Thousand Words, he would surely have named these two alongside Ji Zha, while passing over Yu Fan. Our Emperor Taizu Gao rose like a dragon in the Huai region. Among the great founding ministers from his native locality were Xu Da, who accomplished mighty deeds, and Chang Yuchun, who pacified the Central Plain. These were all helpers who ascended the heights [?] and displayed the prowess of hawks. Had Kong Rong witnessed these two ministers’ glorious achievements, he would surely have set aside all the others and singled them out to inspire his contemporaries and instruct later generations.
Now more than a hundred years have passed since our sagely founder’s rise. The pure and excellent vital energies of the southeast, vast and richly accumulated, have once again converged in its people, turning martial endeavor into advancement through Confucian learning. It will soon be two □□ years since the dynasty’s founding [?]. Thus, recently, in the Metropolitan Examination…

title: 正德八年應天府鄉試錄
text:
遴選是邦之士恒居十二
先帝開進士科得
廷試第一人六是邦之士乃居
其四且秉鈞軸掌
綸翰者仍後先相望使融復見
其然抑不知若何而為揚搉
也今茲奉
===
===
命而來道徐歷揚以入龍江自
長淮南北及大江東南第見
土壤沃衍峯巒秀拔洪流巨
浸浩渺無際前此觀覽之臣
已極狀夫形勢風物之優不
俟重加興歎而後知其為譽
髦之淵藪也比即塲校藝篇

命而來道徐歷揚以入龍江目
長淮南北及大江東南第見
土壤沃衍峯巒秀拔洪流巨
浸浩渺無際蕭此觀覽之臣
已極狀夫形勢風物之優不
俟重加興歎而後知其為譽
髦之淵藪也比即塲校藝篇
punctuated:
遴選是邦之士，恒居十二。先帝開進士科，得廷試第一人六，是邦之士乃居其四。且秉鈞軸、掌綸翰者，仍後先相望。使融復見其然，抑不知若何而為揚搉也。
今茲奉命而來，道徐歷揚，以入龍江。自長淮南北及大江東南，第見土壤沃衍，峯巒秀拔，洪流巨浸，浩渺無際。前此觀覽之臣，已極狀夫形勢風物之優，不俟重加興歎，而後知其為譽髦之淵藪也。比即塲校藝，篇
translation_en:
…among those selected, scholars from this region have consistently accounted for two in ten. Under the late emperor, six men took first place in the Palace Examination for metropolitan graduates (jinshi), and four of them were scholars from this region. Moreover, men who held the reins of government or were entrusted with drafting imperial pronouncements followed one another in an unbroken succession. Had Rong witnessed this too, who knows how he would have extolled it?
This year I came in obedience to the imperial command, travelling through Xu and Yang to enter Longjiang. From the lands north and south of the long Huai River to those east and south of the great Yangzi, everywhere I saw fertile, expansive soil, lofty and graceful peaks, mighty streams and vast waters stretching boundlessly into the distance. Officials who surveyed these places before me have already described to the fullest their splendid terrain, scenery, and local features. There is no need to add fresh exclamations of admiration to recognize this as a gathering place of distinguished scholars. When I reached the examination compound and assessed the candidates’ compositions, the papers…

title: 正德八年應天府鄉試錄
text:
牘郁然或吐芳潤於簡古或
出清麗於醇雅或含質淡於
藻繪玉暉金銑不一而足前
此校閱之臣已盛稱夫文章
之瑰瑋不俟繼為誇詡而後
知其為東南之精華也夫大
厦云構非一木之枝帝王之
===
功非一士之畧諸士今歌鹿
鳴而計偕也仰值我
皇上啓聖興邦之會廣資毗贊以
成化理如金之惟礪濟川之
惟舟楫然將必有梁百尺之
觀航千仞之淵者于以並驅
我元臣而嗣徽前修者矣則

鳴而計偕也仰值我

惟舟楫然將必有梁百尺之
觀航千仞之淵者于以並驅
我元臣而嗣徽前修者矣則
punctuated:
牘郁然，或吐芳潤於簡古，或出清麗於醇雅，或含質淡於藻繪，玉暉金銑，不一而足。前此校閱之臣已盛稱夫文章之瑰瑋，不俟繼為誇詡而後知其為東南之精華也。
夫大厦云構，非一木之枝；帝王之功，非一士之畧。諸士今歌鹿鳴而計偕也，仰值我皇上啓聖興邦之會，廣資毗贊，以成化理。如金之惟礪，濟川之惟舟楫，然將必有梁百尺之觀、航千仞之淵者，于以並驅我元臣而嗣徽前修者矣。則
translation_en:
…the written compositions display abundant refinement: some express fragrant richness through antique simplicity; some bring forth limpid beauty through pure elegance; some enfold unadorned simplicity within ornate embellishment. With the radiance of jade and the sheen of metal, their merits are too numerous to enumerate. Officials who examined such writings before have already lavishly praised their extraordinary excellence. No further praise from us is needed to recognize them as the finest flowering of the southeast.
Now, building a great mansion requires more than the timber of a single tree; the achievements of emperors and kings require more than the talents and plans of a single scholar. You scholars now sing “The Deer Call” and prepare to travel together to the capital for examination. You have the good fortune to encounter a time when our Emperor brings forth his sagely wisdom and invigorates the realm, drawing widely upon assistance to bring about transforming and orderly rule. Just as metal needs a whetstone, and crossing a river requires boats and oars, so surely there will be among you those who can serve as beams for towers a hundred feet high and as vessels across waters a thousand fathoms deep. Thus you will advance alongside our chief ministers and carry on the glorious example of worthy predecessors. Then…

title: 正德八年應天府鄉試錄
text:
夫賁芬邦邑昭見美實前此
登薦之彥已咸其然是又豈
俟爾縷祝望而後建夫儁偉
光明之事功哉惟念天之相
人君莫大於以人遺之近臣
之効職莫要於簡賢而進之
顧慚譾薄謬竽文柄每以不
獲真才為懼茲覽諸士之文
以占素蘊闖然德行之休志
義之宏政事之達舉於是乎
在竊惟所以仰承天意而稱
愜
上心者端藉乎是庶幾蚤夜兢惕
之心差可以少釋焉或乃曰

之効職莫要於簡賢而進之
顧慚譾薄謬竿文柄每以不
===
獲真才為懼茲覽諸士之文
以占素蘊闇然德行之休志
義之宏政事之達舉於是乎
在竊惟所以仰承天意而稱
愜
上心者端籍乎是庶幾蚤夜兢惕
之心差可以少釋焉或乃曰
punctuated: 夫賁芬邦邑，昭見美實，前此登薦之彥已咸其然，是又豈俟爾縷祝望而後建夫儁偉光明之事功哉？惟念天之相人君，莫大於以人遺之；近臣之効職，莫要於簡賢而進之。顧慚譾薄，謬竽文柄，每以不獲真才為懼。茲覽諸士之文，以占素蘊，闖然德行之休、志義之宏、政事之達，舉於是乎在。竊惟所以仰承天意而稱愜上心者，端藉乎是，庶幾蚤夜兢惕之心差可以少釋焉。或乃曰：
translation_en:
… As for bringing distinction and fragrance to their communities [?] and making manifest their admirable substance, the worthy men recommended in earlier examinations have all done so. How could the establishment of outstanding and illustrious achievements depend upon repeated exhortations and expressions of hope [?]?

I reflect that Heaven’s greatest aid to a ruler is to bestow worthy men upon him; and that nothing is more essential to the faithful service of his close ministers than selecting the worthy and advancing them. Yet I am ashamed of my shallow learning and meager abilities, unworthily occupying a position of authority over literary selection, and have always feared failing to obtain men of genuine talent. Now, reading these gentlemen’s compositions to discern what they have long cultivated within, I find revealed therein excellence of moral conduct, breadth of purpose and sense of right, and understanding of governmental affairs—all are present here. I humbly consider that it is precisely upon these men that we must rely to honor Heaven’s intention and satisfy His Majesty’s wishes. Perhaps, then, the apprehension that has kept me vigilant morning and night may be somewhat eased. But someone then said: …

title: 正德八年應天府鄉試錄
text:
兢惕之持自茲方日甚何則
拔士以用世猶導泉以澤物
也使流不以時或為風日所
薄炙而失其紺寒之性或為
塵泥所殽混而喪其潔冽之
真寧不深孤物望而遺導者
之咎乎於乎有是哉諸士其
===
識之行選部
廷而躋華密也慎毋失其性而
變其真焉
奉訓大夫右春坊右諭德兼
翰林院侍講倫文叙謹序
alt_text:

真寧不深孤物望而遺導者

識之行選部
===
廷而躋華密也慎毋失其性而
變其真焉
奉訓大夫右春坊右諭德兼
翰林院侍講倫〔文叙〕謹序
punctuated:
「兢惕之持，自茲方日甚。何則？拔士以用世，猶導泉以澤物也。使流不以時，或為風日所薄炙而失其紺寒之性，或為塵泥所殽混而喪其潔冽之真，寧不深孤物望而遺導者之咎乎？」於乎，有是哉！諸士其識之！行選部廷而躋華密也，慎毋失其性而變其真焉。
奉訓大夫、右春坊右諭德兼翰林院侍講倫文叙謹序。
translation_en:
…“The vigilance one maintains will henceforth only grow more intense each day. Why? Selecting scholars to serve the world is like channeling a spring to nourish living things. If its waters do not flow at the proper time, they may be buffeted and scorched by wind and sun, losing their deep-blue coolness, or become mingled with dust and mud, losing their pristine purity and clarity. Would this not gravely disappoint those who depend upon them and leave the person who channeled them open to blame?” Ah, indeed it would! Let you scholars remember this! When you are selected for service in the ministries and at court [?] and rise to illustrious posts close to the throne, take care never to lose your nature or alter your true character.
Preface respectfully composed by Lun Wenxu, Grand Master for Attending to Instruction, Right Admonisher of the Right Secretariat of the Heir Apparent, concurrently Expositor-in-Waiting of the Hanlin Academy.

title: 正德八年應天府鄉試錄
text:
正德八年應天府鄉試
提調官
應天府府尹歐陽旦〔子相江西安福縣人辛丑進士〕
中順大夫應天府府丞尹梅〔調元直隸靈壽縣人己未進士〕
考試官
奉訓大夫右春坊右諭德兼翰林院侍講倫文叙〔伯疇廣東南海縣人己未進士〕
左春坊左中允兼翰林院修撰賈詠〔鳴和河南臨潁縣人丙辰進士〕
同考試官
江西南昌府儒學教授王德明〔克明浙江慈谿縣人癸卯貢士〕
===
浙江杭州府儒學教授曾大有〔子順福建仙遊縣人甲子貢士〕
湖廣德安府隨州儒學學正陳天祥〔景禎福建閩縣人甲子貢士〕
江西贛州府興國縣儒學教諭鍾華〔美彰廣東順德縣人戊午貢士〕

第壹場

四書

道盛德至善，民之不能忘也。

學而時習之，不亦說乎？有朋自遠方來，不亦樂乎？人不知而不慍，不亦君子乎？

我知言，我善養吾浩然之氣。

易

无所往，其來復吉；有攸往，夙吉。

改邑不改井，无喪无得，往來井井。

君子居其室，出其言善，則千里之外應之，况其邇者乎？

子曰：「書不盡言，言不盡意。」然則聖人之意，其不可見乎？子曰：「聖人立象以盡意，設卦以盡情偽，繫辭焉以盡其言。」

書

迪朕德，時乃功惟叙。

以義制事，以禮制心。

惟先王建邦啓土，公劉克篤前烈，至于太
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

This speaks of flourishing virtue and consummate goodness, which the people cannot forget.

To learn and practice what one has learned at due intervals—is this not a pleasure? To have friends come from afar—is this not a joy? To remain unresentful when others do not recognize one—is this not to be a gentleman?

I understand words, and I am good at nurturing my vast, flowing vital energy.

Book of Changes

If there is nowhere to go, returning brings good fortune; if there is somewhere to go, an early departure brings good fortune.

The settlement may be changed, but the well is not changed. It neither loses nor gains; those who come and go draw from the well.

When a gentleman remains in his room and speaks good words, people a thousand li away respond to him. How much more will those nearby!

The Master said: “Writing does not fully convey words, and words do not fully convey meaning.” Can the sages’ meaning, then, not be apprehended? The Master said: “The sages established images to convey their meaning fully, arranged the hexagrams to convey fully what is genuine and what is false, and appended statements to convey their words fully.”

Book of Documents

Follow my virtue; then your accomplishments will be duly ordered.

Regulate affairs by righteousness; regulate the heart by ritual propriety.

The former kings established the state and opened up its territory. Gong Liu was able to build firmly upon the achievements of his predecessors, down to Tai…

明王立政，不惟其官，惟其人。

詩
七月流火，九月授衣。一之日觱發，二之日栗烈。無衣無褐，何以卒歲？三之日于耜，四之日舉趾。同我婦子，饁彼南畝，田畯至喜。
比物四驪，閑之維則。維此六月，旣成我服。我服旣成，于三十里。王于出征，以佐天子。
質爾人民，謹爾侯度，用戒不虞。
古帝命武湯，正域彼四方。方命厥后，奄有九有。商之先后，受命不殆，在武丁孫子。武丁孫子，武王靡不勝。龍旂十乘，大糦是承。邦畿千里，維民所止，肇域彼四海。

春秋
蔡侯、鄭伯會于鄧，桓公二年。秋七月上辛
translation_en:
…the king laid the foundations of the royal enterprise. Wang Ji labored diligently for the royal house, and my deceased father, King Wen, brought their achievement to completion.
An enlightened king, in establishing government, attends not merely to the offices but to the people who fill them.

Book of Odes
In the seventh month, the Fire Star sinks westward; in the ninth month, winter clothing is distributed. In the days of the first month, the wind whistles; in the days of the second, the cold is biting. Without clothes, without coarse woolen garments, how can we get through the year? In the days of the third month, we attend to our plows; in the days of the fourth, we set foot in the fields. Together with our wives and children, we take food to those southern fields; the agricultural overseer arrives and is pleased.
Four black horses, matched in strength, are trained according to rule. In this sixth month, our equipment is ready. With our equipment ready, we advance thirty li. The king goes forth on campaign, to aid the Son of Heaven.
Settle your people; carefully observe the standards of your lordship, guarding against the unforeseen.
Of old, the Lord on High charged the martial Tang to set right the territories of the four quarters. He everywhere appointed their rulers and possessed all the nine regions. The former rulers of Shang received the mandate without peril; it rests with the descendants of Wu Ding. The descendants of Wu Ding—those martial kings—succeed in all things. Ten chariots bear dragon banners; great offerings of millet are presented. The royal domain extends a thousand li, where the people dwell; he first marked out the territories within the four seas.

Spring and Autumn Annals
The Marquis of Cai and the Earl of Zheng met at Deng, in the second year of Duke Huan. In autumn, in the seventh month, on the first xin day…

… A great sacrifice for rain was performed; on the last xin day, another sacrifice for rain was performed. 〔Twenty-fifth year of Duke Zhao.〕

The Viscount of Chu entered Chen. 〔Eleventh year of Duke Xuan.〕 The Viscount of Chu besieged Zheng. In summer, in the sixth month, on the yimao day, Xun Linfu of Jin led an army into battle against the Viscount of Chu at Bi; the Jin army suffered a crushing defeat. 〔Both in the twelfth year of Duke Xuan.〕 Luan Shu of Jin led an army to relieve Zheng. 〔Sixth year of Duke Cheng.〕 In summer, in the fifth month, on the jiawu day, they thereupon destroyed Biyang. 〔Tenth year of Duke Xiang.〕

The Duke joined the Marquis of Jin, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Wei, the Earl of Cao, Guang, heir apparent of Qi, the Viscounts of Ju, Zhu, and Teng, the Earls of Xue and Qi, and the Viscount of Lesser Zhu in attacking Zheng. In autumn, in the seventh month, on the jiwei day, they jointly concluded a covenant north of the city of Bo. The Viscount of Chu and the Earl of Zheng attacked Song. The Duke joined the Marquis of Jin, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Wei, the Earl of Cao, Guang, heir apparent of Qi, the Viscounts of Ju, Zhu, and Teng, the Earls of Xue and Qi, and the Viscount of Lesser Zhu in attacking Zheng; they met at Xiaoyu. 〔All in the eleventh year of Duke Xiang.〕

Hua Hai, Xiang Ning, and Hua Ding of Song fled from Nanli in Song to Chu. 〔Twenty-second year of Duke Zhao.〕

Record of Rites

Order the Music Master to present the poems, so that the customs of the people may be observed.

Use the four seasons as the guiding principle, so that undertakings may be encouraged; use the sun and stars as the framework, so that undertakings may be arranged in order; use the months as the measure, so that accomplishments may have prescribed limits.

When the mind is dignified, the body is at ease; when the mind is solemn, the countenance is reverent. What the mind delights in, the body will surely find agreeable; what the ruler delights in, the people will surely desire.

Privately borrowing government carts or boats.
Weapons of palace guards.

第叄場
策五道
問輔治之法刑莫尚焉所以禁奸慝而杜
禍亂自虞廷命士夏制常刑於是邦刑
之重掌于卿士而歷代之興率藉以助

當時致治之迹可考也洪惟我

===

大明令一書以詔告天下明民之道可謂至
矣迨七年之際再
命緒正復加

矣不識於舜禹成康之制作其亦脗合

威有所不施不識於唐虞三代之治效

第叄場
策五道

問：輔治之法，刑莫尚焉，所以禁奸慝而杜禍亂。自虞廷命士，夏制常刑，於是邦刑之重掌于卿士，而歷代之興率藉以助理。若成周五刑、五禁之屬，尤為明備，而當時致治之迹可考也。洪惟我太祖高皇帝改元之初，以律令雖行而慮民易犯，乃制《大明令》一書，以詔告天下，明民之道可謂至矣。迨七年之際，再命緒正，復加裁决，集成《大明律》一書，以整齊宇内，繩民之矩可謂嚴矣。不識於舜、禹、成、康之制作，其亦脗合否乎？以故百五十年于兹，刑有所不用，威有所不施，不識於唐虞三代之治效
translation_en:
The elderly and the young are not to be interrogated under torture.

Third Session
Five Policy Questions

Question: Among the means of assisting governance, none surpasses punishment: it restrains wickedness and prevents calamity and disorder. From the appointment of a judicial officer at the court of Yu and the establishment of regular punishments under the Xia, the weighty responsibility for the state's punishments was entrusted to high ministers. Successive dynasties, upon their rise, generally relied on punishment to assist their administration. Such institutions as the five punishments and five prohibitions of the Zhou were especially clear and comprehensive, and the evidence of the good government achieved at that time can be examined.

We reverently reflect that, at the beginning of his reign, our Emperor Taizu Gao, concerned that the people might easily transgress despite the statutes and ordinances already in force, compiled the Great Ming Ordinances and promulgated it throughout the realm. His means of enlightening the people may be called consummate. By the seventh year, he again ordered its revision and correction [?], further adjudicated its provisions, and compiled the Great Ming Code to bring order throughout the empire. The standards by which he regulated the people may be called strict. We ask whether these accorded with the institutions established by Shun, Yu, and Kings Cheng and Kang. 中嚴酷或初峻急而後寬縱固不足舉
似若唐之律令格式宋之勅令格式君
子容或有取焉然其先後之序輕重之
等間亦有合於我
聖祖之制否與且
聖祖之法固善而後世守之亦有其術否與夫

也諸士子少而習之行且推以致用其
敬陳之以占及物之學
問人君之決計用言若臣下之圖事揆策
其或識度淺劣謀用不臧則不免自貽
禍敗而坐受噬臍之悔斯理之常無足
咤者如之何負誠信好謀之資者亦誤
行撓楚之計抱沉幾先物之知者亦幾

===
也諸士子少而習之行且推以致用其
敭陳之以占及物之學
問人君之決計用言若臣下之圖事揆策

punctuated:
其亦聞道否乎？漢之禁網，或前疏闊而中嚴酷，或初峻急而後寬縱，固不足舉似。若唐之律令格式、宋之勅令格式，君子容或有取焉。然其先後之序、輕重之等，間亦有合於我聖祖之制否與？且聖祖之法固善，而後世守之，亦有其術否與？夫《歷代典章》暨《國朝律令》二書，皆備藏學宫而流布坊市者也。諸士子少而習之，行且推以致用，其敬陳之，以占及物之學。
問：人君之決計用言，若臣下之圖事揆策，其或識度淺劣、謀用不臧，則不免自貽禍敗，而坐受噬臍之悔，斯理之常，無足咤者。如之何負誠信好謀之資者，亦誤行撓楚之計；抱沉幾先物之知者，亦幾聽西還之議？神武明畧，殊不世出，一則有郭奉孝若在之思，一則有魏徵若在
translation_en:
…might its achievements likewise compare with those of those ages [?]? Under the Han, the net of prohibitions was sometimes loose at first but harsh midway through, or stringent initially but lax afterward; these are certainly unworthy of comparison. As for the Tang statutes, ordinances, regulations, and procedural rules, and the Song edicts, ordinances, regulations, and procedural rules, a gentleman might perhaps find something worth adopting. Yet in their ordering of priorities and gradations of severity, did they sometimes accord with the institutions of our Sagely Progenitor? Moreover, although the Sagely Progenitor’s laws were certainly good, are there also methods by which later generations may preserve them? The two books, Institutions of Successive Dynasties and Statutes and Ordinances of Our Dynasty, are both held in the government schools and circulate in the book markets. You candidates have studied them since youth and will soon put them into practice. Respectfully set forth your views, so that we may assess your learning in its capacity to benefit others.
Question: When rulers decide upon plans and accept advice, or ministers devise undertakings and weigh strategies, if their discernment is shallow and their judgment poor, and their plans are unsound, they inevitably bring disaster and defeat upon themselves and suffer futile, belated remorse. This is the ordinary course of things and gives no cause for astonishment. How is it, then, that one endowed with sincerity and trustworthiness, and inclined to seek counsel, nevertheless mistakenly carried out a plan to harass Chu; and that one possessed of profound insight into incipient developments and foresight nevertheless nearly accepted a proposal to return west? Men of extraordinary martial prowess and brilliant strategic judgment appear but rarely: yet one thought, “If only Guo Fengxiao were alive,” while another, “If only Wei Zheng were alive…”

之悔英武明睿根於天性或必於石堡
之攻取或昧於靈州之棄守其意何為
與沉毅多大畧胡卒聽三征之請將畧
為舉首胡繼有彭城之敗神識沉敏為
政有實一則敢用諸桓一則輕召內史
知畧足任經濟自許或勸假荊州之地
或輕棄河東之界其計安出與億萬人
之命匪輕也乃懸於一介之區畫千百
年之業匪細也乃本於一時之指揮是
===
不容以不慎重焉慎之重之豈無其術
與抑別有其說與
問聖經賢傳之訓廣博淵深後之求道於
微言者必稽之有以極其大而不遺體
之有以極其量而無外其庶矣乎然究
觀往哲迹其脩己治人之端事君輔友
之實乃有不盡然者如孔門之教有四
或乃曰聖人教人只此二字大學之目
有八或乃曰平生所學惟此四字誠自

之悔。英武明睿，根於天性，或必於石堡之攻取，或昧於靈州之棄守，其意何為與？沉毅多大畧，胡卒聽三征之請？將畧為舉首，胡繼有彭城之敗？神識沉敏，為政有實，一則敢用諸桓，一則輕召內史。知畧足任，經濟自許，或勸假荊州之地，或輕棄河東之界，其計安出與？億萬人之命匪輕也，乃懸於一介之區畫；千百年之業匪細也，乃本於一時之指揮。是不容以不慎重焉。慎之重之，豈無其術與？抑別有其說與？
問：聖經賢傳之訓，廣博淵深，後之求道於微言者，必稽之有以極其大而不遺，體之有以極其量而無外，其庶矣乎！然究觀往哲，迹其脩己治人之端、事君輔友之實，乃有不盡然者。如孔門之教有四，或乃曰：「聖人教人，只此二字。」大學之目有八，或乃曰：「平生所學，惟此四字。」誠自
translation_en:
…the regret that Wei Zheng was no longer alive. Others possessed martial prowess and clear discernment rooted in their very nature, yet one insisted on capturing Shibao, while another failed to discern whether Lingzhou should be abandoned or held. What were their intentions? How could one who was resolute and possessed great strategic ability ultimately assent to the request for three campaigns? How could one ranked foremost in military strategy subsequently suffer defeat at Pengcheng? Of men whose discernment was profound and keen, and whose government achieved substantial results, one ventured to employ members of the Huan clan, while another rashly summoned the Palace Secretary. Of men whose intelligence and strategy qualified them for responsibility, and who prided themselves on their ability to order the realm, one advised lending out the territory of Jingzhou, while another lightly abandoned the territory of Hedong. How did they arrive at such plans? The lives of countless millions are no light matter, yet they hang upon the planning of a single individual; an enterprise enduring for hundreds or thousands of years is no small matter, yet it rests upon a moment’s command. These things cannot be treated without caution and gravity. Is there no method for exercising such caution and gravity? Or is there some other explanation?
Question: The teachings of the sages’ classics and the worthies’ commentaries are broad and profound. Those in later ages who seek the Way in their subtle words must examine them so as to comprehend their full greatness without omission, and embody them so as to realize their full extent, leaving nothing outside. Would they then not come close to the Way? Yet when we closely examine the wise men of the past, tracing their approaches to cultivating themselves and governing others, and their actual conduct in serving rulers and assisting friends, we find cases that do not entirely accord with this. For example, Confucius’s teaching comprised four subjects, yet someone said, “The sage’s teaching consists simply of these two characters.” The Great Learning has eight main articles, yet someone said, “All that I have studied throughout my life consists solely of these four characters.” Sincerity resides in …

title: 正德八年應天府鄉試錄
text:
我存何俟七年之力行而後成信自我
發何須五年之積久而後孚持官之法
果盡於勤謹和緩四字乎勗勵僚屬果
限於廉仁公勤四字乎歷相兩朝悉分
用魯論之全帙夫何其易輔君數載猶
未服行魯論之二言抑何其難指資父
事君一語為讀書之事他篇獨非事乎
揭三代直道而行一句為仕學之要餘
章獨非要乎夫士之學古所以為身心
===
家國之用也與其擇善於簡冊孰若取
則於古人之為要也既取則之可於我
乎隱而不之告邪
問君子之有為於世也其功用同其效當
亦不遠其位遇同其趨當亦不殊若其
始同而終異始異而終或同或不同者
特十之一二而已然亦不可不辨也是
故列國用兵勝負立異究其實皆犯墓
以怖圍城中人耳吳下典計顯晦後殊

則於古人之爲要也旣取則之可於我
乎隱而不之告耶
===
問君子之有爲於世也其功用同其效當
亦不遠其位遇同其趨當亦不殊若其
始同而終異始異而終或同或不同者
特十之一二而已然亦不可不辨也是
故列國用兵勝負立異究其實皆犯墓
以怖圍城中人耳吳下典計顯晦後殊
punctuated:
我存，何俟七年之力行而後成？信自我發，何須五年之積久而後孚？持官之法，果盡於勤謹和緩四字乎？勗勵僚屬，果限於廉仁公勤四字乎？歷相兩朝，悉分用《魯論》之全帙，夫何其易？輔君數載，猶未服行《魯論》之二言，抑何其難？指資父事君一語為讀書之事，他篇獨非事乎？揭三代直道而行一句為仕學之要，餘章獨非要乎？夫士之學古，所以為身心家國之用也。與其擇善於簡冊，孰若取則於古人之為要也？既取則之，可於我乎隱而不之告邪？

問：君子之有為於世也，其功用同，其效當亦不遠；其位遇同，其趨當亦不殊。若其始同而終異，始異而終或同或不同者，特十之一二而已，然亦不可不辨也。是故列國用兵，勝負立異，究其實，皆犯墓以怖圍城中人耳。吳下典計，顯晦後殊。
translation_en:
…resides in oneself: why must it await seven years of strenuous practice before reaching fulfillment? Trustworthiness issues from oneself: why must it require five years of accumulation before winning trust? Are the principles of holding office really exhausted by the four words diligence, circumspection, harmony, and leniency? Is exhorting subordinate officials really confined to the four words integrity, benevolence, impartiality, and diligence? Serving successively as chief minister under two sovereigns, one apportioned the use of the entire Lu recension of the Analects between them: how easy it was! Yet after assisting a ruler for several years, another had still not put two sayings from the Analects into practice: why was it so difficult? If the single saying about drawing upon service to one’s father to serve one’s ruler is designated as the business of studying books, are the other chapters alone excluded from that business? If the sentence about following the straight Way under the Three Dynasties is singled out as the essential principle of learning for office, are the remaining chapters alone inessential? A scholar studies antiquity to apply it to his own person and mind, his family, and his state. Rather than selecting what is good from written texts, would it not be more essential to take the ancients as models? Having taken them as models, could you conceal this from me and not explain it?

Question: When gentlemen undertake action in the world, if their services are alike, their results should not differ greatly; if their positions and circumstances are alike, their courses should likewise not diverge. Cases in which beginnings are alike but endings differ, or beginnings differ but endings may or may not coincide, amount to only one or two in ten. Nevertheless, these too must be distinguished. Thus, when the various states employed troops, victory and defeat immediately set them apart; yet, on examining the facts, all had violated tombs to frighten the people within a besieged city. Those who administered accounts in Wu subsequently differed in whether they attained prominence or remained obscure…

title: 正德八年應天府鄉試錄
text:
原其始皆舉貲以應少主之求耳頽藉
更始已敗乃自歸分國數窘之與不時
至一耳用舍胡乃不倫行人計畫已行
而襲兵卒至說齊之于突厥等耳死生
何為頓分職掌選曹多擢故舊方諸身
為宰輔自以薦賢為任乃却友之求而
不許其義曷據官為防禦內舉其子較
諸位至司空自謂廣收人才顧知子之
賢而不舉者其見何居朝政未恊密啓
===
以聞名執政以之或乃以為不忠乘輿
臨幸徐啓壁門真將軍以之或乃以為
好名凡此皆當悉其肯綮而究其會通
者也析之究之舍格物窮理之士其疇
克之

translation_en:
…If we trace their beginnings, both merely put forward their wealth to meet the young ruler’s requests. Amid collapse and ruin [?], only after Gengshi had been defeated did he submit of his own accord; the divided state repeatedly distressed him [?], which was the same as failing to arrive at the proper time. Why, then, were employment and rejection so inconsistent? The envoy’s plan had already been put into effect, yet attacking troops suddenly arrived. Persuading Qi was comparable to persuading the Tujue; why, then, did their fates diverge so sharply between death and survival? One, charged with the personnel selection bureau, promoted many old associates. Compare him with another who, serving as chief minister and taking the recommendation of worthy men as his responsibility, nevertheless rejected a friend’s request. On what principle did this rest? One, serving as Defense Commissioner, recommended his own son from within his household. Compare him with another who rose to be Minister of Works and professed to recruit talent widely, yet knew his son’s worth and did not recommend him. What view underlay his conduct? When court affairs were not harmonious, one submitted a confidential report to the throne: for this he was acclaimed as a chief minister, whereas another was considered disloyal. When the emperor visited, one opened the camp gate only after a delay: for this he was called a true general, whereas another was considered to be seeking fame. In all these cases, one must fully grasp the crucial points and investigate how their underlying principles connect. Who could analyze and thoroughly examine them other than scholars who investigate things and fathom principle?

Yet, as for words of concern about danger, rather than immediately conveying them to …

title: 正德八年應天府鄉試錄
text:
廟堂孰若且舉一二與諸士子商較之可乎
夫内建百官以善政也而政或有所未
善外設牧守以弘化也而化或有所未
弘疆埸之鎮戍相望而内訌猶莫寧戢
方夏之屯營相屬而椎剽猶或磐牙古
之所患將悍卒驕今則不然古之所禁
民弁俗侈今則異是輕徭所以逸民而
重難弗見損薄賦所以厚下而蠲符莫
或給冒濫之賞何以矯之以循格令之
===
舊脫漏之辜何以裁之以適刑罰之中兹
皆治世所憂而安邦所危也憂之必有
所以弭憂之道危之必有所以持危之
方蓋不可一日不之講也先憂後樂正
韋布之志其敬悉之行將具以
聞于
上

韋布之志其敬悉之行將具以
===
聞于
punctuated: 廟堂，孰若且舉一二與諸士子商較之，可乎？夫内建百官以善政也，而政或有所未善；外設牧守以弘化也，而化或有所未弘。疆埸之鎮戍相望，而内訌猶莫寧戢；方夏之屯營相屬，而椎剽猶或磐牙。古之所患，將悍卒驕，今則不然；古之所禁，民弁俗侈，今則異是。輕徭所以逸民，而重難弗見損；薄賦所以厚下，而蠲符莫或給。冒濫之賞，何以矯之以循格令之舊？脫漏之辜，何以裁之以適刑罰之中？兹皆治世所憂，而安邦所危也。憂之，必有所以弭憂之道；危之，必有所以持危之方。蓋不可一日不之講也。先憂後樂，正韋布之志。其敬悉之，行將具以聞于上。
translation_en:
…the court, would it not be better first to raise one or two matters for discussion with you examination candidates? Within the central government, the various officials are appointed to ensure good administration, yet administration in some respects remains deficient. Outside it, prefects and other local administrators are appointed to extend moral transformation, yet in some respects that transformation has not spread. Frontier garrisons stand within sight of one another, yet internal strife remains unquelled. Military encampments extend throughout the realm, yet violent robbery still has entrenched strongholds. In antiquity, fierce commanders and arrogant soldiers were a source of concern; today this is not so. In antiquity, misconduct among the people [?] and extravagance in customs were prohibited; today things are different. Reducing labor service is intended to ease the people’s lot, yet their grievous burdens show no diminution. Reducing taxation is intended to enrich those below, yet certificates of remission [?] are not issued. How can improperly obtained or excessive rewards be corrected so as to conform to established regulations? How can offenses that have escaped punishment be adjudicated so as to attain the proper balance in penal sanctions?

These are all causes for concern in an age of good government and sources of danger in a secure state. If we are concerned about them, there must be a way to allay that concern; if we perceive their danger, there must be a means of sustaining the state amid peril. Surely these matters must not go undiscussed for even a single day. To be first in concern and last in enjoyment is precisely the aspiration of scholars still clad in commoners’ garments. Address these matters respectfully and fully; your responses will shortly be submitted in full to His Majesty.

First Session
Four Books

“It speaks of flourishing virtue and utmost goodness, which the people cannot forget.”

Xue Hui

Associate Examiner Li, Assistant Instructor, comments: “Interpretations of ‘flourishing virtue and utmost goodness’ differ. This essay clearly presents a firm interpretation, and its language is also coherent and harmonious. It has therefore been selected for inclusion.”

Examiner Lun, Right Admonisher, comments: “It captures the original intention of the author of the commentary.”

In explaining the poem, the author of the commentary says that the gentleman’s virtue reaches its utmost perfection and that all under Heaven are deeply moved by it.

That virtue can move people has long been recognized. Who could say that, when the gentleman’s virtue reaches its utmost perfection, all under Heaven would fail to be deeply moved by it? The third chapter of the commentary to the Great Learning explains ‘resting in utmost goodness.’ This passage discusses it in terms of ‘making bright virtue manifest’ and attaining the proper resting place. 言其必知致于問學之後而講習討論之功熟
行力于自修之餘而省察克治之功深是以涵
養真切而嚴敬為之常存已克而禮無不復渾
然天理之充周也踐履篤實而光輝為之宣著
和積而體無不順藹然天理之流行也善曰至

…speaking of it, his knowledge must have been extended through inquiry and study, bringing his efforts in learning, practice, and discussion to maturity; his conduct must have been strenuously pursued through self-cultivation, deepening his efforts in introspection and overcoming his faults. Thus his inward cultivation is earnest and genuine, and solemn reverence is constantly maintained. The self is overcome [?], and ritual propriety is restored in every respect: the Principle of Heaven fills him as an undivided whole. His practice is steadfast and sincere, and its radiance shines forth. Harmony accumulates, and every aspect of his bearing accords with it: the Principle of Heaven flows abundantly through him. Goodness is called “the highest good” with reference to the ultimate reach of principle. In the realm of earnest and genuine inward cultivation, everything embodies the subtle essence of moral principle, so utterly pure that nothing can be added, possessing something beyond naming. In the realm of steadfast and sincere practice, everything embodies the utmost principles governing affairs, so wholly refined that not the slightest admixture remains, possessing something beyond comparison.

Abundant virtue does not lie outside the highest good; rather, the highest good is what makes virtue abundant in this way. Thus, although the gentleman has no intention of winning the people’s admiration, all who apprehend his virtue through observing him and being moved by him say: “Virtue is common to us all, but the gentleman has attained it in its fullest abundance. How fortunate we are to receive his protection!” Although he has no intention of winning the people’s affection, all who apprehend his goodness even through what little they hear and see say: “Goodness is common to us all, but the gentleman has followed it to its utmost limit. How fortunate we are to have someone on whom to depend!” Thus all upon whom his lingering radiance shines revere and cherish him; no one in the entire age is excluded. For those who share the same virtue necessarily respond to one another. Even if they wished to forget him, could they? Wherever his enduring influence reaches, everyone turns toward him in admiration; throughout the Four Seas, all are alike in this. title: 正德八年應天府鄉試錄
text:
裏交修君子之所以明明德者如此民不能忘
固其所也傳者以之釋詩何其深切而著明哉
不寧是也下引烈文即以新民之實言之蓋大
學之綱領有三莫要於至善而至善之止必由
知而後得故章首三詩備其理此引二詩道其
實咏歎淫泆而始終本末兩無不盡推之天下
之事豈有以異此乎
學而時習之不亦說乎有朋自遠方來不
亦樂乎人不知而不慍不亦君子乎
尹賢
同考試官教諭鍾批此題首一節乃後二節
之本首句尤重是學之用力處學者不察往往三節
平作殊無意味此作深得朱子發明之旨且文詞爾
雅有足式者刻子之文將以破羣疑乎
同考試官教授曾批此是吾夫子教人為學
開卷第一義也學者以其近而忽之故場屋紛紛殊
無的見此作以自得為主而分演功效處深合本傳
是亦學之有得之君子毋謂人不知也

…cultivating the inward together with the outward: such is how the gentleman makes his luminous virtue shine forth. That the people cannot forget him is indeed only fitting. How profound, pertinent, and lucid is the commentator’s use of this to explain the ode! Nor is this all. The subsequent quotation from Illustrious Virtue (Lie wen) speaks of the actual work of renewing the people. The Great Learning has three guiding principles, of which none is more essential than the highest good; yet abiding in the highest good can be attained only through knowledge. Thus the three odes at the beginning of the chapter fully set forth the principle, while the two odes quoted here describe its realization. Through expansive singing and sighing, beginning and end, root and branch, are all exhaustively expressed. If extended to the affairs of the world, how could anything differ from this?

“To learn and practice it at due times—is this not a pleasure? To have friends come from afar—is this not a joy? To remain unresentful when others do not recognize one—is this not to be a gentleman?”

Yin Xian 尹賢

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhong, Instructor: The first section of this topic is the foundation of the following two sections. The opening phrase is especially important: it identifies where effort must be applied in learning. Students fail to perceive this and often treat all three sections on an equal footing, leaving their essays quite devoid of meaning. This essay deeply grasps the purport of Master Zhu’s elucidation. Moreover, its language is refined and offers much worthy of emulation. Might printing your essay dispel the many doubts?

Comment by Associate Examiner Zeng, Professor: This is the very first principle, at the opening of the book, through which our Master teaches people how to learn. Students neglect it because it seems so familiar; hence the profusion of examination essays that utterly lack a clear understanding. This essay takes personal attainment as its central theme, and its separate elaboration of effort and effects accords closely with the original commentary. Here, too, is a gentleman who has attained something through learning. Do not say that others fail to recognize you.

title: 正德八年應天府鄉試錄
text:
考試官左中允賈批聖人立言之㫖此殆近之
考試官右諭德倫批通篇健暢且協朱傳意
聖人之論學也原所得不已之功列所得不已
之效夫功立而效自見也學之不已而有得焉
則其及人之樂成德之地亦豈能自已哉記魯
論者述夫子之言如此意謂人性皆善而覺有
先後後覺者不有待於學乎是故善有未明必
效先覺之知者求以明之使天之賦於我者無
少昏初有未復必效先覺之能者求以復之俾
===
我之得於天者無少歉既知矣而復繹之益續
夫明善之力既能矣而復敦之益崇夫復初之
功如是則事理熟于積習之後喜意油然而進
進不已盖有不能以語人者存焉身心裕於從
容之餘悅意勃然而駸駸不息盖有人所不及
知者寓焉夫學之功立而自得不已如此故其
及於人也同類是從無遠不至皆以我為先覺
而知能之是求善未明也與之以明初未復也
與之以復獨得之妙沛而為同得之美矣懽忻

聖人之論學也，原所得不已之功，列所得不已之效。夫功立而效自見也，學之不已而有得焉，則其及人之樂、成德之地，亦豈能自已哉？記魯論者述夫子之言如此，意謂人性皆善，而覺有先後，後覺者不有待於學乎？是故善有未明，必效先覺之知者，求以明之，使天之賦於我者無少昏；初有未復，必效先覺之能者，求以復之，俾我之得於天者無少歉。既知矣，而復繹之，益續夫明善之力；既能矣，而復敦之，益崇夫復初之功。如是，則事理熟于積習之後，喜意油然而進進不已，盖有不能以語人者存焉；身心裕於從容之餘，悅意勃然而駸駸不息，盖有人所不及知者寓焉。夫學之功立而自得不已如此，故其及於人也，同類是從，無遠不至，皆以我為先覺，而知能之是求。善未明也，與之以明；初未復也，與之以復。獨得之妙，沛而為同得之美矣。懽忻

Examiner Jia, Left Companion to the Heir Apparent, comments: This comes close indeed to the intent behind the sage’s words.

Examiner Lun, Right Exhorter to the Heir Apparent, comments: Vigorous and fluent throughout, it also accords with the meaning of Zhu Xi’s commentary.

In discussing learning, the sage traced the effort through which understanding is gained without cease and set forth the effects of such continual attainment. Once the effort is established, its effects naturally appear. If one learns unceasingly and thereby gains understanding, how could the joy of extending it to others and the attainment of perfected virtue ever cease of themselves? Those who recorded the Analects of Lu recounted the Master’s words in this way. Their meaning is that human nature is universally good, but some awaken earlier and others later. Must not those who awaken later depend upon learning? Thus, wherever goodness has not yet been understood, one must emulate the understanding of those who awakened first and seek to illuminate it, so that nothing of Heaven’s endowment in oneself remains even slightly obscured. Wherever one’s original nature has not yet been restored, one must emulate the abilities of those who awakened first and seek to restore it, so that what one has received from Heaven lacks nothing whatsoever. Having understood, one examines it again, further sustaining the effort to illuminate goodness; having become capable, one reinforces that capacity, further advancing the work of restoring one’s original nature. In this way, after accumulated practice, the principles of affairs become thoroughly familiar, and gladness wells up spontaneously, advancing without cease: something remains here that cannot be conveyed to others in words. Body and mind enjoy ample ease, and delight springs forth, pressing onward without rest: something resides here that others cannot fully know. Such is the unceasing personal attainment that follows when the work of learning is established. Hence, when its influence reaches others, those of the same kind follow, coming from however far away. All regard me as one who awakened first and seek my understanding and abilities. Where their goodness has not yet been illuminated, I help them illuminate it; where their original nature has not yet been restored, I help them restore it. The subtle wonder of individual attainment thus flows abundantly into the beauty of shared attainment. The feelings of joy…

人不我知置之不校一以名爲外物而知能之

translation_en:
…in these feelings, there is no separation between others and oneself: is this not indeed a joy? If things do not altogether turn out so, and others do not recognize me, I let it pass without taking issue. I regard reputation simply as something external and devote my efforts solely to understanding and ability. Since I myself have clarified the good, whence could resentment arise? Since I myself have recovered my original nature, whence could disturbance of mind arise? The learning that rests with oneself is entrusted to the failings that rest with others [?]. With virtue and moral capacity perfected, one joins the company of sages and worthies: is one not indeed a gentleman? Ah! Learning is rooted in practice at due times, and unceasing progress brings one to this point. Should learners not therefore know where to direct their efforts? Moreover, great is the significance of learning! It first appears in the Documents of Shang and is sung again in the Hymns of Zhou: these were indeed the beginnings of sagely learning. Subsequently, the Master's words recorded in this book once again showed learners the gateway to entering the Way and the foundation for accumulating virtue. Ultimately, they culminate in becoming a gentleman, whereby the work is brought to completion. This, in turn, is how sagely learning was continued. Later, what Master Yan loved and what Master Zeng and Zisi transmitted all remained within this scope. Ah! The transmission of the learning of the Way has a long ancestry. Considering these together strengthens our conviction.

“I understand words, and I am skilled at nourishing my vast, flowing vital force.”

Wang Dahua

Comment by Associate Examiner Li, Instructor: He can grasp and apprehend Mencius's meaning in understanding words and nourishing vital force. Moreover, his language is abundant and his vital force full. Might he be one who has studied Mencius and gained something from him?

Comment by Associate Examiner Xu, Instructor: Those who wrote on this topic in the examination hall were generally able to produce complete essays. But in seeking one whose language was upright and grand, and whose vital force was also full, I found only this essay. I have recorded it to serve as a model for scholars…

title: 正德八年應天府鄉試錄
text:
字之務奇者
考試官左中允賈批此等文字非淺學可到
考試官右諭德倫批絕似孟子語
大賢自言其所長異乎時人之所學而已盖知
言養氣大賢之所長也其不動心而異於時人
者非以是歟昔孟子因公孫丑有不動心之疑
異于告子之間故曉之以此謂夫人各有心心
各有主我之所以不動心者亦惟知言養氣焉
耳何則人之有言皆出于心是非得失各有攸
===
當不有以知之可乎我則隨其所在而深究之
一入乎耳即知其中之所存因其所形而深察
之一接乎聰即知其心之所蘊言有是非有以
識是非之所以然如曰詖淫則蔽陷乘之昭然
錙銖之不爽也言有得失有以識得失之所以
然如曰邪遁則離窮因之炳然毫髮之莫違也
我之知言盖如此人之有氣皆本諸天盛大流
行乃其本體不有以養之可乎我則積義以培
其根無所庸於揠拔盖不以力而以理焉遵道

punctuated:
字之務奇者。
考試官左中允賈批：此等文字，非淺學可到。
考試官右諭德倫批：絕似孟子語。
大賢自言其所長，異乎時人之所學而已。盖知言養氣，大賢之所長也。其不動心而異於時人者，非以是歟？昔孟子因公孫丑有不動心之疑、異于告子之間，故曉之以此，謂夫人各有心，心各有主。我之所以不動心者，亦惟知言養氣焉耳。何則？人之有言，皆出于心，是非得失，各有攸當，不有以知之可乎？我則隨其所在而深究之，一入乎耳，即知其中之所存；因其所形而深察之，一接乎聰，即知其心之所蘊。言有是非，有以識是非之所以然。如曰詖淫，則蔽陷乘之，昭然錙銖之不爽也。言有得失，有以識得失之所以然。如曰邪遁，則離窮因之，炳然毫髮之莫違也。我之知言，盖如此。人之有氣，皆本諸天，盛大流行，乃其本體，不有以養之可乎？我則積義以培其根，無所庸於揠拔，盖不以力而以理焉。遵道
translation_en:
…those who strive for novelty in their writing.
Examiner Jia, Left Companion to the Heir Apparent, comments: Writing of this kind lies beyond the reach of shallow learning.
Examiner Lun, Right Admonisher, comments: It sounds exactly like the words of Mencius.
The great worthy speaks of his own strengths, which differ from what his contemporaries study. Understanding words and nurturing vital energy (qi) are indeed the great worthy’s strengths. Is this not why his mind remains unmoved, distinguishing him from his contemporaries? Formerly, Gongsun Chou questioned Mencius about his unmoved mind and how it differed from Gaozi’s [?]. Mencius therefore enlightened him with these words, explaining: Everyone has a mind, and every mind has something that governs it. What enables my mind to remain unmoved is simply understanding words and nurturing vital energy. Why is this so? People’s words all issue from their minds. Their rightness and wrongness, their merits and faults, each have a corresponding source. Can one dispense with a means of understanding them? I investigate deeply wherever that source lies: as soon as words enter my ears, I know what is present within. From their outward expression I examine them closely: as soon as I hear them, I know what their speaker’s mind contains. Words may be right or wrong, and I have the means to discern why they are so. In the case of biased or extravagant words, obstruction and entanglement beset the mind; this is so clear that my discernment errs by not the slightest measure. Words have merits and faults, and I have the means to discern their causes. In the case of perverse or evasive words, departure from the right way and exhaustion of resources underlie them; this is so plain that my discernment deviates by not a hair’s breadth. Such is my understanding of words. The vital energy people possess is rooted in Heaven. Its original substance is vast and flows freely. Can one dispense with a means of nurturing it? I accumulate righteousness to nourish its roots, having no use for tugging at the shoots to make them grow. Thus I rely on principle rather than force. I follow the Way …

title: 正德八年應天府鄉試錄
text:
以豐其源無所事於正助盖不于末而于本焉
氣本至大直以養之而弗害與吾俱生者以全
浩然天地之可塞也氣本至剛正以伸之而弗
撓與吾俱形者以充烈乎金石之可貫也我之
養氣又如此是惟知言則有以明夫道義而於
天下之事無所疑養氣則有以配夫道義而於
天下之事無所懼其當大任而不動心者夫豈
有他道哉雖然孟子之不動心異于告子之冥
然無覺悍然不顧如此者然豈無所自耶盖盡
===
心知性之學開于前善養擴充之功繼于後而
傳受本原亦已遠矣公孫丑不知儗諸告子告
子豈軻之倫耶學者能於此而求之回視告子
之學得失相反大有徑庭疑懼之說將自得之
公孫丑烏足以知此也噫
易
无所往其來復吉有攸往夙吉
尹賢

以豐其源，無所事於正助，盖不于末而于本焉。氣本至大，直以養之而弗害，與吾俱生者以全，浩然天地之可塞也。氣本至剛，正以伸之而弗撓，與吾俱形者以充，烈乎金石之可貫也。我之養氣又如此。是惟知言，則有以明夫道義，而於天下之事無所疑；養氣，則有以配夫道義，而於天下之事無所懼。其當大任而不動心者，夫豈有他道哉？雖然，孟子之不動心，異于告子之冥然無覺、悍然不顧如此者，然豈無所自耶？盖盡心知性之學開于前，善養擴充之功繼于後，而傳受本原亦已遠矣。公孫丑不知，儗諸告子，告子豈軻之倫耶？學者能於此而求之，回視告子之學，得失相反，大有徑庭，疑懼之說將自得之。公孫丑烏足以知此也？噫！

易

无所往，其來復吉；有攸往，夙吉。

尹賢

同考試官教諭鍾批：所往處殆非一事，作者
translation_en:
…to enrich its source, without seeking predetermined results or forcing its growth: the concern is with the root rather than the branches. Vital force is inherently supremely great. By nourishing it with uprightness and doing it no harm, I preserve intact what was born together with me; in its vastness, it can fill Heaven and Earth. Vital force is inherently supremely firm. By extending it through rectitude without bending it, I bring to fullness what took shape together with me; in its power, it can pierce metal and stone. Such, in turn, is how I nourish my vital force. Thus, understanding words enables one to comprehend the Way and righteousness and to have no doubts concerning the affairs of the world; nourishing vital force enables one to accord with the Way and righteousness and to have no fear concerning the affairs of the world. Could there be any other way to shoulder great responsibilities without perturbation of the heart? Yet Mengzi’s unperturbed heart differs in this way from Gaozi’s benighted insensibility and obstinate disregard. Surely this attainment had its source? The learning of fully developing the heart and knowing one’s nature came first; the work of properly nourishing and extending it followed. The origins of this transmission reach far back indeed. Gongsun Chou, failing to understand this, compared him to Gaozi. But how could Gaozi be the peer of Meng Ke? If students can seek understanding here and look back upon Gaozi’s learning, they will see that success and failure stand opposed, with a vast gulf between them; they will come to understand for themselves the explanation concerning doubt and fear. How could Gongsun Chou have understood this? Ah!

Book of Changes

“When there is nowhere to go, returning brings good fortune; when there is somewhere to go, going early brings good fortune.”

Yin Xian

title: 正德八年應天府鄉試錄
text:
惟以兵戰立說殊覺粗淺是篇含蓄不露而意自足
蓋深於易者與
同考試官教授曾批題本平易場中士子競
逞浮詞少當意者此作依題平平敷演詞理俱到且
舂容雋永令人讀之愈嚼愈覺有味誠佳作也
考試官左中允賈批題主安靜為說是篇得之
考試官右諭德倫批得潔靜精微之體
聖人繫解之辭必兩著夫安靜之占焉甚矣動
息之宜貴乎與時推移也時無所往固宜於安
===
靜矣若猶有往又可不以亟濟為安靜之吉耶
昔伏羲畫卦交震坎上而名曰解迨文王繫辭
至此若謂解之為卦變自升來三往居四入於
坤體二居其所而又得中故其占不惟利於平
易抑亦利於安靜何則蹇難既平四海初離荼
毒莫不憚於勤動也坎險既出兆民方脫艱苦
莫不戒於煩擾也當此之際宜審厥宜若亂流
盡殄无一介梗治之夫厲階悉除靡蕞爾不貢
之土斯則无所往矣既无所往顧得妄開釁隙

惟以兵戰立說，殊覺粗淺。是篇含蓄不露，而意自足，蓋深於易者與！

考試官左中允賈批：題主安靜為說，是篇得之。
考試官右諭德倫批：得潔靜精微之體。
聖人繫解之辭，必兩著夫安靜之占焉。甚矣，動息之宜，貴乎與時推移也！時無所往，固宜於安靜矣；若猶有往，又可不以亟濟為安靜之吉耶？
昔伏羲畫卦，交震坎上，而名曰解。迨文王繫辭至此，若謂解之為卦，變自升來，三往居四，入於坤體，二居其所而又得中，故其占不惟利於平易，抑亦利於安靜。何則？蹇難既平，四海初離荼毒，莫不憚於勤動也；坎險既出，兆民方脫艱苦，莫不戒於煩擾也。當此之際，宜審厥宜。若亂流盡殄，无一介梗治之夫；厲階悉除，靡蕞爾不貢之土，斯則无所往矣。既无所往，顧得妄開釁隙
translation_en:
…base their arguments solely on warfare, which seems decidedly crude and shallow. This essay conveys its meaning fully through restrained implication, without laying everything bare. Surely its author has a profound understanding of the Changes!
Associate Examiner Zeng, Prefectural School Professor, comments: The topic is straightforward, yet the candidates in the examination hall compete in displaying empty rhetoric; few satisfy my expectations. This composition follows the topic and develops it in an even, unforced manner, doing full justice to both expression and principle. Moreover, it is leisurely and rich in lasting significance: the more one savors it, the more flavor one discovers. Truly an excellent work.
Examiner Jia, Left Rectifier, comments: The topic takes repose as its central argument. This essay grasps it.
Examiner Lun, Right Admonisher, comments: It achieves the character of purity, stillness, subtlety, and refinement.
When the sage appended the judgment to Deliverance (Jie), he necessarily made the prognostication of repose explicit in both circumstances. How vital it is that the proper choice between action and rest should change with the times! When the times offer nowhere to go, repose is certainly appropriate. Yet if there is still somewhere to go, should not swiftly completing the task likewise constitute the good fortune of repose?
Long ago, when Fu Xi drew the hexagrams, he placed Zhen above Kan [?] and named the hexagram Deliverance. When King Wen came to append its judgment, it was as though he said: Deliverance is a hexagram formed by transformation from Ascending (Sheng). The third line goes to occupy the fourth position, entering the body of Kun; the second remains in its place and also holds the central position. Thus its prognostication favors not only ease but also repose. Why is this? Once difficulties have been pacified, all within the Four Seas have only just escaped bitter suffering, and everyone dreads exertion and activity. Once peril has been escaped, the myriad people have only just emerged from hardship, and everyone is wary of disturbance and harassment. At such a moment, one should carefully assess what is appropriate. If the bands of rebels have all been exterminated, leaving not a single man to obstruct good government, and the sources of calamity have all been removed, leaving not even the smallest territory that fails to present tribute, then there is nowhere to go. Since there is nowhere to go, can one recklessly provoke fresh hostilities…

title: 正德八年應天府鄉試錄

以逞分外之欲乎亦惟來復其所安常處順與
斯民休息於恬養之區返適厥居守貞履素與
斯世嬉遊于富壽之域夫然則衆志堅定而邦
本以固國勢尊安而主威以強豈非處解之吉
乎若遺孽猶存懼微蔓之復滋餘燼未滅慮虐
燄之再然斯則有攸往矣雖有攸往覩得久事
行役以召意外之變乎亦惟籌謀及早不俟終
日即收蕩滅之功弛罷孔亟曾靡逾時頓還安
平之地夫然則往克有濟咸忘羈縶之勞亂庶
===

遄沮于食泰寧之福又非處解之吉乎如或不
爾非多事以自疲則無事以自怠矣其不生患
而長亂也幾希嗟夫世至於解乃亂而復治擾
而復定之時也是雖天運使然何嘗不本諸人
事也故作易聖人不諉諸天惟權時義以為萬
世告而已於乎以為訓猶有勤遠畧以虚耗
海内忽徙戎以貽雲擾之禍者其亦弗思甚矣
可不戒哉

punctuated:
以逞分外之欲乎？亦惟來復其所，安常處順，與斯民休息於恬養之區；返適厥居，守貞履素，與斯世嬉遊于富壽之域。夫然，則衆志堅定而邦本以固，國勢尊安而主威以強，豈非處解之吉乎？若遺孽猶存，懼微蔓之復滋；餘燼未滅，慮虐燄之再然，斯則有攸往矣。雖有攸往，覩得久事行役，以召意外之變乎？亦惟籌謀及早，不俟終日，即收蕩滅之功；弛罷孔亟，曾靡逾時，頓還安平之地。夫然，則往克有濟，咸忘羈縶之勞；亂庶遄沮，于食泰寧之福，又非處解之吉乎？如或不爾，非多事以自疲，則無事以自怠矣。其不生患而長亂也幾希！嗟夫！世至於解，乃亂而復治、擾而復定之時也。是雖天運使然，何嘗不本諸人事也？故作易聖人不諉諸天，惟權時義，以為萬世告而已。於乎！以為訓，猶有勤遠畧以虚耗海内、忽徙戎以貽雲擾之禍者，其亦弗思甚矣！可不戒哉！

君子居其室，出其言善，則千里之外應之。
translation_en:
…to gratify desires beyond one’s proper bounds? One should simply return to one’s place, abide in constancy and accord with what is right, and rest together with the people in a realm of tranquil nurture; return to one’s abode, maintain rectitude and simplicity, and enjoy with the world a realm of prosperity and longevity. Thus the resolve of the multitude will be firm and the foundations of the state secure; the state’s standing will be honored and peaceful, and the ruler’s authority strengthened. Is this not the good fortune of properly managing Deliverance [the hexagram Xie]?

If surviving evildoers remain, there is fear that their slight tendrils may spread again; if embers have not been extinguished, there is concern that their cruel flames may flare up anew. Then there is indeed somewhere to go. Yet even when there is somewhere to go, can one [?] prolong campaigning and thereby invite unforeseen disturbances? One should simply make plans early and, without waiting until the day is over, achieve the complete suppression of the trouble; then demobilize with all speed, without delay, and immediately restore peace and security. Thus the undertaking will succeed, and all will forget the hardships of constraint and service; disorder may swiftly be checked, and the blessings of great peace enjoyed [?]. Is this not also the good fortune of properly managing Deliverance?

If one does otherwise, one will either exhaust oneself by undertaking too much or become negligent through having nothing to do. There is scarcely any chance of avoiding the creation of troubles and the fostering of disorder! Alas! When the world reaches Deliverance, it is a time when disorder gives way again to good government and turmoil to stability. Although the workings of Heaven bring this about, when has it ever failed to rest upon human action? Hence the sage who composed the Book of Changes did not leave the matter to Heaven, but weighed what was fitting for the time and thereby admonished all future ages. Alas! Even with this as instruction, there have still been those who pursued distant conquests and depleted the resources of the realm, or neglected the matter of relocating the Rong peoples and thereby bequeathed the calamity of widespread turmoil. How grievously they failed to reflect! Can one fail to take warning?

“When the gentleman dwells in his chamber and utters words that are good, people a thousand li away respond to him…”

…how much more those nearby?
Wang Ting
Associate Examiner Zhong, an Instructor, comments: Wherever sincerity and trustworthiness exert their influence, nothing obstructs their reach. This essay grasps that point. Moreover, it does not develop its argument exclusively around the ruler: this shows especially clear insight. It is included as a model for elucidating the meaning of the Commentary.
Associate Examiner Zeng, a Professor, comments: Sincerity and trustworthiness are the foundation for moving others, and you alone have been able to articulate this. Every sentence is lucid, vigorous, and pleasing. The conclusion brings out what has not previously been expressed and is particularly striking and unexpected, amply demonstrating your learning and discernment.
Examiner Jia, Left Rectifier, comments: It explains the principle on the basis of the topic, and the writing flows naturally.
Examiner Lun, Right Admonisher, comments: There is not a superfluous sentence in the entire essay.
The argument is that the gentleman’s words, though uttered in his private dwelling, possess a trustworthiness that moves people’s hearts without impediment. How powerful is the capacity of sincerity and trustworthiness to move others! How exalted! When the gentleman speaks and his words are good, they possess trustworthiness. People far and near respond to them; what difference, then, does it make that he is in his private dwelling?
Chapter eight of the Great Commentary sets out examples of comparison and deliberation. It first cites and explains the meaning of the nine in the second place in Inner Trust (Zhongfu). Its point is that nothing is swifter than the mutual responsiveness of human hearts, and nothing is more essential to that responsiveness than sincerity and trustworthiness. Thus, when the gentleman dwells in his chamber, it is merely a space of a few paces and fathoms, unlike the spacious depths of a great court or grand hall that can inspire reverent admiration from far and near. It is merely a place of repose and leisure, without the imposing authority of presiding over the people or addressing an assembled multitude under oath, which can command attention both within and without. title: 正德八年應天府鄉試錄
text:
言出諸口純乎善而不雜如言君而實仁言臣
而實敬則誠信之本於我乎立矣言發乎中一
於善而不妄如言父而實慈言子而實孝則誠
信之道於我乎得矣是雖因事觸發非爲感人
計也然好爵同靡千里之外如彼其遼邈也自
不能已其聲應氣求之篤莫不以君子之言為
夫人之有中初不以私室而或異也雖因事宣
達非爲感人謀也然懿德同好千里之外若彼
其遐逖也自不能遏其心孚意契之誠莫不以
===
君子之言爲嘉言之孔彰初不以私居而或間
也遼邈尚爾况邇而比閭其人乆狎君子之忠
誠吾知聞言之際其應也殆若江河之决矣且
私室之内反以易私屬之聽德也哉遐逖且然
况近而族黨之衆素稔君子之忱恂吾知聞言
之頃其應也殆若桴鼓之捷矣且私居之間反
以便朋比之屬耳也哉是則君子所居雖非公
所一言而善感通猶如此使持是道而揚于王
庭所感抑又何如邪雖然自其感而言之特言

punctuated: 言出諸口，純乎善而不雜，如言君而實仁，言臣而實敬，則誠信之本於我乎立矣。言發乎中，一於善而不妄，如言父而實慈，言子而實孝，則誠信之道於我乎得矣。是雖因事觸發，非爲感人計也，然好爵同靡，千里之外，如彼其遼邈也，自不能已其聲應氣求之篤，莫不以君子之言為夫人之有中，初不以私室而或異也。雖因事宣達，非爲感人謀也，然懿德同好，千里之外，若彼其遐逖也，自不能遏其心孚意契之誠，莫不以君子之言爲嘉言之孔彰，初不以私居而或間也。遼邈尚爾，况邇而比閭，其人乆狎君子之忠誠，吾知聞言之際，其應也殆若江河之决矣。且私室之内，反以易私屬之聽德也哉？遐逖且然，况近而族黨之衆，素稔君子之忱恂，吾知聞言之頃，其應也殆若桴鼓之捷矣。且私居之間，反以便朋比之屬耳也哉？是則君子所居雖非公所，一言而善，感通猶如此，使持是道而揚于王庭，所感抑又何如邪？雖然，自其感而言之，特言
translation_en:
…the words issuing from his mouth are purely good, without admixture: when he speaks of the ruler, he truly embodies benevolence; when he speaks of the minister, he truly embodies reverence. Thus the foundation of sincerity and trustworthiness is established within him. His words arise from within, devoted wholly to goodness and free from falsehood: when he speaks of the father, he truly embodies parental kindness; when he speaks of the son, he truly embodies filial devotion. Thus he attains within himself the Way of sincerity and trustworthiness.

Although these words are prompted by particular circumstances, with no calculation to move others, people nevertheless share his fine cup of wine. Even a thousand li away, remote as that may be, they cannot restrain their profound response, like answering sounds and mutually attracting vital energies. All regard the gentleman’s words as showing that this man possesses inner sincerity; their response is in no way altered because he speaks from a private chamber. Although he expresses himself as circumstances arise, with no design to move others, people nevertheless share a love of admirable virtue. Even a thousand li away, distant as that may be, they cannot suppress the sincerity of their hearts’ trust and their minds’ accord. All regard the gentleman’s words as an illustrious manifestation of excellent speech; their response is in no way interrupted because he speaks from his private dwelling.

If this is so even at such a distance, how much more so among his immediate neighbors, who have long been familiar with the gentleman’s loyalty and sincerity! I know that when they hear his words, their response will be like the bursting forth of the Yangzi and Yellow Rivers. Indeed, might speaking within a private chamber actually make it easier for his close associates to hear his virtue [?]? If this is so even in faraway places, how much more so among the nearby members of his lineage and community, who have long known the gentleman’s sincerity and trustworthiness! I know that the instant they hear his words, their response will be as swift as a drum answering the drumstick. Indeed, might speaking within a private dwelling actually make it easier for his companions to lend their ears [?]?

Thus, although the gentleman does not occupy a public place, a single good utterance can elicit such sympathetic response. Were he to uphold this Way and proclaim it at the royal court, how much greater might its influence be? Nevertheless, considered in terms of what moves others, it is merely speech…

…only speech; how could that compare with the greater importance of conduct? As for what responds to it, this is only human beings; how could that compare with Heaven, the ultimate? 有功咸迪乎朕德矣引斯民於至善我固有德
□之布也今者五長奉行于四海而蹈行有功
□□從是迪矣若華若夷翕然於變之同風有
是地則有是德教之洋溢也何有於弗從者耶
若遠若近熈然敏德之成俗有是地則有是德
化之流通也何有於弗率者耶夫天下化成如
此豈我之所能自致哉良由汝禹贊襄左右竭
八年之勞土功度矣即繼之以弼五服秩秩然

乃功惟叙而吾德教之施始有其地焉宣力四
方勵克勤之節五服弼矣即繼之以立師長井
井然乃功有叙而我德化之行始有其人焉文
命之誕敷雖曰吾主之而師牧宣之然其所以
致是者實汝之功也豈吾所得專哉聲教之四
訖雖曰我出之而五長行之然其所以臻茲者
亦汝之功也豈我所敢居哉夫汝之功叙既已
如此則夫未化之苗民固付之臯陶之刑也何
足慮乎大舜以是歸美於禹其謙德讓善之心

…[?] the extension of moral instruction. Now the regional governors receive and promulgate it throughout the Five Zones, each achieving results in guiding the people, and all lead them toward my virtue. In leading these people to the highest good, I have indeed spread my moral influence [?]. Now the chiefs of the five regions carry it out within the Four Seas and achieve results through putting it into practice; [?] follow this guidance. Whether of the central lands or of the outer peoples, all are transformed together and share the same customs. Wherever there is land, moral instruction spreads abundantly: who could fail to follow it? Whether far or near, all gladly strive for virtue until it becomes customary. Wherever there is land, moral transformation circulates: who could fail to comply?

With the transformation of All-under-Heaven thus accomplished, could I have brought this about by myself? It is truly because you, Yu, assisted me on every side and labored to the utmost for eight years. Once the work of regulating the land was accomplished, you followed it by ordering the Five Zones. Your achievements proceeded in orderly sequence, and only then did the extension of my moral instruction have the territory it required. You exerted your strength throughout the four quarters, holding firmly to diligence. Once the Five Zones were ordered, you followed this by establishing regional leaders. Your achievements proceeded in a well-ordered sequence, and only then did the implementation of my moral transformation have the men it required.

Although it may be said that I preside over the widespread dissemination of civilizing instruction and that the regional governors promulgate it, what has brought this about is truly your achievement. How could I claim the credit exclusively? Although it may be said that instruction reaching the four extremities issues from me and that the chiefs of the five regions carry it out, what has brought matters to this point is likewise your achievement. How could I dare claim the credit? Since your achievements have already unfolded in such orderly succession, the Miao people who remain untransformed may surely be left to Gao Yao’s punishments. What cause is there for concern?

Thus the great Shun attributed the merit to Yu. His disposition to humility and to yielding credit for good deeds to others…

於斯可見矣。抑論自古及今稱治世者，必以唐虞為首，而虞廷無為之治，猶不能無三苗之逆命。盖至化不以是而有加損，而不治之治，又帝王待夷狄之常經也。然舜德誕敷而不自沮，禹謨入告而不少嫌，其君臣都俞吁咈之氣象何如耶？噫！此所以來孔子巍巍之賛於千載之下也。
惟先王建邦啓土，公劉克篤前烈，至于太王肇基王迹，王季其勤王家，我文考文王克成厥勳。

translation_en:
…can be seen in this. Further, whenever people from antiquity to the present have spoken of well-governed ages, they have invariably placed the reigns of Tang Yao and Yu Shun first. Yet even the government through nonaction at Shun’s court could not prevent the Sanmiao from defying his commands. The highest transforming influence is neither augmented nor diminished by this; governing through noninterference is also the constant principle by which emperors and kings deal with the Yi and Di peoples. Yet Shun spread his virtue far and wide without becoming discouraged, while Yu presented his counsels without the slightest misgiving. What a spirit prevailed between this ruler and his minister as they voiced assent and dissent! Ah! This is what elicited Confucius’s praise of their lofty greatness more than a thousand years later.
“Our former kings founded the state and opened up its territory. Gong Liu firmly carried forward his predecessors’ achievements. Then Tai Wang laid the foundations of the royal enterprise, and Wang Ji labored diligently for the royal house. My cultivated deceased father, King Wen, brought their achievement to completion.”
Pan Zhao
Comment by Associate Examiner Li, an Instructor: “The foundations of Zhou’s rise to kingship grew still more flourishing under King Wen. This essay recounts the virtue of successive generations; its style is gracious, elegant, and vigorous, prompting the exclamation, ‘How vast and splendid!’ An exposition of the Classics such as this may serve as a model.”
Comment by Associate Examiner Xu, an Instructor: “The essay sets out how successive generations of the Zhou house founded and continued its enterprise, rendering the relative importance of the events with exact appropriateness. To produce such work beneath the windswept eaves of the examination hall is indeed highly commendable.”
Comment by Examiner Guan, Left Rectifier of the Heir Apparent: “It skillfully recounts the gradual rise of the Zhou house to kingship, and its composition is orderly as well.”

text:
考試官右諭德倫批節序昭晰而詞理簡當
聖君之告諸侯必歷叙王業之所由興而及王
業之所由成焉夫王業之成有所自也聖君推
本而詳叙之豈非所以昭大公而一衆志也哉
昔武王克商之後而告諸侯如此謂夫我周之
業人知其成矣曽知其所以成乎昔我先王后
稷當唐虞之世為農師之官功懋相天而有邰
之邦以建德粒烝民而百里之土以啓斯固有
國之所由始也后稷之孫不有公劉乎匪居匪
康而民人是和乃積乃倉而國家是顯盖至是
而前烈益以篤焉然猶未也迨我古公太王以
九世之孫起公劉之後避狄遷岐而有來如市
之衆脩德服遠而奔喙載路之夷斯則王業之
所由基也太王而下不有王季乎克明克類而
周慶是篤克順克比而帝祉是承盖至是而王
業益以勤焉然亦未也自時厥後文考嗣興備
緝熈敬止之德而姬運為之益昌敷懷保惠鮮
之政而周業為之寢廣九州土地已有其六而

聖君之告諸侯，必歷叙王業之所由興，而及王業之所由成焉。夫王業之成有所自也，聖君推本而詳叙之，豈非所以昭大公而一衆志也哉？昔武王克商之後，而告諸侯如此，謂夫我周之業，人知其成矣，曽知其所以成乎？昔我先王后稷，當唐虞之世，為農師之官，功懋相天，而有邰之邦以建；德粒烝民，而百里之土以啓。斯固有國之所由始也。后稷之孫，不有公劉乎？匪居匪康，而民人是和；乃積乃倉，而國家是顯。盖至是而前烈益以篤焉。然猶未也。迨我古公太王，以九世之孫起公劉之後，避狄遷岐，而有來如市之衆；脩德服遠，而奔喙載路之夷。斯則王業之所由基也。太王而下，不有王季乎？克明克類，而周慶是篤；克順克比，而帝祉是承。盖至是而王業益以勤焉。然亦未也。自時厥後，文考嗣興，備緝熈敬止之德，而姬運為之益昌；敷懷保惠鮮之政，而周業為之寢廣。九州土地，已有其六，而

Examiner Lun, Right Mentor, comments: “The sequence is clearly articulated, and the wording and reasoning are concise and apt.”
When a sage ruler addresses the feudal lords, he must recount in order how the royal enterprise arose and proceed to explain how it reached fulfillment. The fulfillment of a royal enterprise has its origins. In tracing these origins and recounting them in detail, does the sage ruler not make manifest his complete impartiality and unite the wills of all? Such was King Wu’s address to the feudal lords after conquering Shang. His meaning was this: People know that the enterprise of our Zhou has reached fulfillment, but have they understood how it came to fulfillment? Long ago, our former king Hou Ji served as Agricultural Master in the age of Tang and Yu. His achievements were great in assisting Heaven, and the domain of Tai was established; through his virtue he fed the multitude with grain, and a territory one hundred li square was opened up. This was indeed the beginning of our state. Among Hou Ji’s descendants, was there not Gong Liu? Seeking neither repose nor ease, he brought harmony to the people; accumulating supplies and filling granaries, he brought distinction to the state. By this time, the achievements of his predecessors had been further consolidated. Yet this was not all. Then our Gugong Danfu, King Tai, arose as a ninth-generation descendant of Gong Liu. Avoiding the Di, he moved to Qi, and the crowds who came to him were like those gathering at a market. He cultivated virtue and won the allegiance of distant peoples, and the roads were filled with Yi tribespeople hurrying to him [?]. This was how the royal enterprise acquired its foundation. After King Tai, was there not Wang Ji? Capable of discernment and of distinguishing good from evil, he strengthened Zhou’s good fortune; capable of obedience and concord, he received the blessings of the Lord on High. By this time, still greater diligence had been devoted to the royal enterprise. Yet this too was not all. Thereafter, my deceased father, King Wen, arose in succession. Possessing fully the virtues of sustained enlightenment and abiding reverence, he made the fortunes of the Ji lineage flourish all the more. He extended policies that cherished and protected the people, showed kindness, and succored those in distress, and the enterprise of Zhou gradually expanded. 民心之歸也衆祖宗建篤之勳不于是一而集乎
三分天下已有其二而天命之眷也隆先世基
勤之績不于是而成乎夫以我周之業積於累
世而成於文考者其漸如此則夫我今日大統
之集非所以承先志耶抑嘗因是而知有周世
澤之深且長也文武而上開其源者非一人文
武而下浚其流者非一世歷年之永遠超夏商

源深者詎不信夫

translation_en:
…and multitudes of the people gave their allegiance. Were not the achievements by which our ancestors established and strengthened the realm thereby brought together into one? Already possessing two of the three parts of the world, he enjoyed Heaven’s abundant favor. Were not the accomplishments for which earlier generations had laid the foundations and labored thereby brought to fruition? The enterprise of our Zhou accumulated over successive generations and reached fulfillment under my deceased father through just such a gradual process. Is not the supreme succession now devolving upon me, then, the means of carrying forward my forebears’ intentions? From this I have also come to understand how profound and enduring are the blessings handed down through the generations of Zhou. Before Kings Wen and Wu, more than one person opened its source; after Kings Wen and Wu, more than one generation deepened its channel. Its long duration far surpassed that of Xia and Shang. Ultimately, this was simply the result of accumulated merit and benevolence. Earlier Confucian scholars said that its roots were firmly planted and its source was deep: surely this is true!

Book of Odes
“In the seventh month, the Fire Star descends; in the ninth month, winter clothing is distributed. In the first month, the wind blows cold; in the second month, the cold is bitter. Without clothes, without coarse woolen garments, how can we get through the year? In the third month, we attend to the plows; in the fourth month, we set our feet to work. Together with our wives and children, we bring food to those southern fields; the field overseer comes and is pleased.”

Xue Hui

Comment by Associate Examiner Li, Assistant Instructor: The topic is inherently imposing, yet students read it and treat it lightly, so there are scarcely any fine compositions. Its message was: Does Your Majesty know Bin? Originally one of the states under the Xia, it was the old homeland of Zhou. title: 正德八年應天府鄉試錄
text:
所未備則公子無裳而吾民之幼者不免於寒
矣何以卒是歲乎男不服外而褐之出於狩獵
者有所未具則公子無裘而吾民之老者不免
於凍矣何以終是歲乎衣之預也蓋如此自其
為食言之豈飢至而始索耶時維正月斗柄建
寅俯而察之土膏將動田器而往脩矣故二月
舉趾耕焉蓋南畝之方有事壯者皆出在田老
者率婦子而來饁農官適因之而至止斯時也
但見治田早則東作之效可收不惟君祀有所
===
需而吾民之幼者亦無飢矣田畯得不喜耶用
力齊則西成之利可獲不惟君燕有所賴而吾
民之老者亦無餒矣田畯又何怒耶食之預也
又如此吁大寒之候在丑月而圖之於建申之
時收成之候在酉月而慮之於建寅之日憂勤
忠愛之情舉皆見之先公風化王可以不知耶
雖然周公之戒成王不特此耳無逸之書一皆
帝王之心法惓惓言之無非欲知王業之難與
小人之依而已敢並進儒臣有欲繪為圖作為

…were not fully prepared, then the lord’s sons would have no lower garments, and the young among our people could not escape the cold. How could they get through the year? If men did not perform their work outdoors, and the coarse garments supplied through hunting were not fully provided, then the lord’s sons would have no fur robes, and the elderly among our people could not escape freezing. How could they finish the year? Such was their advance provision for clothing. As for providing food, did they wait until hunger arrived before seeking it? In the first month, the Dipper’s handle points toward yin. Looking down to inspect the earth, they see that its fertile moisture is about to stir, and farming implements are taken out for repair [?]. Thus, in the second month they set their feet to plowing. When work is underway in the southern fields, all the able-bodied go out to labor there, while the elderly lead the women and children to bring them food. The agricultural official happens to arrive just then. At such a time, he sees that, because cultivation began early, the benefits of spring planting can be secured. Not only will the ruler’s sacrifices have their required provisions, but the young among our people will also be free from hunger. How could the field overseer fail to rejoice? When all exert themselves together, the benefits of the autumn harvest can be obtained. Not only will the ruler’s banquets have dependable supplies, but the elderly among our people will also be free from hunger. What cause would the field overseer have for anger? Such, too, was their advance provision for food.

Xu Zhu

爾爲君者必揭以道德之訓使閭閻有式而熈

舉席于恬淡之場而後可焉侯度者所受以治
此國者也侯度不謹則法弛而治弗張如國何

樂者有戒罔迷厥政惟明王之刑是共而逸欲

之行不萌于念慮而後可焉夫治民守法常道
修矣然不虞弗戒而變或乘之又如國何必也
身處乎庭除之近慮及乎蠻方之遠車馬以修

…this poem, extending his intention of admonishing himself to these matters. Its meaning is this: the people are those with whom one defends this state. If the people lack integrity, the foundation is shaken and the defenses are insecure. What then becomes of the state? You who rule must set forth the teachings of moral virtue, giving the common people models to follow and fostering a spirit of harmony. You must display standards of dignified conduct, giving both capital and countryside rules to follow and establishing honest customs. Only when the people have support in every circumstance and are all brought into a realm of peace and well-being, when cunning and deceit do not arise and all dwell in tranquility [?], will this suffice.

The standards governing a feudal lord are those he receives for ruling this state. If these standards are not carefully observed, laws grow lax and government loses its effectiveness. What then becomes of the state? You who govern must not overturn your virtue: seek only the laws of the former kings, restraining indulgence in pleasure. You must not go astray in your government: comply only with the statutes of enlightened kings, keeping ease and desire within bounds. Only when you constantly fear violating or forgetting the enduring norms of institutions, rites, and cultural forms, and when thoughts of dissipated wandering and ruinous indulgence never arise, will this suffice.

By governing the people and observing the laws, one cultivates the constant Way. Yet if one takes no precautions against the unexpected, unforeseen troubles may exploit the opening. What then becomes of the state? Though you remain close within your courtyard, your concerns must reach the distant lands of the Man peoples. Keep chariots and horses in readiness, and make your plans comprehensive, thus warding off trouble before danger arises and preparing before events occur. Though your activities consist of the daily routine of sleeping and rising, your mind must attend to the contingency of war. Keep bows and arrows in good order, and let your deliberations reach far ahead, thus preserving order before disorder arises and avoiding mistakes when events confront you.

Places beyond the reach of your eyes and ears may conceal the seeds of disaster. Your thought must reach them, and your plans must ensure complete security. Thus, even in prosperity, there are those who keenly fear that the city wall may collapse back into its moat. In circumstances beyond what one anticipates…

text:
□□釁端之所起見之必預筭無遺策旣濟而
□衣袽之戒者有矣夫事有常變而慮無不周
備無不飭如此君國之道尚何以加之哉大抵
此二言者皆所以為修身齊家治國之道而下
文復以戒慎恐懼為言則又正心誠意之學而
武公及之斯固聖賢之徒歟况進德之功耄而
不倦則其生以文稱沒以武謚睿聖之德非獨
衛人思之三百篇之諷詠相與無窮噫武公國
君也而自修若此君天下者其知所鑒哉
===

…[?] where trouble originates, one must discern it beforehand and leave no measure out of one’s calculations. There are those who, even when all is accomplished, [?] heed the warning to keep cloth ready for caulking a leaking boat. Affairs have both regular courses and unexpected changes; if deliberation is so comprehensive and preparations so thoroughly put in order, what more could be added to the way of ruling a state? Broadly speaking, these two statements both concern the way of cultivating oneself, ordering one’s family, and governing one’s state. The text below speaks further of vigilance, caution, fear, and trembling: this is also the learning of rectifying the mind and making the intentions sincere. Duke Wu attained this; surely he belonged among the sages and worthies! Moreover, he worked tirelessly to advance his virtue even in extreme old age. Thus, during his lifetime he was acclaimed for his civil virtues, and after death he received the posthumous title Wu, “Martial.” His sagely wisdom was cherished not only by the people of Wei: through the recitation and singing of the Three Hundred Odes, it would be celebrated without end. Ah! Duke Wu was the ruler of a state, yet he cultivated himself in this manner. May those who rule all under Heaven recognize the example they should take from him!

“The Marquis of Cai and the Earl of Zheng met at Deng.” Second year of Duke Huan.

“In autumn, in the seventh month, on the first xin day, a great rain sacrifice was performed; on the last xin day, another rain sacrifice was performed.” Twenty-fifth year of Duke Zhao.

title: 正德八年應天府鄉試錄
text:
懼患而忘自强者春秋之所傷弭灾而忘自省
者春秋之所惡此蔡鄭于鄧之會魯昭再雩之
舉皆見譏於春秋也嘅夫楚自西周志存猾夏
周旣東遷始竊僭王肆强蠶食其來遠矣伊昔
殷武興師高宗獲旣平之緒采芑命將宣王收
來威之功修攘之效盖昭昭矣今三國之君懼
憑陵之勢兢業徒集於好會之時而不知天下
莫大於理循天理則無不勝憂懾弁形於禮文
之際而不知天下莫强於信義敦信義則無不
===
克如是荆楚雖大不足畏矣夫何計不出此顧
欲較勝負於地之大小决雌雄於力之强弱先
王脩攘之實果安在哉卒使好講未幾鄧先見
滅蔡亦被虜鄭雖王室之懿終蒙服役之耻楚
勢益張中夏陵遲而不振者非三國所自啓乎
春秋於鄧書會盖傷之也至若昭公嗣魯季氏
專國異呈於鸛鵒之來巢災仍於雲漢之爲虐
雨雹地震其變多矣伊昔祖己訓謀高宗消雉
雊之異側身脩行宣王回蘊隆之災感應之效
