懼患而忘自强者，《春秋》之所傷；弭灾而忘自省者，《春秋》之所惡。此蔡鄭于鄧之會、魯昭再雩之舉，皆見譏於《春秋》也。嘅夫楚自西周，志存猾夏；周旣東遷，始竊僭王，肆强蠶食，其來遠矣。伊昔《殷武》興師，高宗獲旣平之緒；《采芑》命將，宣王收來威之功。修攘之效，盖昭昭矣。今三國之君，懼憑陵之勢，兢業徒集於好會之時，而不知天下莫大於理，循天理則無不勝；憂懾弁形於禮文之際，而不知天下莫强於信義，敦信義則無不克。如是，荆楚雖大，不足畏矣。夫何計不出此，顧欲較勝負於地之大小，决雌雄於力之强弱？先王脩攘之實，果安在哉？卒使好講未幾，鄧先見滅，蔡亦被虜，鄭雖王室之懿，終蒙服役之耻。楚勢益張，中夏陵遲而不振者，非三國所自啓乎？《春秋》於鄧書會，盖傷之也。
至若昭公嗣魯，季氏專國，異呈於鸛鵒之來巢，災仍於雲漢之爲虐，雨雹地震，其變多矣。伊昔祖己訓謀，高宗消雉雊之異；側身脩行，宣王回蘊隆之災。感應之效，
translation_en:
Those who fear trouble yet forget to strengthen themselves are deplored by the Spring and Autumn Annals; those who seek to avert disasters yet forget to examine themselves are condemned by it. Thus the meeting of Cai and Zheng at Deng and Duke Zhao of Lu’s twice performing the rain sacrifice both receive censure in the Spring and Autumn Annals. Alas! Since the Western Zhou, Chu had harbored ambitions to disturb the central states. After the Zhou moved east, Chu began usurping the royal title. Its unchecked aggression and piecemeal encroachments had a long history. In former times, as recounted in “Martial Deeds of Yin,” Gaozong raised an army and achieved pacification; as recounted in “Gathering Millet,” King Xuan commissioned a commander and won the submission of his adversaries. The effects of cultivating strength within and repelling enemies without were surely plain. Now the rulers of the three states feared Chu’s overbearing power, yet their anxious diligence was exercised only at a meeting to cultivate friendly relations. They did not understand that nothing under Heaven is greater than principle, and that by following Heaven’s principle one can prevail in everything. Their fear and apprehension found expression [?] in ceremonial observances, yet they did not understand that nothing under Heaven is stronger than trustworthiness and righteousness, and that by earnestly practicing these one can overcome anything. Had they acted thus, Jing-Chu, though great, would not have been worth fearing. Why did their plans fail to follow this course? Why instead seek to determine victory and defeat by the size of territories, and supremacy by relative strength? Where, indeed, was the substance of the former kings’ practice of internal cultivation and external defense? In the end, before long had passed after their friendly discussions, Deng was the first to be destroyed, and the ruler of Cai was also taken captive. Although Zheng was closely related to the royal house, it ultimately suffered the humiliation of serving Chu. Chu’s power expanded ever further, while the central states declined and failed to recover. Was this not a consequence the three states themselves brought about? In recording the meeting at Deng, the Spring and Autumn Annals surely deplores this.
As for Duke Zhao’s succession in Lu, the Ji lineage monopolized the government. An anomaly appeared when birds described as guanyu [?] came to nest, and disasters followed as drought—the scourge described in “The Milky Way”—wrought havoc. Hailstorms and earthquakes: the aberrations were many indeed. In former times, Zu Ji offered admonition and counsel, and Gaozong dispelled the portent of the crowing pheasant. King Xuan humbled himself and cultivated his conduct, thereby reversing the disaster of oppressive heat. The efficacy of such acts in eliciting a response from Heaven …

title: 正德八年應天府鄉試錄
text:
美彰彰矣今七月之秋為再雩之舉盛樂徒設
於上辛之日而不知天不易勝人則可勝况忠
賢在位國有人耶大雩尋舉於季辛之日而不
知變不易消德則可消况敬畏咎巳天猶眷耶
如是災異雖頻有可禦矣夫何道不由此徒欲
焚巫尫於戲舞之餘而反身之不務黷祀典於
僭妄之末而自省之不知先王感召之誠又安
在哉卒使僭禮虛行天不魯應釋甲執冰終亡
儆戒之心不免遜齊之誚三家益強公室愈弱
===
而不競者非昭公所自致乎春秋大雩書再盖
譏之也吁三國畏人而不務其本昭公畏天而
徒事其末聖人立文示貶亦精且嚴哉大抵春
秋正名以謹華夷紀變以詳災異故于鄧書會
則知三國外制於荆楚夷狄盛而中國微矣再
書大雩則知魯昭内制於强臣人事乖而天道
悖矣嗚呼使當時諸侯舉能以仁自強應天以
實斯可以繼商周之志矣春秋豈復作乎
楚子入陳宣公十一年楚子圍鄭夏六月

美彰彰矣。今七月之秋，為再雩之舉，盛樂徒設於上辛之日，而不知天不易勝，人則可勝，况忠賢在位，國有人耶？大雩尋舉於季辛之日，而不知變不易消，德則可消，况敬畏咎巳，天猶眷耶？如是，災異雖頻，有可禦矣。夫何道不由此，徒欲焚巫尫於戲舞之餘，而反身之不務；黷祀典於僭妄之末，而自省之不知？先王感召之誠，又安在哉？卒使僭禮虛行，天不魯應，釋甲執冰，終亡儆戒之心，不免遜齊之誚，三家益強，公室愈弱而不競者，非昭公所自致乎？《春秋》大雩書再，盖譏之也。吁！三國畏人而不務其本，昭公畏天而徒事其末，聖人立文示貶，亦精且嚴哉！大抵《春秋》正名以謹華夷，紀變以詳災異，故于鄧書會，則知三國外制於荆楚，夷狄盛而中國微矣；再書大雩，則知魯昭内制於强臣，人事乖而天道悖矣。嗚呼！使當時諸侯舉能以仁自強，應天以實，斯可以繼商周之志矣，《春秋》豈復作乎？

楚子入陳，宣公十一年。楚子圍鄭，夏六月。
translation_en:
…the excellence of these effects was plainly manifest. Yet now, in autumn, in the seventh month, the rain sacrifice was performed twice. Elaborate music was vainly presented on the first xin day, without recognizing that although Heaven cannot readily be prevailed upon, human failings can be overcome. How much more so when loyal and worthy men hold office and the state has capable servants! The great rain sacrifice was then performed on the last xin day, without recognizing that although anomalous portents cannot readily be dispelled, virtue can dispel them. How much more so when one is reverent and fearful, blames oneself, and still enjoys Heaven’s regard! With such conduct, even frequent calamities and anomalies could be averted. Why, then, was this way not followed? Instead, he merely wished to burn shamans and the infirm after the ritual dances, without attending to the examination of his own conduct; he profaned the sacrificial ordinances through presumptuous observances, without knowing to examine himself. Where, then, was the sincerity with which the former kings elicited Heaven’s response? In the end, these usurped rites were performed in vain, and Heaven did not respond to Lu [?]. He removed his armor and held ice, yet ultimately lacked any disposition to heed warnings. He could not escape the reproach of having fled to Qi. The three great lineages grew ever stronger, while the ducal house became ever weaker and unable to contend with them. Was this not something Duke Zhao brought upon himself? The Spring and Autumn Annals records the great rain sacrifice as occurring twice: this expresses censure.

Alas! The three states feared other men but neglected the fundamentals; Duke Zhao feared Heaven but concerned himself only with outward observances. How discerning and rigorous was the Sage in framing his text to convey condemnation! In general, the Spring and Autumn Annals rectifies names to maintain carefully the distinction between the Chinese and the non-Chinese, and records unusual occurrences to give a full account of calamities and anomalies. Thus, its recording of the meeting at Deng shows that the three states were subject externally to Jing-Chu: the non-Chinese powers flourished while the central states declined. Its twice recording the great rain sacrifice shows that Duke Zhao of Lu was subject internally to powerful ministers: human affairs were disordered, and Heaven’s course ran contrary to expectations. Alas! Had all the feudal lords of that time been able to strengthen themselves through benevolence and respond to Heaven through substantive conduct, they could have carried on the aspirations of Shang and Zhou. Would the Spring and Autumn Annals then have needed to be written?

宜錄出
===

當心服
考試官右諭德倫批辭健意足僅見此篇
春秋於霸臣用兵而兩失其道者可責用兵而
兩得其道者可予蓋用兵之要惟觀釁制屬而
已今林父昧之以取敗書罃用之而克濟春秋
予奪宜矣且夫春秋中葉楚莊竊霸陳鄭受兵

…On the yimao day, Xun Linfu of Jin led an army into battle against the Viscount of Chu at Bi. The army of Jin suffered a crushing defeat. 〔Both entries are from the twelfth year of Duke Xuan.〕 Luan Shu of Jin led an army to relieve Zheng. 〔The sixth year of Duke Cheng.〕 In summer, in the fifth month, on the jiawu day, they thereupon destroyed Biyang. 〔The tenth year of Duke Xiang.〕
Gu Que 顧礐
Comment by Associate Examiner Li, an Instructor: The underlying commentary makes perfectly clear the principle of observing vulnerabilities and controlling subordinates, yet writers very often confuse it. In discussing the battle at Bi, they occasionally manage to articulate it; but concerning the relief of Zheng and the affair of Biyang, they merely force an explanation in terms of advancing and withdrawing. This essay weaves together the commentary’s text and develops its meaning almost exhaustively. It therefore merits inclusion.
Comment by Examiner Jia, Left Companion to the Heir Apparent: In its assessment of successes and failures in the use of troops, even if the three men were brought back to life, they would surely be convinced at heart.
Comment by Examiner Lun, Right Mentor of the Heir Apparent: Vigorous language and fully developed ideas: this essay alone displays them.
In the Spring and Autumn Annals, ministers serving hegemonic rulers who fail in both principles of warfare deserve censure, while those who succeed in both deserve approval. For the essentials of warfare are simply to observe vulnerabilities and control one’s subordinates. Linfu was blind to these principles and brought defeat upon himself; Shu and Ying applied them and succeeded. The approval and condemnation expressed in the Spring and Autumn Annals are fitting indeed.
Now, midway through the Spring and Autumn period, King Zhuang of Chu usurped the hegemony, and Chen and Zheng came under attack. At that time Duke Jing of Jin held the hegemony. Linfu went to relieve Zheng and engaged the enemy at Bi. Why does the Spring and Autumn Annals absolve Chu and lay the blame exclusively upon Jin? Because in warfare one must first observe vulnerabilities; in resisting an enemy, especially…

title: 正德八年應天府鄉試錄
text:
□於制屬今楚討賊滅陳而尋復封陳恃强入
鄭而旋即平鄭是楚人理直不可敵也三帥及
河而定計欲還先穀逞忿而違命先濟此副屬
輕逞所當誅也使林父苟能獨斷於衷諸帥信
然其策不遷戮而班師按軍法而行辟夫豈不
可奈何惑於分惡竟亦蹈危賞令一聞遂掬舟
中之指三軍半踣大勦奕世之民喪師僨事於
誰責乎故春秋以晉主此戰而獨罪林父者以
此迨夫成襄嗣世楚再伐鄭偪陽附强於時景
悼命將欒書救鄭罃下偪陽春秋何爲深許書
罃之用兵耶盖長於料敵者見可而進善於戰
陣者御下必嚴今晉軍繞角楚人已退移師侵
蔡桑隧復來是晉師遷戮不可逞也許滅偪陽
恐違亂命功成旦夕遽請班師是荀偃逗遛所
當罪也使書罃稍蓄狐疑於心必失兵機之會
乃從三帥而旋師尅期七日而必取事適其可
夫復何疑於時利害甚明左右惟命全師以退
欲戰之帥不敢過投机奮怒荀偃親督而成功

乃從三帥而旋師剋期七日而必取事適其可
夫復何疑於時利害甚明左右惟命全師以退
欲戰之帥不敢遏投机奮怒匄偃親督而成功
punctuated: □於制屬。今楚討賊滅陳，而尋復封陳；恃强入鄭，而旋即平鄭，是楚人理直不可敵也。三帥及河，而定計欲還，先穀逞忿而違命先濟，此副屬輕逞所當誅也。使林父苟能獨斷於衷，諸帥信然其策，不遷戮而班師，按軍法而行辟，夫豈不可？奈何惑於分惡，竟亦蹈危！賞令一聞，遂掬舟中之指；三軍半踣，大勦奕世之民。喪師僨事，於誰責乎？故春秋以晉主此戰，而獨罪林父者，以此。迨夫成襄嗣世，楚再伐鄭，偪陽附强，於時景悼命將，欒書救鄭，罃下偪陽，春秋何爲深許書罃之用兵耶？盖長於料敵者，見可而進；善於戰陣者，御下必嚴。今晉軍繞角，楚人已退，移師侵蔡，桑隧復來，是晉師遷戮不可逞也。許滅偪陽，恐違亂命，功成旦夕，遽請班師，是荀偃逗遛所當罪也。使書罃稍蓄狐疑於心，必失兵機之會。乃從三帥而旋師，尅期七日而必取，事適其可，夫復何疑？於時利害甚明，左右惟命，全師以退，欲戰之帥不敢過；投机奮怒，荀偃親督而成功。
translation_en:
…[illegible] in controlling subordinates. Chu had punished a rebel and extinguished Chen, but soon restored Chen’s ruling house; it had relied on its strength to enter Zheng, but promptly made peace with Zheng. Thus the men of Chu had right on their side and could not be opposed. When the three commanders reached the river, they resolved to return, but Xian Gu [?], indulging his anger, disobeyed orders and crossed first. Such reckless conduct by a subordinate commander deserved execution. Had Linfu exercised independent judgment, with the commanders endorsing his plan, withdrawn his army without directing punishment elsewhere, and imposed the death penalty according to military law, would that not have been acceptable? Why, misled by the notion of sharing the blame, did he himself plunge into danger? Once the order offering rewards was heard, severed fingers could be gathered by the handful inside the boats. Half the army fell, and people whose families had served for generations were slaughtered in great numbers. Who should bear responsibility for losing the army and ruining the undertaking? This is why the Spring and Autumn Annals makes Jin the instigator of this battle and assigns blame to Linfu alone.

When the reigns of Dukes Cheng and Xiang followed, Chu again attacked Zheng, while Biyang attached itself to a powerful state. At that time, Dukes Jing and Dao appointed commanders: Luan Shu relieved Zheng, and Ying captured Biyang. Why does the Spring and Autumn Annals so strongly approve of Shu’s and Ying’s use of troops? Those skilled at assessing the enemy advance when they see an opportunity; those skilled in warfare necessarily exercise strict control over their subordinates. When the Jin army was at Raojiao, the men of Chu had already withdrawn. Jin then moved its army to invade Cai, but Chu returned at Sangsui. Thus the Jin army could not recklessly pursue this transfer of punishment to another state. Having undertaken to destroy Biyang, they feared disobeying an ill-considered command [?]; yet, when success was only a day away, they suddenly requested withdrawal. Xun Yan deserved punishment for such delay. Had Shu and Ying harbored even a little hesitation, they would certainly have missed the opportune moment for military action. Instead, one followed the three commanders’ advice and withdrew; the other set a deadline of seven days and insisted upon taking the city. Each action suited its circumstances: what further doubt could there be? The advantages and dangers were then entirely clear, and those around them obeyed their commands. The army withdrew intact, and the commanders eager for battle dared not overstep their orders. A stool was flung down in fury, and Xun Yan personally supervised the troops and achieved success…

title: 正德八年應天府鄉試錄
text:
□師有紀不亦偉歟故春秋於此書欒書救鄭
□滅偪陽者以此大抵克敵制勝固在乎兵兵
之進退惟繫乎將用將賢否尤繫乎君也林父
非不賢也使剛愎不仁者參焉是景公任將之
不專也書罃亦豈賢於林父哉景悼特任之專
耳故有全師取地之效夫用將之專否成敗有
如是後之命將者觀諸

===

translation_en:
…□ [?] the army maintained discipline: was this not magnificent? This is why the Spring and Autumn Annals here records Luan Shu’s relief of Zheng and □’s destruction of Biyang [?]. In general, defeating the enemy and securing victory certainly depend upon the troops; but their advance and retreat depend entirely upon the commander, and whether worthy commanders are employed depends still more upon the ruler. Linfu was by no means unworthy. By having a headstrong and inhumane man share his command, Duke Jing failed to entrust his commander with undivided authority. Were Shu and Ying really worthier than Linfu? Dukes Jing and Dao merely entrusted them with undivided authority; hence they succeeded in preserving their armies and taking territory. Such are the consequences for success and failure of granting or withholding undivided command. Let those who appoint commanders in later ages consider this!

Record of Rites
“Order the Grand Music Master to present poems, in order to observe the customs of the people.”

Cheng Dan

Comment by Associate Examiner Chen, School Instructor: “What is produced by the ruler’s transforming influence is called ‘custom.’ When the former kings made their inspection tours and observed customs, their purpose was precisely to examine the successes and failures of the regional lords’ governmental commands and accordingly to encourage or chastise them. Most candidates in the examination hall failed to understand this. Some discussed only the inspection tour to the east, an especially narrow interpretation. This composition is precise and judicious in its examination of textual evidence, and its writing is powerful and profound. It has therefore been selected for inclusion.”

Comment by Examiner Jia, Left Mentor: “It elucidates the former kings’ purpose in examining governance thoroughly and exhaustively, and may serve as a model.”

Comment by Examiner Lun, Right Adviser: “Inspecting the regions and observing the people were means of examining oneself. This essay grasps that point.”

When the former kings made their inspection tours, they ordered the people’s words to be recounted, thereby examining the ruler’s transforming influence. For the ruler’s transforming influence is embodied in the people’s customs, and the embodiment of customs in words has a long history.

title: 正德八年應天府鄉試錄
text:
非命官述而觀之抑何所知哉記王制者之意
以爲昔我先王建萬國親諸侯當五年之期舉
巡守之禮豈不以民習之繫於一國者為風民
言之形於一時者為詩欲觀其風必陳其詩是
詩也雖曰閭里童稚之言而上之所感者深雖
曰民俗歌謠之詞而化之所被者遠是以因所
歷之地命大師之官采而錄之如春之東夏之
南凡東南之所詠者自閨門以及鄉黨言有是
非悉陳於岱衡之下不以鄙俚而或遺焉秋之
===
西冬之北凡西北之所歌者自國都以及閭巷
言有邪正舉列於華恒之間不以俗陋而或隱
焉夫民言之所在即民風之所在盖志形於言
者有是非則風之正變關焉故即岱衡所陳者
而觀則東南之民風可知而政令得失亦因以
覘而為黜陟之地矣民詩之所存即民俗之所
存盖志發於詩者有邪正則俗之美惡寓焉故
即華恒所述者而觀則西北之民俗可知而政
令善否亦因以考而為慶讓之所矣夫風以化

punctuated:
非命官述而觀之，抑何所知哉？記《王制》者之意，以爲昔我先王建萬國，親諸侯，當五年之期，舉巡守之禮，豈不以民習之繫於一國者為風，民言之形於一時者為詩？欲觀其風，必陳其詩。是詩也，雖曰閭里童稚之言，而上之所感者深；雖曰民俗歌謠之詞，而化之所被者遠。是以因所歷之地，命大師之官采而錄之。如春之東，夏之南，凡東南之所詠者，自閨門以及鄉黨，言有是非，悉陳於岱衡之下，不以鄙俚而或遺焉；秋之西，冬之北，凡西北之所歌者，自國都以及閭巷，言有邪正，舉列於華恒之間，不以俗陋而或隱焉。
夫民言之所在，即民風之所在。盖志形於言者有是非，則風之正變關焉。故即岱衡所陳者而觀，則東南之民風可知，而政令得失亦因以覘，而為黜陟之地矣。民詩之所存，即民俗之所存。盖志發於詩者有邪正，則俗之美惡寓焉。故即華恒所述者而觀，則西北之民俗可知，而政令善否亦因以考，而為慶讓之所矣。夫風以化
translation_en:
…Unless officials were commanded to recount these words so that he could examine them, how could he know? The intention of those who recorded the Royal Regulations was this: formerly, our ancient kings established the myriad states and maintained close relations with the feudal lords. At five-year intervals they performed the rites of inspection tours. Was this not because the people's habits, as attached to a particular state, constitute its customs, while their words, as expressed at a particular time, constitute its poetry? To examine their customs, one must have their poems presented. Although these poems are said to be the words of children in the village lanes, the influence exerted upon them by those above is profound; although they are said to be the lyrics of popular songs, the transforming influence they receive reaches far. Thus, wherever the king traveled, he commanded the Grand Music Master to collect and record them. When he went east in spring and south in summer, everything sung in the east and south, from the inner chambers to the local communities, whether its words were right or wrong, was presented at the foot of Mount Dai and Mount Heng. Nothing was omitted because it was rustic or vulgar. When he went west in autumn and north in winter, everything sung in the west and north, from the capitals of the states to the village lanes, whether its words were wayward or upright, was laid out before him at Mount Hua and the northern Mount Heng. Nothing was concealed because it was crude or uncouth.
Where the people's words are found, there too are their customs. For intentions expressed in words may be right or wrong, and upon this depends whether customs retain their proper character or depart from it. Thus, by examining what was presented at Mount Dai and Mount Heng, the king could know the customs of the people in the east and south. Through these he could also discern the successes and failures of governmental commands, providing a basis for demotion and promotion. Where the people's poems survive, there too do their customary practices survive. For intentions expressed in poetry may be wayward or upright, and in these reside the good and bad qualities of customary practices. Thus, by examining what was recounted at Mount Hua and the northern Mount Heng, the king could know the customary practices of the people in the west and north. As for the poems of the feudal lords, these too had to be collected and presented to the sovereign. They likewise came under the charge of the music officials, to be preserved and rehearsed at the proper times. This was the origin of the institution of observing popular customs. In later ages, the rites of inspection tours were abandoned, and officials charged with collecting poems were no longer appointed. Fortunately, the practice of reporting on the discharge of one’s duties alone survived, still preserving the former kings’ intention of examining the quality of government. title: 正德八年應天府鄉試錄
text:
樂莫逾於古也君子於旣作之終而語之其道
曷有旣乎昔子夏因魏文侯厭古樂而好鄭衛
之音告之盖謂君之厭古樂者以其無可好之
音耳孰知古樂之中有可言之道乎是故君子
之於古樂方其未作之先固無得而語之也迨
其正作之際亦無暇而語之也八音旣闋矣得
之於心者自不能不形於言萬舞旣畢矣會之
於神者自不容不宣於聲不曰進旅退旅則曰
和正以廣與夫會守拊鼓皆亹亹於議論焉不
曰始奏以文則曰復亂以武與夫治亂訊疾皆
諄諄於答述焉所以語者豈有他哉誠以古樂
之正初非鄭音好濫淫志之可倫也亦非衛音
趨數煩志之可擬也肅乎其敬有雍乎其和者
在味之而有無窮之趣本之以仁有制之以義
者存究之而有益深之蘊修身以之齊家以之
君子心得其道焉得不於樂終而道之邪治國
以之平天下以之君子神會其妙惡得不於樂
終而論之邪是則古樂之中有可言之道如此

punctuated: 樂莫逾於古也！君子於旣作之終而語之，其道曷有旣乎？昔子夏因魏文侯厭古樂而好鄭衛之音，告之，盖謂君之厭古樂者，以其無可好之音耳，孰知古樂之中有可言之道乎？是故君子之於古樂，方其未作之先，固無得而語之也；迨其正作之際，亦無暇而語之也。八音旣闋矣，得之於心者，自不能不形於言；萬舞旣畢矣，會之於神者，自不容不宣於聲。不曰進旅退旅，則曰和正以廣，與夫會守拊鼓，皆亹亹於議論焉；不曰始奏以文，則曰復亂以武，與夫治亂訊疾，皆諄諄於答述焉。所以語者，豈有他哉？誠以古樂之正，初非鄭音好濫淫志之可倫也，亦非衛音趨數煩志之可擬也。肅乎其敬，有雍乎其和者在，味之而有無窮之趣；本之以仁，有制之以義者存，究之而有益深之蘊。修身以之，齊家以之，君子心得其道，焉得不於樂終而道之邪？治國以之，平天下以之，君子神會其妙，惡得不於樂終而論之邪？是則古樂之中有可言之道如此。
translation_en:
…in music, nothing surpasses the ancient! When the gentleman speaks of it after the performance has ended, how could the principles he discusses ever be exhausted? Formerly, because Marquis Wen of Wei disliked ancient music and preferred the sounds of Zheng and Wei, Zixia instructed him. His meaning was surely this: you dislike ancient music merely because it offers no sounds that please you; yet who recognizes that ancient music contains principles worthy of discussion?

Thus, before ancient music has begun, the gentleman has nothing yet to discuss; while it is being performed, he has no leisure to discuss it. Once the eight classes of instruments have fallen silent, what he has grasped in his heart cannot but take shape in words. Once the wan dance has ended, what he has apprehended in spirit cannot but find expression in speech. He speaks either of advancing and retreating together, or of harmony, correctness, and breadth; and concerning the ensemble’s awaiting the cue of the struck drum, too, his discussion is tireless. He speaks either of beginning the performance with the civil dance, or of concluding it with the martial dance; and concerning the ordering of the concluding passage and its swift execution [?], too, his explanations are earnest and sustained.

Could there be any other reason for such discussion? Truly, the correctness of ancient music cannot be compared with the sounds of Zheng, which delight in excess and debauch the will, nor with the sounds of Wei, whose hurried rhythms agitate the will. Within its solemn reverence resides a gracious harmony: savor it, and its delights are inexhaustible. Grounded in benevolence, it also contains the restraints of righteousness: investigate it, and its significance grows ever deeper. Through it one cultivates oneself; through it one orders one’s family. When the gentleman has grasped its principles in his heart, how could he fail to speak of them when the music ends? Through it one governs the state; through it one brings peace to all under Heaven. When the gentleman has apprehended its subtleties in spirit, how could he fail to discuss them when the music ends? Such, then, are the principles within ancient music that are worthy of discussion.

translation_en:
…to the reigning sovereign, it could serve as a rule for preserving what has been achieved.

Examiner Lun, Right Mentor, comments: Bold and unrestrained, freely flowing, with striking variations emerging in quick succession—here indeed is a hand skilled in writing discourses! An excellent scholar! An excellent scholar!

Those who inherit a great undertaking should reflect on the difficulty of its accomplishment and fully carry out the way of preserving it. A great undertaking is not easily accomplished, nor is it easily preserved. If one does not understand how to reflect upon the difficulty of accomplishing it, one will surely regard its preservation as easy rather than difficult. If one regards its preservation as easy, failing to recognize its difficulty, reverence and awe will slacken daily, and indulgence in ease and pleasure will know no end. Though an undertaking has been accomplished, one dare not speak of it [?]; how could one be capable of preserving it? Only by recognizing the greatness of the undertaking—that it was not accomplished suddenly, and that accomplishing it was difficult—does one understand that inheriting it requires more than merely holding on to it, and that preserving it is not easy. With anxious vigilance, one fully follows its proper way, daring not depart from it; cultivates one’s virtue, daring not indulge in ease; and maintains its laws, daring not let them lapse. This is how lasting peace and enduring order are secured, and how one ultimately enjoys boundless tranquility. Such are the words of Sima, Duke Wenzheng: truly an enduring mirror for all who inherit great undertakings through the ages! Let me attempt to discuss this.

Where nothing has been done by predecessors sufficient to transmit to posterity, one cannot speak of an undertaking; where nothing is done by successors sufficient to carry on what their predecessors began, one cannot speak of preservation. To establish what is to be established: all efforts to bequeath a line of succession and devise plans for providing for grandsons and bringing peace to sons constitute an undertaking. title: 正德八年應天府鄉試錄
text:
為繼志述事之舉者皆守也夫業無所成
固難於責守業成而不知所以守之者抑
人何耶况太平之業業之大也開之有自
致之有道成之非一人積之非一日君人
者惟不知創之之難則曰自我受之自我
由之而已守將何哉不知守之之難則曰
自我有之自我為之而已守復何哉謂天
下一家也中國一人也作威作福惟辟而
已誰敢侮予不惟不庸守而亦不必守矣
===
萬方一統也萬姓一心也有罪無罪惟我
而已誰敢遏予不惟不必守而亦不假守
矣謂逸欲為無傷而宴安之氣勝謂奢泰
為無害而儆戒之志微謂太平何時也以
三光則得其明以四時則得其序以五辰
則得其正以庶類則得其所是業也確乎
泰山之安夫焉慮乎以九州則得其貢以
四海則得其心以九夷則得其賓以八蠻
則得其臣是業也巍然磐石之固夫何虞

translation_en: …all undertakings that carry on a predecessor’s intentions and continue his works constitute preservation. When an enduring achievement has not been established, it is certainly difficult to demand its preservation. But when it has been established and someone does not know how to preserve it, what sort of person is he [?]? Moreover, the achievement of Great Peace is the greatest of achievements. Its foundation has a source, and its attainment has a way. It is accomplished by more than one person and accumulated over more than a single day. A ruler who does not understand the difficulty of founding it says, “I have inherited it; I shall simply do as I please with it.” What preservation can there then be? If he does not understand the difficulty of preserving it, he says, “I possess it; I shall simply act as I please.” Again, what preservation can there be? He thinks: “All under Heaven is one household, and the Central States are as one person. The dispensation of punishments and blessings belongs to the sovereign alone. Who dares slight me?” He considers preservation not merely unnecessary, but something he need not undertake at all. “The myriad regions are united under one rule, and the myriad families are of one mind. Guilt or innocence rests with me alone. Who dares thwart me?” He considers preservation not merely unnecessary, but something he has no need to resort to. He regards indulgence in ease and desire as harmless, and a spirit of complacent comfort prevails; he regards extravagance as innocuous, and his resolve to remain vigilant weakens. He asks: “What sort of age is this age of Great Peace? The three luminaries have their proper brilliance; the four seasons have their proper sequence; the five planets have their proper courses; and the myriad kinds of beings have their proper places. This achievement is as secure as Mount Tai. What is there to worry about? From the Nine Provinces I receive their tribute; from all within the Four Seas I gain their allegiance; from the Nine Yi peoples I receive submission as guests, and from the Eight Man peoples submission as subjects. This achievement stands lofty and firm as a massive rock. What is there to fear…”

title: 正德八年應天府鄉試錄
text:
乎殊不知可樂者莫如太平而可慮者亦
莫如太平無虞者莫如太平而可虞者亦
莫如太平一日不謹或以貽四海之憂一
念不謹或以致千百年之患彼般樂之易
於荒珍竒之易於侈蠹太平之業者莫甚
焉我其除之聲色之易於惑貨利之易於
溺戕太平之業者莫大焉我其杜之甘言
之來夫諛泛恩之啓夫僭摧太平之業者
又孰甚耶我其抑之故嗜慾之必節好尚
===

之必謹一念之萌罔有弗欽不如是恐蠹

一心之動罔有弗敬不如是恐戕吾太平
之業也聽納之必審勸懲之必嚴一政之

世已治矣洞屬之心視若未治治已成矣
戰慄之心視若未成念創造之難必曰開
之者誰歟而敢易耶天命之奉盖不敢不
謹也懼嗣守之難必曰成之者誰歟而敢

translation_en:
… be feared? Yet one utterly fails to realize that nothing affords greater joy than peace, and nothing gives greater cause for concern than peace; nothing is freer from anxiety than peace, and nothing gives greater grounds for apprehension than peace. A single day’s lack of care may leave all within the Four Seas in distress; a single careless thought may bring calamity lasting hundreds or thousands of years. Indulgence in pleasure readily leads to dissipation, and rare treasures readily lead to extravagance. Nothing more grievously eats away at the foundations of peace: I must eliminate these things. Music and sensual beauty readily beguile, and wealth and profit readily engulf. Nothing more seriously injures the foundations of peace: I must bar these things. Sweet words invite flattery, and indiscriminate favors open the way to usurpation of rank. What could more grievously undermine the foundations of peace? I must restrain these things.
Thus appetites and desires must be moderated, and tastes and preferences carefully guarded. No budding thought may be treated without reverent care; otherwise, I fear that it will eat away at the foundations of our peace. Joy and anger must be measured, and love and hatred properly directed. No stirring of the heart may be treated without reverence; otherwise, I fear that it will injure the foundations of our peace. Advice must be carefully weighed before it is accepted, and rewards and punishments must be rigorously administered. No measure of government may be enacted without earnest care; otherwise, I fear that it will undermine the foundations of our peace.
Though the world is already well governed, with a vigilant heart [?] one must regard it as still ungoverned. Though good government has already been achieved, with a trembling heart one must regard it as still unachieved. Reflecting on the difficulty of founding the realm, one must ask: “Who was it who first established it? How could I dare treat it lightly?” Thus, in upholding Heaven’s Mandate, one surely dares not be anything but circumspect. Fearing the difficulty of preserving what one has inherited, one must ask: “Who was it who brought it to completion? How could I dare…”

title: 正德八年應天府鄉試錄
text:
忽耶天討之行盖不敢不恭也守誠難矣
獨不觀諸巨室乎前人遺之將為無窮之
規必植其堂基壯其柱石強其棟梁厚其
茨盖高其垣墉嚴其關鍵既成而復得人
以守之日省月視欹者正之敝者補之危
者持之顛者扶之如是則亘千百年而無
壞矣守太平者寧異是耶民者國之堂基
也我其植之禮法者柱石也我其壯之所
以奠吾太平之業也公卿者棟梁也我其
===
強之官吏者茨盖也我其厚之所以輔吾
太平之業也將帥者垣墉也我其高之甲
兵者關鍵也我其嚴之所以衛吾太平之
業也由是天下一家推之則準中國一人
動之則化萬方一統無分崩也萬姓一心
無離貳也天位乎上天道以之而清也地
位乎下地道以之而寧也萬物位乎中萬
物以之而育也三光明四時序五辰正庶
類蕃九州貢四海服九夷賓八蠻臣諸福

translation_en:
…neglect it? In carrying out Heaven’s punishments, one surely dares not fail to act reverently. Preservation is indeed difficult! Have you not considered a great house? When predecessors bequeath it, intending to provide for an endless future, they must firmly establish its foundations, strengthen its pillars and their stone bases, reinforce its ridgepole and beams, thicken its thatch, raise its enclosing walls, and secure its gates and bolts. Once it is completed, if they also find someone to preserve it, inspecting it daily and examining it monthly, straightening whatever leans, repairing whatever is worn, supporting whatever is endangered, and propping up whatever is falling, then it can endure for hundreds and thousands of years without ruin. How could preserving Great Peace be any different?

The people are the foundations of the state: let us establish them firmly. Ritual and law are its pillars and stone bases: let us strengthen them. These are the means of securing the foundations of our achievement of Great Peace. The dukes and ministers are its ridgepole and beams: let us reinforce them. Officials and clerks are its thatch: let us make it substantial. These are the means of sustaining our achievement of Great Peace. Generals and commanders are its enclosing walls: let us raise them high. Armor and weapons are its gates and bolts: let us secure them. These are the means of defending our achievement of Great Peace.

Thus all under Heaven becomes one family: extend these principles, and they serve as the standard. The central realm becomes one person: set it in motion, and transformation follows. The myriad regions are united under one rule, without fragmentation or collapse; the myriad families share one heart, without estrangement or divided allegiance. Heaven occupies its place above, and through this the Way of Heaven becomes clear. Earth occupies its place below, and through this the Way of Earth becomes tranquil. The myriad things occupy their places between, and through this they are nourished. The three luminaries shine brightly; the four seasons follow their proper sequence; the five planets keep their proper courses; all kinds of beings flourish. The Nine Provinces offer tribute; the Four Seas submit; the Nine Yi come as guests; the Eight Man acknowledge themselves as subjects; all the blessings…

title: 正德八年應天府鄉試錄
text:
之物可致之祥駢臻畢備史不絶書而混
一靈長之統保合太和之治將衍之萬世
而無斁矣如此而曰守太平之業信乎其
能守矣抑稽諸古太平之盛莫如帝王若
堯之萬邦協和舜之四方風動禹之黎民
敏德湯之兆民允殖文武之天下咸和四
海永清皆是業也致之未必無本而守之
亦未必無要遡而求之放勳之言方形於
書而精一之心法已見於授受之際而為
===
帝舜之兢兢重華之語方播為典而執中
之正統已見於咨爾之時而為大禹之孜
孜建中之德既肇有商之業而說命伊訓
之書又懇懇乎交陳文武之德既成有周
之業而七月無逸之篇又諄諄乎夾輔萬
世之下誦二帝之功想三王之治康衢之
謠擊壤之歌四百載之曆六百禩之統八
百年之籙卒為有道之長者雖皆德盛而
元勳佐命之功亦不可誣也下迨漢唐宋

translation_en:
…auspicious objects and portents that could be brought forth would arrive together in their full array, and historians would record them without cease. The unified and enduring imperial succession, and the government that preserves and harmonizes supreme concord, would extend through ten thousand generations without failing. If this is called preserving the achievement of Great Peace, then truly it can be preserved!

Yet, examining antiquity, no flourishing of Great Peace equaled that under the sage emperors and kings. Yao brought the myriad states into concord; Shun moved the four quarters as the wind moves things; under Yu, the common people diligently pursued virtue; under Tang, the multitudes truly prospered; and under Wen and Wu, all under Heaven were harmonious and the four seas forever tranquil. These were all instances of this achievement. Bringing it about surely had its foundation, and preserving it surely had its essentials.

Tracing these back to their source, just as the words concerning Yao’s “far-reaching achievement” took form in the Documents, the teaching of the mind—refinement and single-mindedness—was already manifest when sovereignty was transmitted and received, becoming Emperor Shun’s vigilant reverence. Just as the account of Shun’s “successive brilliance” was being disseminated as a canon, the orthodox succession of holding fast to the mean was already manifest in the address “Oh, you,” becoming the Great Yu’s unremitting diligence. The virtue of establishing the mean had founded the enterprise of Shang, while the writings “The Charge to Yue” and “The Instructions of Yi” further set forth earnest counsels in concert. The virtue of Wen and Wu had established the enterprise of Zhou, while the chapters “The Seventh Month” and “Against Luxurious Ease” further sustained it with repeated admonitions.

Ten thousand generations later, we recite the achievements of the Two Emperors and contemplate the government of the Three Kings: the rhyme of the broad thoroughfare, the song of striking the ground, the four-hundred-year span, the six-hundred-year succession, and the eight-hundred-year mandate. translation_en:
…their rulers’ virtue was not entirely pure, and the means by which they established an age of great peace were not wholly good. Neither the rulers who succeeded them nor the ministers who assisted them could fully match those of the age of the ancient emperors and kings. Thus, what they maintained remained open to criticism, and there were reasons why they ultimately fell short of antiquity. We reverently reflect that our ancestral sovereigns, sage succeeding sage, founded our magnificent enterprise. The ministers who assisted them likewise pledged their hearts and joined their efforts to help bring about great peace. Their sage sons and divine grandsons have all shared one virtue, setting their hearts on emulating their ancestors, employing the worthy, revering Heaven, and diligently caring for the people. This is how the enterprise of great peace has been continued down to the present day, matching the flourishing rule of the emperors and kings of remote antiquity. How fortunate I, in my humble capacity, am to witness it in person!

Memorial

A memorial in the voice of Wei Zheng, Director of the Palace Library under the Tang, presenting Essentials of Governance from Collected Books (Qunshu liyao), in the fifth year of Zhenguan [631].
By Tang Gao.

Comment by Associate Examiner Li, Instructor: “It is not difficult to compose a piece in parallel prose; the difficulty lies in encompassing the essential concerns of the time. This piece recounts matters fully and amply, employs elegant and proper diction, and conveys loyal and earnest intentions. If Wenzhen [Wei Zheng] could return to life, he too would surely nod his approval. It should be recorded as a model.”

Comment by Examiner Jia, Left Mentor: “Elegant, ample, and well ordered: it fully demonstrates the writer’s learning and discernment.”

On the twenty-seventh day of the ninth month of the fifth year of Zhenguan, your servant Wei Zheng, Director of the Palace Library, and his colleagues respectfully submit the Essentials of Governance from the Collected Books that we have compiled. With utmost fear and trepidation, we bow our heads to the ground and repeatedly kowtow, addressing the throne as follows:
We humbly consider that grandly welcoming Shang’s blessings meant fulfilling the instruction to acquire extensive knowledge; diligently magnifying martial achievements meant seeking out the text of the Great Plan. The ruler who called himself “your sire” inquired into the learning of earlier times and commanded the compilation of the New Discourses; in the Yuankang era, inquiries were made into the Great Way, and an imperial edict was broadly issued. Expounding the Classics without feeling weariness helped accomplish the great enterprise of dynastic restoration; “What can increase divine wisdom?” became a celebrated saying without equal through the ages. Thus, a ruler who wishes to accomplish great things must diligently study antiquity in governing.
We reverently reflect that Your Majesty—

—is discerning and magnanimous, divinely martial and sagely in civil accomplishments. Responding to Heaven and following the people’s wishes, you took over the isolated Sui and swept away the bands of rebels in scarcely more than six years. title: 正德八年應天府鄉試錄
text:
家躊駁欲强探力取懼勞而少功将周覧
泛觀柰博而寡要爰
命臣等採摭諸書凡子民君國之議言精粗
備錄參諸子而本六經若濟世康時之故
實優劣兼收訖晉年而原五帝棄華掇實
肯抽鸞鳳之羽毛舉要刪繁詎截象犀之
牙角馳雲車於文苑轍迹可尋張天網於
書林綱目自舉有倫有緒越公理之昌言
不矯不偏陋子真之政論經時裒次五帙
===
彙成邈乎數千載治忽之端派分鱗萃富
矣億萬言聖賢之蘊星麗河明豈俟收籍
關中乃悉秦亡之故奚庸觀典魯國始知
周道之興盖生人育物之良劑而濟理致
平之令典也念禹俞益賛矧帝拜陶歌陳
述雖職於臣鄰允迪類存乎元首悅而知
繹但從寬問一篇此自足用泛矣無歸徒
使俊陳三易多亦奚為伏願
游心於濩濩之常

translation_en:
…the various schools are confused and contradictory [?]. To probe them forcibly and wrest out their meaning would risk much labor for little gain; to survey them comprehensively and read them widely would yield breadth but few essentials. Thus Your Majesty commanded us, your servants, to gather selections from the books. All discussions of nurturing the people and governing the state, whether refined or coarse, were to be recorded, consulting the various masters while taking the Six Classics as the foundation. Historical precedents for aiding the world and bringing peace to the age were to include both superior and inferior examples, extending down to the Jin and tracing their origins back to the Five Emperors.

Discarding ornament and gathering substance, would we willingly pluck away the feathers of the luan and phoenix? Selecting essentials and cutting excessive detail, would we sever the elephant’s tusks or the rhinoceros’s horn? We drive a cloud carriage through the garden of letters, leaving tracks that can be followed; we spread a celestial net through the forest of books, and its main cords and meshes fall into order of themselves. Ordered and coherent, the work surpasses Gongli’s Forthright Discourses; neither distorted nor partial, it makes Zizhen’s Discourse on Government seem inadequate. After prolonged collecting and arranging, it has been compiled into five book wrappers.

Across the distant span of several thousand years, the causes of good government and disorder are distinguished like branching streams and assembled like overlapping scales. The abundant wisdom of sages and worthies, contained in countless words, is arrayed like stars and shines like the Milky Way. Why wait to collect books in Guanzhong before fully understanding the reasons for Qin’s fall? Why need to examine the records in Lu before recognizing how the way of Zhou arose? This is indeed an effective remedy for sustaining the people and nurturing all things, and an excellent canon for furthering good government and achieving peace.

We recall Yu’s assent and Yi’s commendation, and, further, the emperor’s bow and Gao Yao’s song. Although setting forth counsel is the duty of ministers close to the throne, faithfully putting it into practice rests with the sovereign. To delight in it and understand how to draw out its meaning—even a single piece responding to Kuan’s question [?] would itself suffice for use. To range widely without arriving anywhere—even merely having Jun set forth the Three Changes [?]—what use would there be in abundance? We humbly wish that Your Majesty would let your mind dwell upon the enduring principles of vastness [?]…

…devote Your attention to this in the intervals between overseeing affairs. Thoroughly investigate the course of three thousand years: what brought obstruction, and what brought flourishing? Examine the rise and decline of fourteen dynasties: which offer examples to follow, and which offer warnings? Follow the illustrious footsteps of enlightened kings, tracing upward to the origins of the transmission among the Three Sages. Follow the proper paths of the various masters, bringing together the established methods of the Six Classics for achieving good government. Like fish finding water in which to swim, do more than merely peruse and enjoy earlier writings; like birds furnished with wings to soar, be sure to put these teachings into practice. Thus may You bring virtue and achievement to their fullest realization and secure the foundations of an enduring imperial enterprise. We, Your servants, gaze toward Heaven and look up to Your sagely majesty with the utmost fervor and trembling reverence. 之弗豫而遽一之虐之肆也齊之無本而
punctuated:
聖祖仁天下之心著於立法之初，抑以見我列聖仁天下之心寓於行法之際。噫！子殆誦習之有素矣，高薦何忝！

同考試官教諭梁批：皇祖立法令以教民於先，律以一民於後，有以仰追舜禹成康之遺制，而非漢唐宋所能及也。列聖嗣守良法，克臻治效。此策援古證今，鑿鑿有實，蓋服習聖製而有得焉者。推以致用，權度自不忒矣。

同考試官教授王批：發問之旨，具有乎聖製序文「教」「齊」二字中，作者多昧之。是篇序述詳明，而詞致沉着，豈邃於古今訓典者與？

考試官左中允賈批：我聖祖律令之設，真有符於虞周制刑之意。子能仰窺而會其指歸，豈嘗究心而服膺者與？宜冠本房。

…our sagely progenitor’s benevolent concern for all under Heaven manifested at the inception of legislation, but also our successive sage emperors’ benevolent concern for all under Heaven embodied in the administration of the laws. Ah! You must have long been versed in reciting and studying these writings. How could you be unworthy of a high recommendation!

Successive sage emperors upheld these excellent laws and achieved effective government. This policy essay invokes antiquity to substantiate the present, offering definite and solid evidence. This essay’s exposition is detailed and clear, and its expression composed and assured. Is its author deeply versed in the authoritative teachings of past and present?

Comment by Examiner Jia, Left Companion to the Heir Apparent: Our sagely progenitor’s establishment of penal laws and ordinances truly accords with the intent underlying the institution of punishments under Shun and the Zhou. title: 正德八年應天府鄉試錄
text:
驟論之忍之為也此有天下之君撫億兆
之衆威制非所先而軌訓為尚法禁非所
急而播告惟勤其猶弗率乃致辟焉則民
與我皆無憾而仁與義亦並行矣詎非經
邦之令猷御世之大防與愚於是有以知
有虞成周制刑之意我
太祖高皇帝立法之旨暨歷代興辟陳臬之端
矣夫天地化生萬物既舒之以陽不能不
慘之以陰聖人子育黎庶既煦之以和不
===
能不肅之以威然其好生之德未嘗不行
于明罰勅法之先不忍之心未始不著于
鈇鉞鞭扑之外故有虞之時雖命伯夷播
刑之迪然三禮之典實先降之于以折民
邪妄之心使之入禮而不入於刑禮之弗
率而後戮辱加之是豈帝舜之本心哉不
得已而用耳成周之時雖命司寇掌五刑
之政然五禁之法實隨布之于以嚴民未
然之防俾之遠罪而不犯禁之弗戢而後

punctuated:
驟論之，忍之為也。此有天下之君，撫億兆之衆，威制非所先，而軌訓為尚；法禁非所急，而播告惟勤。其猶弗率，乃致辟焉，則民與我皆無憾，而仁與義亦並行矣。詎非經邦之令猷、御世之大防與？愚於是有以知有虞、成周制刑之意，我太祖高皇帝立法之旨，暨歷代興辟陳臬之端矣。
夫天地化生萬物，既舒之以陽，不能不慘之以陰；聖人子育黎庶，既煦之以和，不能不肅之以威。然其好生之德，未嘗不行于明罰勅法之先；不忍之心，未始不著于鈇鉞鞭扑之外。故有虞之時，雖命伯夷播刑之迪，然三禮之典，實先降之，于以折民邪妄之心，使之入禮而不入於刑。禮之弗率，而後戮辱加之，是豈帝舜之本心哉？不得已而用耳。成周之時，雖命司寇掌五刑之政，然五禁之法，實隨布之，于以嚴民未然之防，俾之遠罪而不犯。禁之弗戢，而後
translation_en:
…to pass judgment on them precipitately is an act of cruelty. Thus the ruler who possesses all under Heaven and cares for its teeming multitudes does not give priority to coercion through authority, but esteems instruction in proper conduct; he does not make legal prohibitions his most urgent concern, but diligently issues proclamations. Only when the people still fail to comply does he impose punishment. Then neither the people nor the ruler has cause for regret, and benevolence and righteousness operate together. Is this not an excellent plan for governing the realm and a great safeguard for ruling the world? From this, I in my humble understanding can grasp the intent behind the establishment of punishments under Youyu and Chengzhou, the purpose of our Emperor Taizu Gao in instituting laws, and the underlying reasons why successive dynasties established punishments and promulgated legal standards.
Heaven and Earth transform and generate the myriad things: having fostered their growth through yang, they cannot but subject them to the severity of yin. The sage nurtures the common people as his children: having warmed them with harmony, he cannot but discipline them through authority. Yet his life-loving virtue invariably operates before he clarifies punishments and sets the laws in order; his heart, unable to bear others’ suffering, invariably manifests itself beyond the axes of execution, whips, and rods. Thus, in the time of Youyu, although Bo Yi was commanded to promulgate guidance concerning punishments [?], the ordinances of the three rites were in fact issued first. These were intended to check the people’s wayward and reckless impulses, bringing them within the rites rather than within the reach of punishment. Only after they failed to follow the rites were execution and humiliation imposed upon them. Could this have been Emperor Shun’s original intention? He employed them only because he had no alternative. In the time of Chengzhou, although the Minister of Justice was commanded to administer the five punishments, the regulations governing the five prohibitions were in fact promulgated alongside them. These were intended to strengthen safeguards against misconduct before it arose, so that the people would keep far from crime and commit no offenses. Only after the prohibitions failed to restrain them did…

title: 正德八年應天府鄉試錄
text:
剪伐及焉是豈成康之所願哉不得已而
施耳洪惟我
太祖高皇帝撫有華夏思滌夷風乃倣有虞成
周遺意為
大明律令二書其
大明令之頒布在改元之正月大而紀綱倫
理之重小而器用輿服之差凡律令所張
弛罔不具載為條一百四十有五兼他
訓誥率亦稱是則
===
聖製所謂令以教之於先之旨可謂周盡而懇
切矣
大明律之刪定在七年之二月揭名例六曹
為綱列職制以下為目統括事類愜比情
理為條四百有六十視諸舊律倫要獨全
則
聖製所謂律以齊之於後之義可謂審慎而昭
晰矣由是畫一良規迄今率由重以欽恤
之厚培諸

translation_en:
…only then did punitive destruction befall them. Could this have been what Kings Cheng and Kang desired? They imposed it only when no alternative remained. Our august Emperor Taizu Gao, having taken possession of the Chinese realm, sought to cleanse it of barbarian customs. Accordingly, he followed the surviving intentions of the age of Shun and the Zhou dynasty, producing the two works, the Great Ming Code and the Great Ming Ordinances. The Great Ming Ordinances were promulgated in the first month of the year in which the new reign era began. From weighty matters of governing principles and ethical relationships to minor distinctions in utensils, carriages, and dress, everything that the code and ordinances regulated, whether strictly or leniently, was fully recorded in 145 articles. His other instructions and admonitions were generally consonant with these. Thus the purpose expressed in the imperial composition—“use ordinances to instruct them beforehand”—may indeed be called comprehensive and earnest.
The Great Ming Code was revised and settled in the second month of the seventh year. General Principles and the Six Ministries provided its main divisions, with the official establishment and subsequent subjects arranged beneath them. It comprehensively classified affairs and fitted its provisions to circumstances and principles, forming 460 articles. Compared with earlier codes, it alone was complete in its essential organization. Thus the meaning expressed in the imperial composition—“use the code to bring them into conformity afterward”—may indeed be called judicious and clear. title: 正德八年應天府鄉試錄
text:
列聖審克之至嗣以群賢於是四方風動之休
萬邦刑措之美真無愧於有虞成周之世
矣是豈漢唐宋諸君所能及哉何以明其
然也唐之制刑以尊卑貴賤之等為令百
司所常行為格所常守為式三者有違始
一斷以律其教刑之序亦得矣然品官衣
服高下之式待馬周而始建白隋季明輕
明重之弊至永徽猶未刋除節目之脫畧
若此果可以望我
===
聖祖憲度之藩籬邪宋之制刑以設於此而待
彼之謂格使彼效之之謂式禁於未然之
謂令禁於已然之謂敕其齊導之倫亦著
矣然嫡孫承祖之服至宋敏求而始定大
中故殺之令至杜曾而始釐疵類之猥多
如此果可以窺我
聖祖法理之堂奧邪無怪乎中葉叔世科條屢
增法守寖奪紀綱因而墮廢鼎祚遂以顛
隮是固作者之過然繼統承序之君亦豈

列聖，審克之至嗣以群賢。於是四方風動之休，萬邦刑措之美，真無愧於有虞、成周之世矣。是豈漢、唐、宋諸君所能及哉？何以明其然也？唐之制刑，以尊卑貴賤之等為令，百司所常行為格，所常守為式，三者有違，始一斷以律。其教刑之序亦得矣。然品官衣服高下之式，待馬周而始建白；隋季明輕明重之弊，至永徽猶未刋除。節目之脫畧若此，果可以望我聖祖憲度之藩籬邪？

宋之制刑，以設於此而待彼之謂格，使彼效之之謂式，禁於未然之謂令，禁於已然之謂敕。其齊導之倫亦著矣。然嫡孫承祖之服，至宋敏求而始定；大中故殺之令，至杜曾而始釐。疵類之猥多如此，果可以窺我聖祖法理之堂奧邪？無怪乎中葉叔世，科條屢增，法守寖奪，紀綱因而墮廢，鼎祚遂以顛隮。是固作者之過，然繼統承序之君亦豈
translation_en:
…the successive sage emperors, with the utmost care in adjudication carried on by worthy men. Thus the blessings of transforming influence spread throughout the realm, and the splendid condition in which punishments could be set aside prevailed in every region. This truly bore comparison without shame to the ages of Shun and the flourishing Zhou. Could the rulers of the Han, Tang, and Song possibly have matched it? How can this be demonstrated? In the Tang system of penal law, ordinances prescribed distinctions between superior and inferior, noble and humble; regulations governed the regular business of the various offices; and procedural rules governed their customary observances. Only when one of these three was violated was judgment rendered uniformly according to the penal code. Its ordering of instruction and punishment was indeed appropriate. Yet standards distinguishing the clothing of ranked officials were first proposed only when Ma Zhou appeared; and the abuses of making punishments lighter or heavier at will [?], inherited from the closing years of the Sui, had still not been eliminated by the Yonghui era. With such omissions in its detailed provisions, could it possibly have come within sight of even the outer fence of our sagely founder’s laws and institutions?

In the Song system of penal law, what was established here to govern cases arising elsewhere was termed a regulation; what others were required to follow as a model was termed a procedural rule; what prohibited acts before they occurred was termed an ordinance; and what prohibited acts after they had occurred was termed an edict. Its principles for regulating and guiding the people were also clearly expressed. Yet the mourning obligations of a grandson in the direct line who succeeded his grandfather were settled only in the time of Song Minqiu; and the Dazhong-era ordinance concerning intentional killing [?] was rectified only in the time of Du Zeng. With defects of so many kinds, could it possibly have glimpsed the inner chambers of our sagely founder’s principles of law? No wonder that, in the middle and declining periods of those dynasties, statutory provisions repeatedly multiplied, established legal observances were gradually undermined, the governing framework consequently fell into disrepair, and the dynastic mandate ultimately collapsed. These were certainly faults of those who framed the laws; yet could the rulers who inherited the imperial succession also possibly…

title: 正德八年應天府鄉試錄
text:
能辭其玩忽之咎哉由是觀之則夫為□
之計欲維持百年無弊之法以開萬世不
拔之基者亦惟人法兼任持之以簡以有
限治無窮不使比議繁滋以啓二門之奸
如桓譚所疏可也上下一心蒞之以公絕
疵於五過明清于單辭不令曲當妙鑒奪
徵文之直準如劉頌所啓可也然皆聖哲
之上明察之官之任也愚生何為者邪
第二問
===
同考試官教諭鍾批古人行事得失昭然莫
掩然非億說所能斷述也是篇援據詳悉評議切當
且他篇稱是擢于於眾中以冠本房非獨見子學問
之該博而已它時進用
廟堂臨大事决大疑吾知迎刃而解必矣
同考試官教授曾批此策正欲觀士子平日
胸中權度而此篇能歷歷剖析明白無毫髮疑滯他
日獨謀

translation_en:
…can they escape blame for their negligence? Viewed in this light, anyone planning for □ [?], who wishes to maintain laws free of defects for a hundred years and thereby lay an unshakable foundation for ten thousand generations, must rely on both men and laws, upholding them with simplicity and using what is finite to govern limitless circumstances. One must prevent deliberations based on precedents from proliferating and opening the way to abuses through two channels, as Huan Tan proposed in his memorial. Those above and below must be of one mind and administer affairs impartially, eliminating the faults associated with the five judicial errors and discerning the truth even in the testimony of a single party. One must not allow finely tailored judgments and subtle discernment to displace the straightforward standard of consulting written provisions, as Liu Song proposed in his memorial. Yet these are all responsibilities of a sage and wise sovereign and discerning officials. What standing has an ignorant student such as I?
Second Question
Comment by Associate Examiner Zhong, Instructor: The successes and failures of the ancients’ actions are plain and cannot be concealed; nevertheless, they cannot be judged and recounted through conjecture. This essay adduces evidence in thorough detail, and its assessments are apt. The other essays are of comparable quality. In selecting you from among the candidates to rank first in this examining section, I recognize more than merely the breadth of your learning. When you are advanced to service at court and confront great affairs and resolve great uncertainties, I know that these will surely yield readily to your judgment, like something severed at the touch of a blade.

text:
王斷國知其必出人一頭地而王謝之流豈足言哉甄拔之際有士
此差亦足以報
上矣

會得失成敗之迹如指諸掌末復舉經訓以為準的

title: 正德八年應天府鄉試錄
text:
不爾寧能逭夫噬臍之悔亡身僨國之慘
乎愚嘗讀歷代史述及諸傳記有以悉夫
君臣决計用言之畧圖事揆策之大較於
指掌間矣請得而陳之方漢祖之圍滎陽
也酈生一鼓撓楚權之舌遽命刻印立國
以時莫有爭之者耳迨聞張良借筯之言
遂立罷之雖幾敗乃公事亦豈害其為誠
信好謀邪世祖之困於薊北也群議一倡
還長安之便即欲卷甲西歸以時未有規
===
之者耳及聽邳彤廷對之言遂立止之雖
瀕失事機亦豈害其為沉幾先物邪魏武
乘破荊之威欲帖江東舟師熸潰顛沛而
還始興郭奉孝若在不使孤至此之思愚
以為使奉孝果可作决不能善赤壁之役
何則恐喝之初周瑜已策其有四敗之形
矣唐文皇矜中國之盛親征高麗靺鞨犯
陳幾陷不測尋發魏徵若在吾豈有此行
之思愚以為使魏徵果無恙斷莫能遏遼

punctuated:
不爾，寧能逭夫噬臍之悔、亡身僨國之慘乎？愚嘗讀歷代史述及諸傳記，有以悉夫君臣决計用言之畧、圖事揆策之大較於指掌間矣。請得而陳之。

方漢祖之圍滎陽也，酈生一鼓撓楚權之舌，遽命刻印立國，以時莫有爭之者耳。迨聞張良借筯之言，遂立罷之。雖幾敗乃公事，亦豈害其為誠信好謀邪？世祖之困於薊北也，群議一倡還長安之便，即欲卷甲西歸，以時未有規之者耳。及聽邳彤廷對之言，遂立止之。雖瀕失事機，亦豈害其為沉幾先物邪？

魏武乘破荊之威，欲帖江東，舟師熸潰，顛沛而還，始興「郭奉孝若在，不使孤至此」之思。愚以為使奉孝果可作，决不能善赤壁之役。何則？恐喝之初，周瑜已策其有四敗之形矣。唐文皇矜中國之盛，親征高麗，靺鞨犯陳，幾陷不測，尋發「魏徵若在，吾豈有此行」之思。愚以為使魏徵果無恙，斷莫能遏遼
translation_en:
…If they did otherwise, could they possibly escape the regret of biting their own navels—regret that comes too late—or the calamity of destroying themselves and bringing their states to ruin? I have read historical accounts of successive dynasties and various biographies and records, and have thereby come to understand, as clearly as the palm of my hand, the methods by which rulers and ministers settled plans and adopted advice, and the broad principles by which they planned undertakings and weighed strategies. Allow me to set these out.

When Han Gaozu was besieged at Xingyang, Master Li had only to deploy his tongue in a proposal to undermine Chu’s power, and Gaozu immediately ordered seals to be engraved and kingdoms established, simply because no one at the time disputed the proposal. Once he heard Zhang Liang’s argument, illustrated with borrowed chopsticks, he immediately abandoned it. Although he had nearly ruined “your old man’s enterprise,” how could this detract from his sincerity and willingness to seek counsel? When Shizu was trapped north of Ji, his advisers had only to advocate the advantages of returning to Chang’an, and he immediately wished to pack up his troops’ armor and return west, simply because no one at the time had remonstrated with him. Once he heard Pi Tong’s reply before the court, he immediately stopped. Although he had nearly lost his strategic opportunity, how could this detract from his penetrating grasp of incipient developments and ability to anticipate events?

Wei Wudi, riding the prestige of his conquest of Jingzhou, wished to subdue Jiangdong. His naval force was destroyed and scattered, and he returned in distress. Only then did he reflect: “Had Guo Fengxiao been alive, he would not have let me come to this.” I believe that even if Fengxiao could indeed have risen from the dead, he certainly could not have brought the Chibi campaign to a successful conclusion. Why? At the very outset of the threats and intimidation, Zhou Yu had already identified four circumstances pointing to Wei Wudi’s defeat. Tang Wenhuang, proud of the Central Kingdom’s strength, personally campaigned against Gaoli. The Mohe attacked his battle formation, and he nearly met with disaster. Soon afterward he reflected: “Had Wei Zheng been alive, would I ever have undertaken this expedition?” I believe that even if Wei Zheng had indeed remained alive and well, he could certainly never have halted the advance against Liao…

title: 正德八年應天府鄉試錄
text:
兵之鋒何則議討之初褚遂良巳極夫支
體之諫矣二君之自用而不悟其非亦何
貴乎神武謀畧為哉石堡城之攻取所得
不酬所失王忠嗣籌之熟矣唐玄宗乃眩
於庸將之請勤兵吐蕃久無成功繼命哥
舒翰拔之士卒果死亡畧盡一何忍人也
靈州之孤危可棄而不可守楊億論之確
矣宋真宗惑於中外之說仍命關中飛輓
不絕卒為李繼遷據之兵民陷沒殆億計
===
一何後時也二君之聽言而不訂其是亦
奚貴於英武明睿為哉司馬師之東圖孫
亮也惑三征謬請而黜傅嘏之昌言猥致
關東之敗夫師之沉毅大畧豈忽於料敵
者邪倖速成功以基篡業而巳不然何蜀
捷交至而昭之九錫即加也吳明徹之北
伐彭城也適王軌濟師而拒摩訶之請擊
遂為周人所執夫以明徹之將畧人才豈
昧於决機者邪坐狃常勝輕視敵人而巳

兵之鋒何則議討之初楮遂良已極夫支
體之諫矣二君之自用而不悟其非亦何
貴乎神武謀畧為㦲石堡城之攻取所得
不酬所失王忠嗣籌之熟矣唐玄宗乃眩

punctuated:
兵之鋒。何則？議討之初，褚遂良巳極夫支體之諫矣。二君之自用而不悟其非，亦何貴乎神武謀畧為哉？

石堡城之攻取，所得不酬所失，王忠嗣籌之熟矣。唐玄宗乃眩於庸將之請，勤兵吐蕃，久無成功，繼命哥舒翰拔之，士卒果死亡畧盡，一何忍人也！靈州之孤危，可棄而不可守，楊億論之確矣。宋真宗惑於中外之說，仍命關中飛輓不絕，卒為李繼遷據之，兵民陷沒殆億計，一何後時也！二君之聽言而不訂其是，亦奚貴於英武明睿為哉？

司馬師之東圖孫亮也，惑三征謬請，而黜傅嘏之昌言，猥致關東之敗。夫師之沉毅大畧，豈忽於料敵者邪？倖速成功以基篡業而巳。不然，何蜀捷交至而昭之九錫即加也？吳明徹之北伐彭城也，適王軌濟師，而拒摩訶之請擊，遂為周人所執。夫以明徹之將畧人才，豈昧於决機者邪？坐狃常勝，輕視敵人而巳。
translation_en:
… the army’s advance. Why? When the campaign was first discussed, Chu Suiliang had already remonstrated to the utmost, using the analogy of the limbs and body. These two rulers insisted on their own judgment without recognizing their errors: what, then, was so admirable about their divine martial prowess and strategic ability?

In capturing Shibao City, the gains would not compensate for the losses: Wang Zhongsi had weighed this thoroughly. Yet Emperor Xuanzong of Tang was beguiled by an ordinary general’s request and wearied his troops in campaigns against Tubo, long without success. He subsequently ordered Geshu Han to take the city, and indeed almost all the soldiers perished. How cruel he was! Lingzhou was isolated and imperiled; it could be abandoned but could not be defended. Yang Yi had argued this conclusively. Emperor Zhenzong of Song, misled by arguments from within and outside the court, nevertheless ordered uninterrupted deliveries of supplies at speed from Guanzhong. In the end, Li Jiqian occupied the city, and soldiers and civilians lost numbered nearly a hundred million [?]. How late he was to act! These two rulers listened to advice without determining whether it was right: what, then, was so admirable about their heroic martial prowess and enlightened discernment?

When Sima Shi planned an eastern campaign against Sun Liang, he was misled by the mistaken requests of the three Generals Who Conquer and rejected Fu Gu’s sound advice, thereby bringing about the defeat east of the passes. Given Shi’s composure, resolution, and broad strategic ability, could he have been careless in assessing the enemy? He merely hoped for a quick success to lay the foundation for usurpation. Otherwise, why were the Nine Bestowals immediately conferred upon Sima Zhao when reports of victories in Shu arrived in succession? When Wu Mingche campaigned north against Pengcheng, Wang Gui happened to bring reinforcements across, but Mingche rejected Mohe’s request to attack and was consequently captured by the men of Zhou. Given Mingche’s strategic ability as a commander and his personal talents, could he have failed to discern the decisive moment? He had simply grown accustomed to constant victory and treated the enemy lightly.

title: 正德八年應天府鄉試錄
text:
不然何伐齊之役而陳之北境盡復也桓
温不臣其親從豈宜居位謝安乃舉諸桓
而用之用之未必是也然衆翕然樂之安
亦豈能違衆而廢黜之邪權以濟事國用
乂安不亦得乎蘇峻懷逆其萌蘖豈宜久
稔庾亮則稱詔旨以召之召之未必非也
然勢危然可憂亮亦豈能違勢而誅鋤之
邪剛愎自用國反危辱不亦僨乎二臣經
邦一臧一否安之沉敏足稱而亮之政實
===
則未之或徵也玄德之假荆州也吳之宿
将咸以為非宜而魯肅獨勸其主曰帝王
之興皆有驅除卒為關羽所資真内不能
辦而外為大言耳仲謀評之當矣蕭禧之
来求分水嶺界也宋之故相皆以為不可
而王安石獨違衆議曰将欲取之必固與
之卒中遼人之計誠莫知所却而謬為大
言耳洪邁譏之是矣二臣行事異世同符
肅之知畧少損而安石之經濟則未之或

punctuated:
不然，何伐齊之役而陳之北境盡復也？桓温不臣，其親從豈宜居位？謝安乃舉諸桓而用之，用之未必是也。然衆翕然樂之，安亦豈能違衆而廢黜之邪？權以濟事，國用乂安，不亦得乎？蘇峻懷逆，其萌蘖豈宜久稔？庾亮則稱詔旨以召之，召之未必非也。然勢危然可憂，亮亦豈能違勢而誅鋤之邪？剛愎自用，國反危辱，不亦僨乎？二臣經邦，一臧一否。安之沉敏足稱，而亮之政實，則未之或徵也。
玄德之假荆州也，吳之宿将咸以為非宜，而魯肅獨勸其主曰：「帝王之興，皆有驅除。」卒為關羽所資，真内不能辦而外為大言耳，仲謀評之當矣。蕭禧之来求分水嶺界也，宋之故相皆以為不可，而王安石獨違衆議曰：「将欲取之，必固與之。」卒中遼人之計，誠莫知所却而謬為大言耳，洪邁譏之是矣。二臣行事，異世同符。肅之知畧少損，而安石之經濟，則未之或
translation_en:
… Otherwise, how was it that the campaign against Qi recovered all of Chen’s northern territory? Huan Wen was disloyal to his sovereign: how could his relatives and followers properly hold office? Yet Xie An recommended members of the Huan clan and employed them. Employing them was not necessarily right. But everyone welcomed this unanimously; how could An have gone against them all and dismissed these men? He exercised expedient judgment to accomplish the task, and the state thereby enjoyed peace and order. Was this not a success? Su Jun harbored rebellious intentions: how could their shoots properly be allowed to mature unchecked? Yu Liang invoked the imperial edict to summon him. Summoning him was not necessarily wrong. Yet the situation was perilous and troubling; how could Liang have acted against the circumstances and rooted him out? Stubbornly trusting his own judgment, he instead brought danger and humiliation upon the state. Was this not a failure? Of these two ministers’ conduct of government, one was good and the other bad. An’s composure and quick judgment deserve praise, whereas evidence of Liang’s actual achievements in government is nowhere to be found.
When Xuande borrowed Jingzhou, Wu’s veteran generals all considered it inappropriate, but Lu Su alone urged his ruler to agree, saying, “Whenever an emperor rises, there are always those who clear the way for him.” In the end, Jingzhou became a resource for Guan Yu. Su truly could not manage matters at home and merely made grand pronouncements abroad. Zhongmou’s assessment of him was apt. When Xiao Xi came to demand that the watershed ridge be made the boundary, Song’s former chief councillors all considered this unacceptable. Wang Anshi alone opposed their collective judgment, saying, “If you wish to take something, you must first give it.” In the end, he fell into the Liao people’s scheme. Truly, he did not know how to repulse their demands and merely made empty, grand pronouncements. Hong Mai’s criticism of him was correct. These two ministers acted in different ages, yet their conduct matched. title: 正德八年應天府鄉試錄
text:
聞也是則臨大事遇大患率以用人而
自用而敗從衆則安違衆則危如此然則
後世作事之君獻計之臣惡可不知所法
哉亦惟以高帝為階世祖為蹊而馴至于
舍己從人改過弗吝之盛德可也必以謝
安為勸安石為戒而謹守乎主善為師大
猶是經之明訓可也夫然則勳烈如之何
不俊偉民物如之何不蕃阜宗社如之何
不靈長也何以見其然哉亦惟驗諸
===
今日而已
第三問
王大化
同考試官教諭李批首閱初場旨趣深長文
詞雅健心固奇之及觀此策歴論昔賢學于古訓所
得淺深之等無不切當其學識所造可槩知矣
畿甸之士若此豈非涵濡
聖化之深而脫然穎出者乎健羨健羨
同考試官教諭徐批先哲格言至論散于子

開也是則臨大事遇大患率以用人□
自用而敗從衆則安違衆則危如此然則
後世作事之君獻計之臣惡可不知所法
哉亦惟以高帝爲階世祖爲蹊而馴至乎
舍己從人改過弗吝之盛德可也必以謝
安爲勸安石爲戒而謹守乎主善爲師大
猶是經之明訓可也夫然則勲烈如之何
不俊偉民物如之何不蕃阜宗社如之何
不靈長也何以見其然哉亦惟驗諸
===
今日而已
第三問
王大化
同考試官教諭李　批〔首閱初場旨趣深長文詞雅健心固奇之及觀此策歷論昔賢學于古訓所得淺深之等無不切當其學識所造可槩知矣幾甸之士若此豈非涵濡〕
聖化之深而脱然穎出者乎健羨健羨
同考試官教諭徐　批〔先哲格言至論散于子〕
punctuated:
聞也。是則臨大事，遇大患，率以用人而自用而敗，從衆則安，違衆則危，如此。然則後世作事之君、獻計之臣，惡可不知所法哉？亦惟以高帝為階，世祖為蹊，而馴至于舍己從人、改過弗吝之盛德可也。必以謝安為勸，安石為戒，而謹守乎主善為師、大猶是經之明訓可也。夫然則勳烈如之何不俊偉，民物如之何不蕃阜，宗社如之何不靈長也？何以見其然哉？亦惟驗諸今日而已。
第三問
王大化
同考試官教諭李批：首閱初場，旨趣深長，文詞雅健，心固奇之。及觀此策，歴論昔賢學于古訓所得淺深之等，無不切當，其學識所造可槩知矣。畿甸之士若此，豈非涵濡聖化之深而脫然穎出者乎？健羨，健羨！
同考試官教諭徐批：先哲格言至論，散于子
translation_en:
…has been heard of. Thus, when confronting great affairs and encountering grave troubles, rulers generally, through employing others [?], but fail through relying on themselves; following the counsel of others brings security, while opposing it brings danger. Such is the lesson. How, then, could rulers of later ages who undertake affairs, and ministers who offer plans, fail to know what to emulate? They need only take Gaozu as their stepping stone and Shizu as their path, gradually attaining the consummate virtue of setting aside their own views to follow others and correcting their faults without hesitation. They must take encouragement from Xie An and warning from Wang Anshi, faithfully observing the clear injunctions to take goodness as their teacher and to order affairs by great principles. Then how could their achievements fail to be outstanding, the people and all living things fail to flourish, or the ancestral temples and altars of state fail to endure in blessed perpetuity? How can we know this to be so? We need only examine the present day.
Third Question
Wang Dahua
Comment by Associate Examiner Li, Instructor: When I first read his first-session work, its purport was profound and far-reaching, and its language elegant and vigorous; I already found it exceptional. On reading this policy essay, I found that his successive discussions of the varying depths of understanding that former worthies gained from studying ancient teachings were all precisely apt. From this one can broadly discern the attainments of his learning and judgment. That a scholar from the metropolitan region should be like this—surely it is because he has been deeply imbued with the sagely transforming influence of the throne that he stands out so distinctly? Most admirable, most admirable!
Comment by Associate Examiner Xu, Instructor: The exemplary sayings and consummate discussions of earlier sages are scattered through the writings of the masters…

title: 正德八年應天府鄉試錄
text:
史中句句可以為身心之資惟無意於為己者則視
若長物而忽之者多矣此篇隨荅無遺義非平日潜
心於理學者也且他策皆善叅之初中二場文字又
皆淡而旨正而華簡而徹是知明理之學無所施而
不可以之試春官與天下士較其裒然而頴出者吾
端有所望焉
考試官左中允賈批理道之言儒先類有所得而
程朱為統會此篇的有所見而條荅無遺謂非潜心
之久者能之乎
===
考試官右諭德倫批賢哲學力所造自有等級非
私意淺見可得而軒輊之也稱量當而去取公無如
此作是用錄之以為稽古者勸
甚矣古訓之富而有待乎人也大用之則
大有所立小用之則小有所成殆無施而
不可無修而不善無推而不準焉是豈局
於一偏狃於一曲宜於甲而乖於乙通乎
近而泥乎遠也人之資禀不同而位遇亦
異故隨其流品而取則有廣狹因其素位

史中句句可以爲身心之資誰謂無意於爲己者能觀
若長物而忽之者多矣此篇隨答無遺義誠乎日躋
心於理學者也且他策皆無參之初中二場文學又
皆淡而旨正而華簡而徹是知明理之學無所施而
不可以之試春官與天下士較其臭然而顯出若吾
端有所望焉
考試官左中允賈　批〔理道之言儒先類有所得而程宋爲統會此篇的有所見而條答無遺謂非潛心〕
之久者能之乎
===
考試官右諭德倫　批〔賢哲學力所造自有等級非私意淺見可得而軒輕之也稱量當而去取公無如〕
此作是用錄之以爲稽古者勸
甚矣吉訓之富而有待乎人也大用之則
大有所立小用之則小有所成殆無施而
不可無修而不善無推而不準焉是豈局
於一偏狃於一曲宜於甲而乖於乙通乎
近而泥乎遠也人之資稟不同而位遇亦
異故隨其流品而取則有廣狹因其素位
punctuated:
史中，句句可以為身心之資。惟無意於為己者，則視若長物而忽之者多矣。此篇隨荅無遺義，非平日潜心於理學者也。且他策皆善，叅之初中二場文字，又皆淡而旨、正而華、簡而徹。是知明理之學，無所施而不可。以之試春官，與天下士較，其裒然而頴出者，吾端有所望焉。
考試官左中允賈批：理道之言，儒先類有所得，而程朱為統會。此篇的有所見，而條荅無遺，謂非潜心之久者能之乎？
考試官右諭德倫批：賢哲學力所造，自有等級，非私意淺見可得而軒輊之也。稱量當而去取公，無如此作，是用錄之，以為稽古者勸。
甚矣，古訓之富而有待乎人也！大用之，則大有所立；小用之，則小有所成。殆無施而不可，無修而不善，無推而不準焉。是豈局於一偏，狃於一曲，宜於甲而乖於乙，通乎近而泥乎遠也？人之資禀不同，而位遇亦異，故隨其流品而取則有廣狹，因其素位
translation_en:
…in the histories, every sentence can provide nourishment for one's person and mind. Yet among those who have no intention of learning for their own moral improvement, many regard these sayings as superfluous and neglect them. This essay answers each point without omitting any meaning; could this have been achieved without habitual dedication to the learning of principle? [?] His other policy essays are all good as well. Comparing them with his compositions from the first and second sessions, we find that all are restrained yet rich in meaning, correct yet elegant, concise yet lucid. This shows that learning directed toward understanding principle can be applied successfully everywhere. When he competes with scholars from throughout the realm in the Metropolitan Examination, I have firm hopes that he will distinguish himself conspicuously.
Examiner Jia, Left Companion to the Heir Apparent, comments: Earlier Confucian scholars generally attained some understanding in their discussions of principle and the Way, while Cheng and Zhu brought these insights together into a coherent whole. This essay displays definite insight and answers the questions point by point without omission. Could someone who had not devoted himself to this study for a long time have accomplished it?
Examiner Lun, Right Admonisher to the Heir Apparent, comments: The attainments of worthy and wise men through their scholarly efforts have their own gradations. These cannot be ranked according to personal prejudice or shallow understanding. No composition matches this one in the appropriateness of its assessments and the impartiality of its judgments of acceptance and rejection. We have therefore recorded it to encourage those who study antiquity.
How abundant are the teachings of antiquity, and how much they depend upon people to put them into practice! Applied on a large scale, they enable great accomplishments; applied on a small scale, they enable lesser achievements. There is scarcely any application in which they are unsuitable, any cultivation they fail to improve, or any extension in which they fail to provide a sound standard. How could they be confined to one partial standpoint or restricted to one narrow corner, suitable for one thing but contrary to another, effective for what is near but obstructed when applied to what is distant? People's natural endowments differ, and so too do their positions and circumstances. Thus, according to their respective capacities, the models they draw upon vary in breadth; according to their existing stations …

title: 正德八年應天府鄉試錄
text:
而擬議有時宜譬猶群汲江河器殊巨細
而濟生人之用則一而已何則道之大原
出於天而備載於六經闡明於大學論語
諸書孔曾思孟傳之于前周程張朱繼之
于後是故博我以文約我以禮顏子稱孔
子教人語也作聖之功莫切乎此故程伊
川指博約而言曰聖人教人只此二字誠
孔門闡教之的焉自格物致知以至治國
平天下大學中綱領之條目也告君之言
===
莫先乎是故朱晦庵聞正心誠意之語而
應曰平生所學惟此四字真大人格君之
事焉盡心行己莫要乎誠是以劉器之服
膺師訓力行七年而誠之為德始成然猶
惑於司戶不貪之對至讀楊子避礙通理
之言而意乃釋其篤信好學者與理郡專
城莫尚乎信是以張忠定再領益州拊循
五載而信之一字始成然猶不免外間背
服之疑至聞李畋何待今日之語而心始

punctuated: 而擬議有時宜。譬猶群汲江河，器殊巨細，而濟生人之用則一而已。何則？道之大原出於天，而備載於六經，闡明於大學、論語諸書。孔曾思孟傳之于前，周程張朱繼之于後。是故「博我以文，約我以禮」，顏子稱孔子教人語也。作聖之功莫切乎此，故程伊川指博約而言曰：「聖人教人，只此二字。」誠孔門闡教之的焉。自格物致知以至治國平天下，大學中綱領之條目也。告君之言莫先乎是，故朱晦庵聞正心誠意之語而應曰：「平生所學，惟此四字。」真大人格君之事焉。盡心行己，莫要乎誠，是以劉器之服膺師訓，力行七年，而誠之為德始成。然猶惑於司戶不貪之對，至讀楊子避礙通理之言而意乃釋，其篤信好學者與！理郡專城，莫尚乎信，是以張忠定再領益州，拊循五載，而信之一字始成。然猶不免外間背服之疑，至聞李畋何待今日之語而心始

…and in deliberating upon them, take account of what is appropriate to the circumstances. It is like people all drawing water from rivers: their vessels differ in size, yet their purpose of supplying human needs is the same. Why is this? The great source of the Way comes from Heaven. It is fully recorded in the Six Classics and elucidated in such books as the Great Learning and the Analects. Kongzi, Zengzi, Zisi, and Mengzi transmitted it in earlier times; Zhou, Cheng, Zhang, and Zhu continued their work afterward.

Thus, “He broadens me through learning and restrains me through ritual” were the words with which Master Yan described Kongzi’s teaching. Nothing is more essential to the work of becoming a sage. Hence Cheng Yichuan, referring to broadening and restraint, said, “In teaching people, the sage uses only these two words.” This is indeed the central aim of the teachings expounded in the school of Kongzi. From investigating things and extending knowledge to governing the state and bringing peace to all under Heaven: these are the constituent articles under the overarching principles of the Great Learning. Nothing takes precedence over these in addressing a ruler. Thus, when Zhu Hui’an heard the words “rectifying the mind and making the intention sincere,” he replied, “All that I have studied throughout my life lies in these four words.” This is truly the work of a great man in rectifying his ruler.

In fully applying one’s heart and conducting oneself, nothing is more essential than sincerity. Thus Liu Qizhi took his teacher’s instructions to heart and diligently practiced them for seven years before he attained sincerity as a virtue. Yet he remained perplexed by the Revenue Manager’s reply about not being avaricious. Only when he read Master Yang’s words about avoiding impediments and comprehending principle did his doubts dissolve. Was he not one who believed steadfastly and loved learning?

In administering a commandery and holding sole charge of a city, nothing ranks above trustworthiness. Thus Zhang Zhongding, during his second tenure in charge of Yizhou, nurtured and cared for its people for five years before he realized the single word “trustworthiness.” Yet he still could not escape doubts about whether people outside his immediate circle opposed him or submitted to him. title: 正德八年應天府鄉試錄
text:
安其善政得民者與士之守官勤則下無
壅滯謹則行罔玷缺和則與物無忤緩則
處事精當人能持此四字職業蔑不舉矣
張思正道之以教新進其知言哉州縣之
職一吏軌民非廉弗率愛人利物非仁弗
濟决獄齊衆非公弗服剸煩治劇非勤弗
辦舉能行此四字化理罔不振矣真西山
以之勗勵僚屬其名言哉趙中令歷相兩
朝自謂以半部論語佐太祖半部論語佐
===
太宗其功烈有足稱者然海物之獻涪陵
之獄果公綽不欲以道事君似乎亦幾於
侮聖言矣宜其晚節之不醇李文靖輔相
真宗自謂如論語節用而愛人使民以時
尚未能行其語儲若自謙者然遼夏未附
息肩無期欲節勞損費施舍已責得乎誠
篤於畏聖言矣宜其相業之終偉于仲文
對主讀書之問謂資父事君忠孝而已忠
孝豈能括夫讀書之事然乃臣子立身之

punctuated: 安，其善政得民者與！士之守官，勤則下無壅滯，謹則行罔玷缺，和則與物無忤，緩則處事精當。人能持此四字，職業蔑不舉矣。張思正道之以教新進，其知言哉！州縣之職，一吏軌民，非廉弗率；愛人利物，非仁弗濟；决獄齊衆，非公弗服；剸煩治劇，非勤弗辦。舉能行此四字，化理罔不振矣。真西山以之勗勵僚屬，其名言哉！趙中令歷相兩朝，自謂以半部《論語》佐太祖，半部《論語》佐太宗，其功烈有足稱者。然海物之獻、涪陵之獄，果公綽不欲、以道事君，似乎亦幾於侮聖言矣，宜其晚節之不醇。李文靖輔相真宗，自謂如《論語》「節用而愛人，使民以時」，尚未能行。其語儲若自謙者，然遼夏未附，息肩無期，欲節勞損費、施舍已責，得乎？誠篤於畏聖言矣，宜其相業之終偉。于仲文對主讀書之問，謂資父事君，忠孝而已。忠孝豈能括夫讀書之事？然乃臣子立身之
translation_en:
…was set at ease. Was he not one who won the people through good government! When a scholar holds office, diligence ensures that business below him encounters no obstruction or delay; caution keeps his conduct free from blemishes; harmony prevents friction with others; and an unhurried approach makes his handling of affairs precise and appropriate. If a person can maintain these four qualities, none of his official duties will go unfulfilled. Zhang Sizheng taught these principles to newcomers to office: how well he understood the import of words! In prefectural and county office, bringing clerks into line and setting standards for the people requires integrity if they are to follow; loving people and benefiting others requires benevolence if it is to succeed; deciding lawsuits and bringing the multitude into order requires impartiality if they are to submit; and handling complicated and demanding business requires diligence if it is to be accomplished. If all can practice these four qualities, moral transformation and good government will invariably flourish. Zhen Xishan used them to exhort his subordinate officials: what memorable words!

Secretariat Director Zhao served as chief councillor in two reigns. He himself said that he assisted Taizu with half the Analects and Taizong with the other half. His achievements certainly merit praise. Yet, regarding the offering of marine delicacies and the Fuling judicial case, did he truly display Gongchuo’s freedom from desire and serve his ruler according to the Way [?]? He seems indeed to have come close to slighting the sage’s words. It is fitting that his conduct in his later years was not unblemished. Li Wenjing served as chief councillor to Zhenzong. He himself said that he had not yet been able to practice such teachings of the Analects as ‘Be frugal in expenditure and love the people; employ the people’s labor at the proper seasons.’ His words seem to express modesty [?]. Yet, with Liao and Xia still unsubdued and no prospect of respite from these burdens, could he have reduced toil and expenditure, bestowed relief, and canceled debts? He was truly earnest in his reverence for the sage’s words. It is fitting that his achievements as chief councillor were great to the end.

When Yu Zhongwen answered his ruler’s question about reading, he said that it amounted simply to loyalty and filial devotion: drawing upon service to one’s father in serving one’s ruler. Can loyalty and filial devotion encompass all that reading involves? Yet they constitute, for a minister and son, the foundation of personal conduct…

title: 正德八年應天府鄉試錄
text:
大節也大節不虧而後百行始得而修焉
有子以孝弟為仁之本斯言其近之廖德
明語人仕學之要惟用三代直道而行一
句直道豈能盡仕學之方然乃有司應務
之宏幹也宏幹不撓而後衆事始依以立
焉孟子謂枉己不能直人斯言其庶矣夫
伊川之立教晦庵之格君得經傳之綱要
而聖賢之道在是矣噐之之力行西山之
忠告得經傳之旨趣而聖賢之道庶幾矣
===
餘則或辭夫杯勺或慕夫高美或涉夫近
似而已雖於斯道邈乎其未聞然視既其
文而不既其實聞其號而未燭其理者寧
不大有間邪愚生幼味糟魄嘗出入乎諸
子而未始有得伊欲窺西山門戶以企及
乎程朱之堂室不知執事其肯進教否
第四問
程旦

第四問
程旦

同考試官學正陳批：事實散見諸史，答者多
translation_en:
…the cardinal principles by which one establishes oneself. Only when these cardinal principles remain unimpaired can all other forms of conduct be cultivated. Youzi regarded filial devotion and respect for elder brothers as the foundation of benevolence; these words come close to his meaning. In explaining to others the essentials of serving in office and learning, Liao Deming relied solely on the phrase concerning the Three Dynasties, “proceed along the straight Way.” How could the straight Way encompass every method of official service and learning? Yet it is the great supporting trunk by which officials attend to their duties. Only when that trunk does not bend can the many affairs of government be established upon it. Mencius said that one who bends himself cannot straighten others; these words closely approach that meaning.

Yichuan’s establishment of teachings and Hui’an’s correction of his ruler grasped the essential framework of the Classics and their commentaries: therein lies the Way of the sages and worthies. Qizhi’s vigorous practice and Xishan’s loyal admonitions grasped the purport of the Classics and their commentaries and came close to the Way of the sages and worthies. The others either declined a cup or ladleful, admired what was lofty and excellent, or merely touched upon something resembling the Way. Although they were far from having heard this Way, was there not nevertheless a great difference between them and those who mastered its wording without mastering its substance [?], or heard its name without illuminating its principles?

Since childhood, I, your foolish student, have tasted the dregs of learning. I have ranged among the various philosophical masters but have never gained any real understanding. I wish to glimpse Xishan’s gateway, hoping thereby to reach the halls and inner chambers of Cheng and Zhu. I do not know whether you would be willing to offer me further instruction.

Fourth Question
Cheng Dan

text:
不能悉此策不獨於古人同異之迹歷歷能述之且
究其本末考其是非區別其成敗得失昭如指掌先
正論凡讀史不徒要記事迹正謂此也其必積學待
問有素之士乎得士如此校文之責可少逭矣行將
捷南宮對
大廷而措諸用亦何疑於天下之理何難於天下之事哉餘策稱是惜
不能盡錄
考試官左中允費批古人心迹異同自有確論求
其評品精當而詞氣舂容者僅見此篇噫胸中無尺
===
度而欲較物之短長其不謬者幾希子殆有窮理之
學乎
考試官右諭德倫批是策乃比類體其間曲折始
難折衷此篇抑揚進退各當其歸非貫穿經傳低昂
權衡者不能也得士如子亦可以自慶矣

其迹者不可不考其是非甚哉迹之不可
拘而亦不可棄也徒因其同而不究夫事
之本末則眩於疑似彷彿而不準其實者

…cannot give a complete account. This policy essay not only recounts clearly, one by one, the similarities and differences in the outward deeds of the ancients; it also investigates their origins and outcomes, examines their rightness and wrongness, and distinguishes their successes and failures, gains and losses, making everything as clear as the palm of one’s hand. When a former worthy argued that reading history should not merely mean remembering events, this was precisely what he meant. Surely this must be a scholar who has long accumulated learning in readiness for questioning! Having found such a man, we may be somewhat relieved of our responsibility for judging the examination essays. Soon he will succeed in the Metropolitan Examination, answer before the great imperial court, and put his learning into practice. What doubt will he then have about the principles of the world, and what difficulty will he find in its affairs? His other policy essays are of comparable quality; regrettably, we cannot record them all.

If one has no standard of measurement in one’s mind but wishes to compare the lengths of things, how rarely will one escape error! You must surely have studied the investigation of principle!
Comment by Examiner Lun, Right Admonisher to the Heir Apparent: This policy question takes the form of comparison by categories; the intricacies within it make a balanced judgment difficult at the outset [?]. This could be achieved only by someone thoroughly versed in the classics and their commentaries and able to weigh their relative merits. Having found a scholar such as you, I too may congratulate myself.

title: 正德八年應天府鄉試錄
text:
多矣徒信其異而不考夫事之得失則拘
於界分形迹而不覈其當者衆矣故欲究
觀往事而區別其成敗得失必極盡古人
之底蘊披拓古人之心胸庶持諸已有定
論施諸用有成轍俟諸後世將亦占其必
信而不惑矣夫明問舉此以策末進意獨
至矣如學未足以通方何哉粤昔成周之
季晉文騎劫之伐齊曹也咸用犯墓之謀
以怖敵人然晉但稱舍於墓若將發塚然
===
故曹人懼而晉遂入曹燕則實發之以激
怒齊人故齊反乘衆忿擊敗燕軍其本實
不同也無怪其末之不同焉呂範周谷之
奉孫權也咸用所掌之財以應私求然範
每遇權索取必關白于策故權後以為忠
實而任之谷則慮抵譴每為之掩焉故權
後以為欺妄而黜之其本盖有異也無怪
其末之亦異焉項籍已滅季布懼嘗窘高
祖滕公待間為言之即召拜郎中更始已
