…there are many such people. Those who merely trust in the differences between events without examining their merits and faults are likewise often confined by distinctions and outward appearances, failing to investigate what was appropriate. Thus, to scrutinize past events and distinguish their successes and failures, gains and losses, one must fully explore the underlying purposes of the ancients and lay open their hearts and minds. Only then may one reach settled judgments for oneself and find established paths to follow in practice; awaiting the judgment of later ages, one may also anticipate that these conclusions will command confidence without perplexity. Your discerning question raises these matters to test us junior candidates: its intention is most thoughtful. Yet what can I do when my learning is insufficient for a comprehensive understanding?

In the latter days of Zhou, Duke Wen of Jin and Qi Jie, in their campaigns against Qi and Cao [the targets are given in reversed order here], both employed the threat of violating graves to frighten their enemies. Jin, however, merely announced that it would encamp among the graves, as though preparing to open the tombs. The people of Cao were therefore frightened, and Jin succeeded in entering Cao. Yan actually opened the tombs, thereby enraging the people of Qi; Qi consequently turned the populace’s anger to advantage and defeated Yan’s army. Their initial actions were in fact different, so it is no wonder that their outcomes differed.

When Lü Fan and Zhou Gu served Sun Quan, both used funds under their charge to meet his private requests. Whenever Quan demanded funds, however, Fan invariably reported the matter to Sun Ce. Quan therefore later regarded him as loyal and trustworthy and entrusted him with office. Gu, by contrast, feared incurring reprimand and always concealed the matter for Quan. Quan therefore later regarded him as deceitful and dismissed him. Their underlying conduct differed, so it is no wonder that their outcomes also differed.

title: 正德八年應天府鄉試錄
text:
敗馮衍始幅巾河內世祖以衍不時至遂
終身擯棄夫不時至者人臣盡忠所事之
大節非觀望之為也衍亦布同耳顧不得
如布詎非命邪唐儉說頡利歸欵李靖乘
虜懈弛潜兵赴之儉以脫身走免酈食其
說田廣稱藩韓信掩齊無備渡師襲之食
其坐賣敵見烹夫掩不備者乃謀將倖隙
貪功之譎計非行人之罪也食其亦儉侔
耳顧不得如儉詎非數邪何晏典選曹諸
===
與有舊者多擢用之裴垍為宰相故人求
除判司拒不之許謂不敢傷朝廷至公孰
不以為晏厚於垍也殊不知任官惟賢才
非其人虽私之如名器之濫何垍得之矣
尹勲為防禦以子才可用特薦進之呂公
著為司空自謂當世善士收拾畧盡乃置
子之賢不試孰不謂公著愈於勲也殊不
知內舉不避親惟其才是視耳何恤議之
足卹公著失之矣趙抃為參知政事遇朝

…was defeated, Feng Yan only then withdrew to Henei, wearing the plain headcloth of a private man. Because Yan had not come promptly to submit, Shizu excluded him from office for the rest of his life. Yet his failure to come promptly exemplified the great principle that a minister should remain wholly loyal to the ruler he serves; it was no act of watching and waiting to see which side would prevail. Yan was just like Ji Bu, yet he did not receive the same treatment as Bu. Was this not fate?

Tang Jian persuaded Jieli to submit, but Li Jing took advantage of the enemy’s relaxed vigilance and secretly advanced his troops against them. Jian escaped with his life by fleeing. Li Yiji persuaded Tian Guang to acknowledge himself a vassal, but Han Xin took Qi unprepared, crossing the river with his army to attack it. Yiji was accused of betraying Qi to its enemy and was boiled to death. Attacking an unprepared enemy was the crafty scheme of a calculating general, exploiting an opening in his greed for military glory; it was no fault of the envoy. Yiji was just like Jian, yet he did not fare as Jian did. Was this not destiny?

Who would not consider Yan more generous than Ji? Yet this overlooks the principle that appointments should go only to the worthy. If someone lacks the requisite ability, however much one favors him, what of the indiscriminate bestowal of official rank and insignia? Ji acted rightly.

When Yin Xun was a Defense Commissioner, he considered his son capable of service and specifically recommended him for advancement. When Lü Gongzhu was Minister of Works, he declared that he had gathered into service nearly all the worthy men of the age, yet left his own worthy son untried. Who would not say that Gongzhu surpassed Xun? Yet this overlooks the principle that, in recommending those close to oneself, one need not avoid relatives: ability alone is what matters. Why should one fear criticism [?]? Gongzhu acted wrongly.

title: 正德八年應天府鄉試錄
text:
政有未恊者必密啓聞李沆為相則否真
宗嘗問之沆對曰公事則公言之人臣有
密啓者非讒即佞夫事涉機要慮防宣泄
則權用密啓以杜猜嫌無易由言之戒不
可忽也若中外公共之政自宜宰執僉議
揚于王庭以聽君命不得與機要例也又
惡用密啓為哉周亞夫屯兵細柳適文帝
乘輿臨幸入不以時王猛伐燕圍鄴符堅
遠赴之猛迎曰亞夫前却人主以求名臣
===
竊少之夫文帝之來勞軍而已則閫以外
亞夫專之其却天子先驅軍令當爾若堅
率十萬眾赴鄴時乃天子自將閫外之事
堅實兼之不得與細柳比也猛安得不潜
謁之哉然豈特數子為然禹稷救世顏子
修已其迹異矣然處之各當其理故孟子
曰禹稷顏回同道季文子妾不衣帛公孫
弘身服布被其迹同矣然心之所存不同
故史謂其有體之與利之之異若但槩其

…whenever something in court government was amiss, he invariably reported it confidentially to the throne. Li Hang, however, did otherwise as chief councillor. Emperor Zhenzong once asked him about this, and Hang replied: “Public matters should be discussed publicly. A minister who submits confidential reports is either slandering others or currying favor.” Now, when a matter involves crucial secrets and disclosure must be guarded against, confidential reporting may be used as an expedient to forestall suspicion. The admonition “Do not speak lightly” must not be disregarded. But matters of government that concern the public, both at court and in the provinces, should naturally be discussed jointly by the chief councillors and other executive ministers, openly presented at the royal court, and submitted to the ruler for his decision. They cannot be treated in the same way as confidential affairs. What use, then, is confidential reporting for these?

Your servant privately holds him in low esteem for this.” Now, Emperor Wen had come merely to offer encouragement to the troops; command outside the palace gates therefore belonged exclusively to Yafu. In turning back the Son of Heaven’s advance escort, he acted as military regulations required. When Jian led a force of one hundred thousand to Ye, however, the Son of Heaven was commanding in person, and Jian himself also assumed responsibility for affairs outside the palace gates. This cannot be compared with Xiliu. How, then, could Meng fail to seek a private audience with him [?]?

title: 正德八年應天府鄉試錄
text:
振
祖宗之法殊未見其有濟也人蓋有善居室者
矣棟欹則正之榱敝則易之斯屋宇常固
而風雨非所憂亦有善養身者矣否則通
之鬱則散之斯血氣常和而寒暑非所慮
保治之道亦何異於是哉
國朝法古為理內而百官之政外而兵民之
司大而爵賞刑獄之務次而徭役度數之
繁莫不有不易之規畫一之度存焉故百
===
五十年于茲守而勿失
兩畿十三省之民帖然以寧執事猶以為政
或有未善化或有未洽內訌未盡寧椎剽
未盡息為

文帝康乂之世乎夫政或有未善者非輕
變以失初意則遷就以徇時好耳化有未
弘者非官使多邪僻則生養未完復耳長
技不修師律不肅能免內訌之警乎材武

國朝法古為理，內而百官之政，外而兵民之司，大而爵賞刑獄之務，次而徭役度數之繁，莫不有不易之規、畫一之度存焉。故百五十年于茲，守而勿失，兩畿十三省之民帖然以寧。執事猶以為政或有未善，化或有未洽，內訌未盡寧，椎剽未盡息，為今日之憂危者，豈非以賈誼之痛哭而發於文帝康乂之世乎？夫政或有未善者，非輕變以失初意，則遷就以徇時好耳。化有未弘者，非官使多邪僻，則生養未完復耳。長技不修，師律不肅，能免內訌之警乎？材武
translation_en:
…revive the laws of our dynastic ancestors, there would certainly be no prospect of success. There are those who know how to maintain a house: when a ridgepole leans, they straighten it; when a rafter decays, they replace it. Thus the house remains sound, and wind and rain cause no concern. There are also those who know how to nourish their bodies: they clear obstructions and disperse stagnation. Thus blood and vital energy remain harmonious, and cold and heat cause no anxiety. How is the way of preserving good government any different?
Our dynasty models its government on antiquity. Within the court, the administration of the hundred offices; beyond it, the authorities responsible for soldiers and civilians; the major matters of ranks, rewards, punishments, and judicial proceedings; and the lesser complexities of corvée service, measures, and numerical regulations—all have fixed rules and uniform standards. Thus, for a hundred and fifty years now, these have been maintained without being lost, and the people of the two metropolitan regions and thirteen provinces have lived peacefully and securely. Yet you, honored examiners, consider that administration may still be imperfect, moral transformation may not yet have reached everywhere, internal strife has not been entirely pacified, and violent robbery has not wholly ceased, and regard these as causes for anxiety and alarm today. Is this not like Jia Yi’s bitter weeping in the peaceful and well-governed age of Emperor Wen? Where administration remains imperfect, this results either from rash changes that lose sight of the original intent, or from compromises made to indulge the preferences of the times. Where moral transformation has not spread widely, this results either from widespread perversity among officials and their agents, or from the people’s livelihoods not yet having fully recovered. If specialized military skills are not cultivated and military discipline is not strict, can the danger of internal strife be avoided? Military talent and valor…

punctuated: 不振，尺籍徒存，能禁椎剽之奸乎？斯皆目前之弊也。蒐其弊，則法可得而復焉。執事又以為民徭未輕，民賦未薄，賞間失重，刑間失輕，為今日之憂危者，豈非以鮮于侁之大息而發於神宗勵精之日乎？夫徭有未輕者，他籍日增，見戶日減耳；民賦未薄者，度支寖廣，科派轉滋耳。功序弗明，希求弗抑，賞能不失於重乎？守文不確，權斷太寬，罰能不失於輕乎？斯皆近日之弊也。薅其弊，則法可得而舉焉。若謂將悍卒驕、民弁俗侈，古以為病，今也則無者，愚竊以為未盡然也。何則？徒以目之所接，偶見夫畏懦蹴踖，無介胄不可犯之色；羸憊剽輕，乏山嶽不可撼之威，遂以為惜其不悍不驕，得驕悍者挫折磨礪而用之，猶勝於筋骨委頓而銜勒靡所施者也。是固或然，然安知熊羆之將、貔貅之旅，不混於尋常士伍中邪？其弊則
translation_en:
…if military talent and valor languish and muster rolls exist in name alone, can violent robbery be checked? These are all present abuses. Investigate these abuses, and the established institutions can be restored. You further regard the people's corvée burdens remaining heavy, their taxes remaining high, rewards sometimes erring on the side of excess, and punishments sometimes erring on the side of leniency as causes for anxiety and alarm today. Is this not like Xianyu Shen's deep sighs being uttered in the days when Emperor Shenzong was striving earnestly to govern well? Corvée burdens remain heavy simply because other registers increase daily while the households currently registered decrease daily. The people's taxes remain high simply because state expenditure gradually expands and additional levies multiply. When the ranking of merits is unclear and solicitations for favor go unchecked, how can rewards fail to become excessive? When adherence to the written law is uncertain and discretionary judgments are too lenient, how can punishments fail to become too light? These are all recent abuses. Root them out, and the established institutions can be put into effect.

But if you say that overbearing generals, arrogant soldiers, grasping commoners [?], and extravagant customs were regarded as afflictions in antiquity but no longer exist today, I humbly venture to think this is not entirely so. Why? Merely because one happens to encounter men who are timid and cringing, without the unassailable bearing of warriors in armor, or men who are weak, exhausted, and flighty, lacking the immovable might of mountains, one comes to lament that they are neither overbearing nor arrogant. One thinks that obtaining arrogant and overbearing men, checking and tempering them, and then employing them would still be better than having men whose sinews and bones are so enfeebled that there is nowhere to apply the bridle and reins. This may indeed be so. Yet how do we know that generals fierce as bears and troops valiant as mythical beasts are not mingled among the ordinary ranks? Their failing, then, …

title: 正德八年應天府鄉試錄
text:
坐乎銳氣不作勇力不完之故耳求其所
以不作不完者而去之良將勁卒不於此
而在乎是乃立法之本意也第見夫閭閻
下戶缾盎無宿舂之儲聚落窮民居服罕
圬湼之飾遂以為惜其不并不侈得并侈
者節約限制而使之猶勝於皮毛不攝而
繭絲無所著者也是固或爾然安知盖藏
之積貲筭之厚不本於身佚力舒乎其弊
則坐夫本不獲以盡務用不由以自節之
===
故耳要其所以不獲不由者而除之豪家
富室不即此而有乎是乃立法之初旨也
茲又伯益陳遊逸淫樂之戒于虞廷之比
焉顧豈有是哉特過防之計耳雖然堤决
蟻孔氣洩針芒誠有天下國家者之所深
慮也是以怨豈在明不見是圖夏后氏未
始不為未然之防也惟事事乃其有備有
備無患殷人未始不為未然之防也徹彼
桑土綢繆牖戶周人未始不為未然之防

焉顧豈有是哉特過防之計耳雖然隄決
蟻孔氣洩針芒誠有天下國家者之所深

始不為未然之防也惟事事乃其有備有
備無患殷人未始不為未然之防也徹彼
桑土綢繆牖戶周人未始不為未然之防
punctuated:
坐乎銳氣不作、勇力不完之故耳。求其所以不作不完者而去之，良將勁卒不於此而在乎？是乃立法之本意也。第見夫閭閻下戶，缾盎無宿舂之儲；聚落窮民，居服罕圬湼之飾，遂以為惜其不并不侈，得并侈者節約限制而使之，猶勝於皮毛不攝而繭絲無所著者也。是固或爾，然安知盖藏之積、貲筭之厚，不本於身佚力舒乎？其弊則坐夫本不獲以盡務、用不由以自節之故耳。要其所以不獲不由者而除之，豪家富室不即此而有乎？是乃立法之初旨也。
茲又伯益陳遊逸淫樂之戒于虞廷之比焉。顧豈有是哉？特過防之計耳。雖然，堤决蟻孔，氣洩針芒，誠有天下國家者之所深慮也。是以「怨豈在明？不見是圖」，夏后氏未始不為未然之防也；「惟事事乃其有備，有備無患」，殷人未始不為未然之防也；「徹彼桑土，綢繆牖戶」，周人未始不為未然之防
translation_en:
…lies simply in their fighting spirit failing to rise and their courage and strength being impaired. Find and remove what prevents that spirit from rising and that strength from being complete: would not capable generals and strong soldiers then be found among these very men? This is the fundamental intention of establishing regulations. Yet one merely sees humble households in the lanes whose jars and bowls hold no reserve of pounded grain, and poor villagers whose dwellings and clothing show little embellishment with plaster or dye. One consequently regrets that they neither engross wealth nor live extravagantly, thinking that people who do engross wealth and live extravagantly could be restrained and regulated, and put to use—still preferable to those whose skin and hair are scarcely covered and upon whom silk has nowhere to be applied [?]. This may indeed be so. Yet how can one know that accumulated stores and substantial wealth do not depend upon freedom from bodily exhaustion and relief from excessive toil? Their predicament lies simply in being unable to devote themselves fully to agriculture, the fundamental occupation, and lacking the means to regulate their own expenditure. Identify and remove what prevents these things: would not wealthy households and prosperous families arise among these very people? This is the original purpose of establishing regulations.
This, too, resembles Bo Yi presenting his admonition against idle roaming and excessive pleasure at the court of Shun. Could such things actually have existed there? It was merely a precaution carried beyond immediate necessity. Nevertheless, a dike can burst through an ant hole, and air can escape through an opening as fine as a needle’s point. These are truly matters for deep concern among those who possess the realm and govern states. Thus: “Must resentment be manifest? Take thought for what is unseen.” The rulers of Xia certainly took precautions against troubles before they arose. “In every affair, make preparations; with preparations, there will be no calamity.” The people of Yin certainly took precautions against troubles before they arose. “Strip the bark from those mulberry roots; bind fast the windows and door.” The people of Zhou certainly took precautions against troubles before they arose…

title: 正德八年應天府鄉試錄
text:
也誦詩書之言則三代之訓于以制治于
未亂保邦于未危使釁孽不萌而
宗社永底苞桑之固者端有望於
今日之
明良焉若夫滯而不舉矯而或過之偏雖三
代之法所不能免是又俟夫規措已定乃
徐議之兹未得以并告也惟執事恕其狂
而擇焉

也誦詩書之言則三代之訓于以制治于
未亂保邦于未危使釁孽不萌而
宗社永底苞桑之固者端有望於
今日之
明良焉若夫滯而不舉矯而或過之偏雖三
代之法所不能免是又俟夫規措已定乃
徐議之茲未得以并告也惟執事恕其狂
而擇焉
punctuated: 也。誦詩書之言，則三代之訓，于以制治于未亂，保邦于未危，使釁孽不萌，而宗社永底苞桑之固者，端有望於今日之明良焉。若夫滯而不舉、矯而或過之偏，雖三代之法所不能免，是又俟夫規措已定，乃徐議之，兹未得以并告也。惟執事恕其狂而擇焉。
translation_en: … indeed. Reciting the words of the Book of Odes and the Book of Documents, we find in the teachings of the Three Dynasties the means to establish order before disorder arises and to safeguard the state before danger appears, preventing the seeds of calamity from sprouting and securing the dynastic ancestral temples and altars of soil and grain forever, as firmly as a clump of mulberry trees rooted in the earth. For this, we place our hopes squarely in the enlightened ruler and worthy ministers of today. As for the shortcomings of allowing measures to languish unimplemented or carrying corrective action too far, even the laws of the Three Dynasties could not escape them. These matters must await the settling of arrangements and then be discussed at leisure; I cannot address them together here. I ask only that you, sir, pardon my presumption and select what is worth adopting.

translation_en:
Postface to the Record of the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination

Our dynasty regards the southern and northern capitals and their metropolitan territories as its foundation. It has therefore specially established two Provincial Examinations, held once every three years. These select men alongside the provinces, but with larger quotas. For the responsibility of evaluating the essays, however, it selects ministers serving in close attendance upon the emperor to preside. This distinctive treatment reflects the importance of the task.

In the eighth month of autumn in the guiyou year of Zhengde [1513], when the appointed time for selecting men arrived, your servant Ju of Yingtian Prefecture, following the regulations, first submitted a request for Examiners. We, your servants Wenxu and Yong, were thereupon commanded to suspend our lecturing duties and undertake this appointment. Day and night, reverent and apprehensive, we respectfully received from above…

translation_en:
…His beneficent virtue—could we dare not respond to this exceptional distinction with due gravity? We therefore traveled by forced stages to arrive and, following established practice, entered confinement in the examination compound and conducted the three examination sessions. After two ten-day periods, the work was completed and the thorn barriers removed. We gathered together the successful candidates, compositions worthy of serving as models, and the various names and native places of all those officiating, and had them compiled and printed as a record, to be deposited in the imperial archives and circulated throughout the realm for encouragement and admonition.
Yong once wrote at the end by way of a concluding preface: “Scholars advance through the examinations; selection in the examinations rests on literary composition; composition takes principle as its guiding concern; and principle is given fullness by vital energy. Thus, when principle is profound, vital energy flourishes; when vital energy flourishes, composition is refined, and the excellence of a scholar’s talents is fully displayed. On this basis, scholars are selected through the examinations and presented to the Emperor, to further moral transformation and orderly government and thereby attain consummate governance. This …

title: 正德八年應天府鄉試錄
text:
聖天子汲汲求賢之意亦詠等司
校閱者之愚悃也苟文焉而
不根于理空言而不達諸用
競為浮誇靡麗乖舛怪誕之
說以闘纖富為工夫然氣雖
昌而實無補如文何易曰觀
乎天文以察時變觀乎人文
===
以化成天下是也夫文以時
而變化以文而成唐虞三代
之文尚矣秦漢而下文不逮
古唐襲八代之衰韓愈氏變
之終唐之世三變而後定宋
襲五代之衰歐陽子變之歷
宋之運再變而始一二時豪

punctuated:
聖天子汲汲求賢之意，亦詠等司校閱者之愚悃也。苟文焉而不根于理，空言而不達諸用，競為浮誇靡麗、乖舛怪誕之說，以闘纖富為工夫，然氣雖昌，而實無補，如文何？《易》曰：「觀乎天文，以察時變；觀乎人文，以化成天下。」是也。
夫文以時而變，化以文而成。唐虞三代之文尚矣，秦漢而下，文不逮古。唐襲八代之衰，韓愈氏變之；終唐之世，三變而後定。宋襲五代之衰，歐陽子變之；歷宋之運，再變而始一。二時豪
translation_en:
…the sage Son of Heaven’s earnest intention in seeking worthy men, and also the humble, sincere wish of Yong and the others charged with evaluating the examination papers. If writing is not rooted in principle, if its empty words have no practical application, and if writers compete to produce inflated, ornate, discordant, and outlandish statements, making rivalry in subtle elaboration and richness their craft, then, however abundant their vital force, they offer no actual benefit. What good is such writing? The Book of Changes says: “Observe the patterns of Heaven to discern changes in the seasons; observe human culture to transform and bring order to all under Heaven.” This is precisely the point.
Literary writing changes with the times, while moral transformation is accomplished through writing. The writing of the ages of Tang Yao and Yu Shun and of the Three Dynasties was exalted indeed. From the Qin and Han onward, writing fell short of antiquity. The Tang inherited the decline of the Eight Dynasties, and Han Yu transformed it; over the course of the Tang, it underwent three changes before becoming settled. The Song inherited the decline of the Five Dynasties, and Master Ouyang transformed it; over the course of the Song, it underwent two changes before attaining unity. The outstanding men of these two eras…

title: 正德八年應天府鄉試錄
text:
傑爭自奮厲以名科目猗歟
盛哉肆我
祖宗開基應運以來右文弘化遠
軼前軌近刬胡元而上之陋
設科取士百有餘年文之體
裁盖嘗屢變而盡無不純矣
詠嘗兩同校禮闈士之文而
===
得其槩茲又謬主是考則
南畿士之文含英咀華以自
見其才美者益得徧觀而盡
識之況諸士子生當根本之
地幸而膺崇重特異之典又
幸而際
文明之運覩文物之美漸文化

得其槩茲又謬主是考則
南畿士之文含英咀華以自
見其才美者益得徧觀而盡

地幸而膺崇重特異之典又
幸而際
文明之運覩文物之美漸文化
punctuated:
傑爭自奮厲，以名科目，猗歟盛哉！肆我祖宗開基應運以來，右文弘化，遠軼前軌，近刬胡元而上之陋。設科取士百有餘年，文之體裁盖嘗屢變，而盡無不純矣。
詠嘗兩同校禮闈士之文，而得其槩。茲又謬主是考，則南畿士之文，含英咀華以自見其才美者，益得徧觀而盡識之。況諸士子生當根本之地，幸而膺崇重特異之典，又幸而際文明之運，覩文物之美，漸文化
translation_en:
…outstanding men vied to exert themselves and gain distinction in the examinations. Ah, how flourishing it was! Ever since our imperial ancestors founded the dynasty in accordance with Heaven’s appointed course, they have honored literary learning and extended its transforming influence, far surpassing earlier precedents and, more immediately, sweeping away the shortcomings of the non-Han Yuan and preceding dynasties. For more than a hundred years, officials have been recruited through examinations. Literary forms and styles have indeed changed repeatedly, yet all have attained purity.
I, Yong, have twice served as Associate Examiner, assessing candidates’ writings at the Metropolitan Examination, and thus gained a general understanding of them. Now, undeservedly entrusted with presiding over this examination, I have had a still fuller opportunity to survey and thoroughly appreciate the writings of the Southern Metropolitan Region’s candidates, who savor literary blossoms and their finest essence to reveal the excellence of their talents. Moreover, these candidates were born in the land that forms the dynasty’s foundation. They are fortunate to receive exceptionally distinguished treatment, and fortunate also to live in an age of cultural brilliance, to behold the splendor of its cultural achievements, and to be steeped in its civilizing influence…

德意之所以重且異者而益勉
之植特立之操尚以文經邦

國潤太平期收化成之效于
punctuated: 之先，其必有首藩省而特出焉者。今觀其文之沉浸醲郁，雖風簷寸晷不足盡見，殆極所養而後發，理邃氣昌，渾厚典則，絕無浮誇靡麗、乖舛怪誕之習，而纖富之工一切不校。燁乎炳然，信一時之盛，而亦信乎其異哉！名登茲錄，行將與藩省士會比南宮，進明天子之廷，奉清對而躋膴仕。其思德意之所以重且異者而益勉之，植特立之操，尚以文經邦國、潤太平，期收化成之效于
translation_en:
…among the first to be imbued with cultural transformation, they must surely include men who stand foremost among the provinces and distinguish themselves. Now, observing the depth and richness of their writing, although the brief time beneath the wind-swept eaves of the examination hall does not suffice to reveal it fully, I find that they seem to have expressed themselves only after bringing their cultivation to its fullest extent. Their principles are profound, their vital force abundant; their writing is substantial, balanced, and in keeping with classical standards. It is entirely free of ostentation and florid extravagance, of perversity and bizarre conceits; skill in “subtlety and richness” [?] is not weighed at all. Brilliant and resplendent, it truly attests to the flourishing achievement of this age—and indeed to their distinction!
Those whose names appear in this record will soon compete alongside scholars from the provinces at the Ministry of Rites in the Metropolitan Examination, advance to the court of the enlightened Son of Heaven, respectfully present their answers at the Palace Examination, and rise to eminent office. May they reflect upon why the imperial benevolent regard for them is so weighty and exceptional, and exert themselves all the more. May they establish an integrity that stands independently, and through their literary learning administer the realm and enrich its great peace, hoping to realize the effects of transforming and perfecting the people in…
